courseMetadata.title: Practical AI for Developers
courseMetadata.description: A hands-on course that takes a working software engineer from understanding what modern AI actually is to scoping, building, evaluating, deploying and operating LLM-powered systems inside a real engineering organisation. Learners ship three portfolio artifacts: a compounding retrieval-augmented capstone over a domain corpus they choose, a brownfield integration case study, and a small model-adaptation experiment benchmarked against a prompt-only baseline.

prerequisites.description: Proficiency in at least one common programming language, ideally Python; Java or TypeScript is acceptable with some translation effort.
Comfort with core data structures (lists, maps, trees) and the ability to reason about time and space cost.
Working familiarity with git, the command line, and calling a REST/HTTP API.
No machine learning, linear algebra or statistics background is assumed or required.

interleavingGroups.rationaleNote: Measurement is the course's central habit and is seeded in section 3 long before its dedicated treatment in section 7. Injecting evaluation retrieval items into prompt, RAG, adaptation and deployment experiences keeps the habit alive across the whole arc rather than letting it decay into a single-section topic.

The same evaluate-level decision skill recurs at five different scales: which model, which vector store, which adaptation strategy, which deployment target, build vs buy. Interleaving these prevents learners from treating each as a separate memorised answer and forces them to notice the shared reasoning pattern.

Hallucination is introduced mechanistically in section 2 and only becomes actionable in sections 6 and 7. Re-injecting the mechanism while learners debug retrieval is what converts an abstract explanation into a diagnostic instinct.

Every increase in model autonomy is simultaneously a security question. Pairing loop design and orchestration with the tool-calling authorisation boundary stops learners from learning capability in section 8 and safety as a separate afterthought in section 10.

Cost begins as token arithmetic in section 2 and ends as production unit economics in section 10. Interleaving keeps the arithmetic fresh so that the section 10 optimisation work builds on a live skill rather than a half-remembered one.

The brownfield artifact built in section 4 is assessed against the section 11 portfolio rubric. Interleaving these keeps learners aware from early on that their daily-workflow work is portfolio evidence, which materially changes how carefully they document it.

probeQuestions.prompt: A logistics company has twelve months of structured shipment records and wants to predict which deliveries will arrive late. Which approach fits best?
options: Gradient-boosted trees trained on the historical shipment table
A large language model prompted with each shipment's details
The largest frontier model available, because it has the strongest reasoning
An embedding model that stores shipments as vectors and finds similar past shipments

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Structured tabular input with a closed numeric output is the canonical strength of classical machine learning, and it will beat a generative approach on accuracy, cost and explainability.
This treats a tabular prediction problem as a language problem, costing orders of magnitude more per prediction for worse accuracy.
Parameter count does not transfer to tabular prediction; fit to the task dominates raw scale.
Nearest-neighbour retrieval is a weaker, less calibrated way to do what supervised learning does directly, and gives you no feature importances.

routingRules.action: Offer to compress section s01 to its environment-setup activity only, and surface the s01 assessment as an optional challenge.
Flag s01 as required and pre-load the misconception ail-m1-ai-means-llms into the section opener.

probeQuestions.prompt: A model is asked for the clause number governing overtime in a company handbook it has never seen. It confidently answers 'Clause 7.3.' What best explains this?
options: It is predicting the most plausible continuation, and with no grounding data a plausible-looking clause number is exactly what that mechanism produces
It retrieved a similar handbook from its training data and returned the wrong one
This is a known defect that is being fixed in newer model releases
The temperature setting was too high

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Fabrication and correct recall are the same operation; the distribution simply has nothing specific to concentrate on for private data.
There is no retrieval step at inference time; generation runs over learned weights, not a searchable store.
Newer models fabricate less on common knowledge, but the mechanism is unchanged and private data remains outside the distribution entirely.
At temperature zero the model would still produce a fabricated clause number, just the same one every time.

routingRules.action: Mark s02 objectives s02-o1 and s02-o3 as likely-known; keep s02-o4 and s02-o5 required.
Flag as miscalibrated and make the s02 generation-trace experience mandatory before any section 5 build work.

probeQuestions.prompt: A model emits a tool call requesting `get_customer_record(customer_id="88213")`. The authenticated user is customer 44190. What must your handler do?
options: Execute it, since the model determined this was the right record to fetch
Reject it, because authorisation is evaluated against the session identity rather than arguments the model supplied
Execute it but redact sensitive fields from the result
Ask the model to confirm that the user is authorised

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct answer is B. Executing here builds a data-leak endpoint with a natural-language interface.
Correct. The handler is the security boundary; the model may propose what to look up but never who is permitted to look.
Redaction limits blast radius but the access-control violation has already happened, and confirming the record exists is itself a leak.
Delegating an authorisation check to the component you are trying to constrain defeats the control entirely.

routingRules.action: Unlock the advanced variant of the s05 tool-boundary experience, which adds mutating tools and idempotency requirements.
Make the s05 tool-boundary experience mandatory and schedule the s05 assessment before section 8 begins.

probeQuestions.prompt: Users search a parts catalogue using exact part numbers such as `MS21042L3`. Semantic (dense) retrieval performs poorly on these queries. Why?
options: The embedding model needs fine-tuning on the catalogue
The chunks are too large
Embedding models represent rare alphanumeric identifiers weakly, because their meaning is not semantic
Something is misconfigured, since semantic search outperforms keyword search

optionFeedback.feedback: Adaptation cannot make an arbitrary identifier semantically meaningful; the mismatch is in the technique, not the training.
Chunk size affects context and dilution, not the ability to match an exact string.
Correct. Exact identifiers carry no semantic content to embed, which is why hybrid retrieval combining lexical matching is the standard remedy.
The premise is false: dense and lexical retrieval are complementary techniques with genuinely different strengths.

routingRules.action: Offer the accelerated s06 path: skip the embeddings primer, go straight to the chunking comparison activity.
Keep the full s06 path and inject evs-m1-semantic-always-beats-keyword into the section opener.

probeQuestions.prompt: A team says: 'We'll fine-tune the model on our internal documentation so it knows our procedures.' What is the strongest objection?
options: Fine-tuning requires far more data than they are likely to have
Fine-tuning reliably teaches form, style and task behaviour, but is a poor and expensive way to inject retrievable facts, which belong in retrieval
Fine-tuning is too computationally expensive for most companies
Nothing is wrong; this is the standard way to give a model private knowledge

optionFeedback.feedback: Data volume is rarely the binding constraint; parameter-efficient methods work with a few hundred well-curated examples.
Correct. This is the single most common and most expensive misdiagnosis in applied AI work, and retrieval is the right tool for facts.
LoRA on a small model is a single-GPU or even laptop exercise; cost is not the primary objection.
Facts learned in weights cannot be updated, cited or permission-filtered, which is why retrieval exists.

routingRules.action: Unlock the advanced s09 track: a full LoRA run with a held-out benchmark rather than the guided variant.
Flag s09 as high-priority and surface this probe again as a review item after section 7.

probeQuestions.prompt: A team ships a prompt change because the outputs 'look better in the playground.' What is the core problem with that reasoning?
options: The playground uses different model settings than production
Playground models are usually older versions
Single-sample inspection of a probabilistic system cannot establish that a change helped, or reveal what it quietly broke
Nothing — for prompts, expert judgement is the accepted professional standard

optionFeedback.feedback: A real risk, but secondary; the reasoning error would remain even with identical settings.
Sometimes true, but this is not the flaw in the reasoning being demonstrated.
Correct. Without a regression set and a measured pass rate there is no basis for the claim and no way to detect the subset that regressed.
Expert judgement should design the test set; it cannot substitute for running one.

routingRules.action: Mark the learner as evaluation-ready; s03 regression harness becomes a build task rather than a guided walkthrough.
Make the s03 regression harness experience mandatory and gate section 7 entry on completing it.

probeQuestions.prompt: An agent has been running for 40 minutes on a refactoring task, reporting progress each iteration while costs climb. What does this most likely indicate about the loop's design?
options: No external validator and no budget, so the agent is judging its own progress with nothing to stop it
The model is too small and should be upgraded
The task should be split across several cooperating agents
This is normal for agentic work and simply requires patience

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Self-assessed progress with no budget is precisely the condition under which loops run long while achieving nothing.
A more capable model inside an undesigned loop fails the same way, just more expensively.
Adding agents compounds error rates and cost; it does not supply the missing external validator.
Treating the framework's default loop as a given is the underlying error this course sets out to correct.

routingRules.action: Unlock the multi-architecture s08 variant requiring a justified choice between four loop patterns.
Keep the full s04 loop-design path and schedule this probe for review one day later.

probeQuestions.prompt: In your own words: a team has a working AI demo that stakeholders loved. Roughly what proportion of the total work is done, and what specifically remains? Answer in three or four sentences.
scoringCriteria: Recognises that a demo represents a small fraction of total effort, typically cited as around ten percent
Names at least three of: evaluation, edge-case handling, security review, cost control, observability, deployment, ongoing operations
Identifies that non-determinism is what makes the remaining work qualitatively different from ordinary software delivery
Avoids the claim that remaining work is mostly a matter of scaling infrastructure

routingRules.condition: Self-rated Strong and names four or more remaining work categories
routingRules.action: Offer the accelerated s11 path focused on portfolio packaging rather than delivery fundamentals.

routingRules.condition: Self-rated Weak, or names fewer than two categories
routingRules.action: Surface deliver-m1-demo-means-nearly-done at the start of section 1 as a framing hook, and re-ask at the end of section 10.

competencies.title: Modern AI Landscape Literacy
competencies.description: Accurately place LLMs within the broader field — classical ML, deep learning, supervised versus self-supervised learning, generative versus discriminative models, multimodal systems, embeddings — and identify which class of technique a given business problem actually calls for.

desiredOutcomes.description: Given an unfamiliar business request, classify it into the AI technique family most likely to solve it and justify the classification, including recognising when the answer is 'not AI'.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Names the technique family, states the output contract, and gives at least one reason grounded in input shape, output shape or knowledge location rather than in model popularity.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: AI basically means large language models now — if we're doing AI, we're prompting a model.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Most production AI value still comes from tabular machine learning, ranking, forecasting and classical computer vision. Framing every problem as a prompt produces solutions that are slower, more expensive and less accurate than a gradient-boosted tree would have been.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Present four requests from one organisation where only two are language problems, and require the learner to assign a technique family and defend it before any code is written. Follow with a cost-and-accuracy comparison on the tabular case.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Neural networks work like the human brain, so the model understands and remembers things the way a person would.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The biological analogy is historical branding. It predicts nothing about observed behaviour and actively misleads, because it makes people expect memory, understanding and consistent reasoning that the architecture does not provide.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Replace the metaphor with the mechanism: have the learner trace a single token prediction end to end, then ask them to predict three model behaviours using the mechanism and three using the brain analogy, and check which set matched reality.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: More parameters means a better model, so pick the biggest one you can afford.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Capability is a function of data quality, training compute, post-training and fit to the specific task. A well-tuned small model routinely beats a frontier model on a narrow task at a fraction of the cost.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner rank four approaches for a high-volume classification task, then re-rank the same list after the volume constraint is changed from 40 items a day to 40,000, making explicit that constraints determine the ranking rather than model size.

competencies.title: How LLMs Are Built and How They Behave
competencies.description: Explain tokenization, embeddings, attention, next-token prediction, the pretraining to supervised fine-tuning to preference-optimization pipeline, and how decoding parameters, context windows and training data produce the observable behaviours developers hit daily.

desiredOutcomes.description: Explain an observed model behaviour — fabrication, apparent forgetting, sycophancy, formatting habits — by reference to the generation mechanism or a specific training stage.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Attributes the behaviour to a named mechanism or training stage, and states whether it is fixable by prompting, by architecture, or not at all.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The model looks things up — it has some kind of database or index it searches when answering.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Generation is next-token prediction over learned weights. There is no retrieval step unless you build one, which is precisely why both hallucination and retrieval-augmented generation exist.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Trace one input string through tokenization, attention, logits and sampling, then ask the learner to predict what happens when the required fact is absent from training data, and verify the prediction against a live model.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Hallucination is a bug that model providers will eventually patch out.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Fabrication is the same mechanism as correct generation, applied where the training distribution underconstrains the answer. It is mitigated architecturally through grounding, constraint and verification, not fixed by a release.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner rank five mitigations and discover that instructing the model not to hallucinate ranks last, because the model has no internal signal distinguishing recall from construction.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The model remembers our earlier conversation, so it will recall what we discussed before.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The API is stateless. Apparent memory is the entire prior transcript being resent as input tokens, which makes context management a cost and correctness problem rather than a user-experience detail.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner plot cumulative token cost across a twenty-turn conversation with no context management, then locate the 'forgetting' bug in their own application code rather than in the model.

competencies.title: Model Selection and Tradeoff Analysis
competencies.description: Compare models and hosting options — frontier API, open-weights, self-hosted, small task-specific — across capability, latency, cost per token, context length, privacy posture and licensing, and defend a selection against a stated requirement set.

desiredOutcomes.description: Recommend a model and hosting approach for a requirement set that includes at least one non-cost constraint, and defend it against two named alternatives.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Identifies which constraint is actually decisive, shows token and cost arithmetic, and does not appeal to benchmark rank as primary evidence.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Just use whichever model is top of the leaderboard — that's the best one.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Public benchmarks are contaminated, aggregated across tasks unlike yours, and silent on cost, latency, privacy and licensing. Selection requires a task-specific evaluation set built from your own inputs.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give the learner a requirement set where confidentiality and context length are decisive and cost is trivial, and have them observe that benchmark rank changes nothing about the correct answer.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Open-weights models are cheaper because you're not paying per token.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Self-hosting shifts cost to GPUs, operations and engineering time. Below a certain sustained throughput, APIs are materially cheaper once staff time and idle capacity are counted.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner compute monthly API cost for a realistic workload, then compute the fully-loaded cost of the GPU capacity and on-call time needed to serve it, and identify the crossover throughput.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: We picked our model at the start of the project, so that decision is settled.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A model is a swappable dependency whose price and capability move faster than almost anything else in your stack. Teams that cannot substitute cheaply stop re-evaluating, and quietly overpay for years.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Require a provider abstraction in the section 5 build even though only one provider is in use, then in section 10 have the learner substitute a cheaper model for part of the traffic and measure the saving.

competencies.title: Prompt and Context Engineering
competencies.description: Design reliable, testable model inputs — role and task framing, decomposition, few-shot exemplars, output-format constraints, reasoning elicitation, context ordering and budgeting — and iterate against measured outcomes rather than impressions.

desiredOutcomes.description: Diagnose a prompt failure mode and select the technique that targets it specifically, rather than applying general prompting advice.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Names the failure mode, names the matching remedy, and explains why the obvious alternative remedies would not address it.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Prompting is about finding the right phrasing — the magic words that unlock better output.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Reliability comes from specification quality: explicit constraints, examples and formats. Techniques that survive measurement do so because they add information, constraint or demonstration, not because of their wording.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner test a phrasing-only change and a constraint-adding change against the same regression set, and compare the measured pass rates.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: It worked when I tried it, so the prompt is good.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Single-sample success on a stateless probabilistic system is not evidence. Prompts need regression sets like any other logic, or you cannot tell whether a change helped or what it silently broke.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Require every prompt change in the course to be accompanied by a pass rate across at least twenty real inputs run three times, and surface the variance between runs.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Bigger context windows mean I should give the model everything I have.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Irrelevant context degrades accuracy through distraction and position effects, while raising cost and latency. Curation beats accumulation.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner measure accuracy on the same questions with two relevant documents versus ten documents of which two are relevant, and observe the degradation directly.

competencies.title: AI-Augmented Development Workflow
competencies.description: Integrate coding assistants and agentic tools into real engineering practice — scaffolding, refactoring, test generation, debugging, code review, documentation, legacy comprehension — with task-appropriate delegation and disciplined verification.

desiredOutcomes.description: Choose an assistance mode appropriate to a task's specificity and verification cost, and apply a verification protocol proportionate to the risk of the change.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Justifies the mode using both delegation conditions, and describes a verification step that is cheaper than re-reading the whole diff.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The AI writes the code and I review it — that's the workflow.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Review effort scales with unverified volume, and reviewing code you did not write is slower per line than writing it. Accepting large diffs means either spending more time than writing would have taken, or shipping unread code.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner time themselves reviewing a 400-line generated diff properly, compare against writing the same change, then repeat the task using a failing test as the contract and compare all three.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Relying on AI assistance is cheating and will erode my real engineering skills.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The durable skills are specification, decomposition and verification, and those are exercised more under this workflow rather than less. Uncritical acceptance genuinely does erode debugging ability, but the mitigation is verification discipline, not abstinence.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner log a week of assisted and unassisted tasks, then identify which specific skills each mode exercised, distinguishing the real risk from the imagined one.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Whatever I paste into my coding assistant stays private.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Data handling depends entirely on the vendor tier and its configuration. Consumer, business and enterprise tiers of the same product frequently differ in retention and training-use terms, and secrets or proprietary code require an explicit policy check.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Require the learner to locate and quote the actual terms for their own tier, configure exclusions, and then verify the exclusions work rather than assuming an untested ignore file is a control.

competencies.title: Programmatic LLM Integration Patterns
competencies.description: Build production-shaped application code against model APIs: streaming, structured and schema-constrained output, tool and function calling, multi-turn state, retries and backoff, timeouts, token accounting, graceful degradation and provider abstraction.

desiredOutcomes.description: Build a service around a model API that survives malformed output, provider failure, unbounded conversation growth and a model substitution.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Demonstrates schema validation with a bounded repair path, retry rules distinguishing retryable from non-retryable failures, an enforced context budget, and a provider abstraction.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: I asked for JSON, so I can just parse the response.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Without schema-constrained decoding and validation, malformed responses are a routine runtime event rather than an edge case — fenced output, preambles and truncation all appear at volume.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner run 200 requests against a prompt-only JSON instruction, count the failures, then repeat with provider-side schema enforcement and compare.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: When the model calls a tool, it executes the function.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The model emits a structured request. Your code decides whether and how to execute it, which is where authorisation lives. Treating the model's arguments as authorising the call turns a helpful assistant into an open data endpoint.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give the learner a tool call requesting another user's record and require them to write the handler, making explicit that identity comes from the session and never from the model's arguments.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Setting temperature to zero makes the system deterministic and therefore auditable.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Low temperature reduces variance but does not guarantee reproducibility across batching, hardware or model versions. Auditability comes from logging inputs, outputs and versions, not from sampling settings.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner run the same zero-temperature prompt 50 times across a model version change and inspect the variation, then design the logging that would actually satisfy an auditor.

competencies.title: Embeddings and Vector Retrieval
competencies.description: Explain vector representations and similarity metrics, choose and apply chunking strategies, generate and index embeddings, operate a vector database, and tune retrieval with metadata filtering and hybrid search.

desiredOutcomes.description: Measure retrieval quality on a real corpus, categorise the failures, and select the intervention that addresses the dominant cause.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reports recall@k before and after, names the failure categories found by inspection, and links each intervention to a specific category rather than to general best practice.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Semantic search is strictly better than keyword search — that's the whole point of embeddings.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Embeddings lose exact identifiers, error codes, part numbers and rare tokens, because those carry no semantic content to represent. Hybrid dense-plus-lexical retrieval is the strong default.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner run a query set containing both conceptual questions and exact identifiers against dense-only retrieval, inspect which fail, and then add lexical fusion and re-measure.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A vector database is a fundamentally new kind of database that you need for any AI project.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It is an index over vectors with approximate nearest-neighbour search and filtering. Postgres with pgvector is sufficient for a large share of real workloads, and a managed service is a scale and operations decision rather than a capability one.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner implement the same retrieval against an embedded store and against pgvector, then articulate the specific throughput or operational condition that would justify a managed service.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Chunking is just a preprocessing detail — pick a size and move on.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Chunk boundaries determine what can ever be retrieved together. Nothing downstream recovers information split apart at ingestion, which makes it the highest-leverage knob in most underperforming retrieval systems.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner measure recall with fixed-size chunking on a corpus containing tables, inspect the failures, then re-chunk structure-aware and observe the size of the improvement relative to any prompt change.

competencies.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Architecture
competencies.description: Design and implement end-to-end RAG — ingestion and parsing, indexing, query transformation, retrieval, reranking, context assembly, grounded generation with citations — and diagnose which stage is responsible for a given failure.

desiredOutcomes.description: Build a complete RAG pipeline and, given a bad answer, attribute it to the responsible stage and select a targeted remediation.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Correctly separates retrieval failure from generation failure using stage-level evidence, and proposes a fix at the identified stage rather than a general prompt change.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Once we add RAG, the model stops hallucinating.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Retrieval constrains and grounds generation, but the model can still misread passages, over-generalise, or fall back on its priors when retrieval returns nothing useful. Citations and explicit abstention behaviour have to be engineered deliberately.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner ask their own RAG system a question whose answer is genuinely absent from the corpus, observe the confident answer, then implement an abstention path and re-test.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: RAG is just: embed the docs, take the top k results, stuff them into the prompt.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Naive top-k is the demo, not the system. Production quality lives in parsing, chunking, query rewriting, reranking and filtering, and skipping those stages is why demos plateau at mediocre accuracy.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner measure a naive pipeline, then add query rewriting and reranking as separate measured steps so each stage's contribution is visible as a number.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: With million-token context windows, RAG is obsolete — just put everything in the prompt.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Cost, latency, retrieval precision, freshness and per-document access control all still favour retrieval, and accuracy degrades measurably over stuffed context. Long context changes the tradeoff without removing it.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner compare answer accuracy and cost for the same question set using full-corpus stuffing versus retrieval, and include a permission-filtered query that stuffing cannot satisfy at all.

competencies.title: Evaluating AI Systems
competencies.description: Build evaluation harnesses for non-deterministic systems — golden datasets, retrieval metrics such as recall@k and MRR, generation metrics such as groundedness and correctness, LLM-as-judge with its caveats, human review, and regression gating in CI.

desiredOutcomes.description: Construct a staged evaluation harness that separates retrieval quality from generation quality and can gate a deployment.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Defines a golden set from real inputs, reports at least one retrieval and one generation metric separately, and specifies a pass threshold that would block a release.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: I'll just look at the outputs and see if they're good.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Manual spot-checking cannot detect regressions or support a change decision on a probabilistic system, and it is the single most common reason teams stall permanently at 'the demo works'.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner make a change they are confident improves things, measure it against a golden set, and confront the subset that regressed while overall accuracy rose.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Using a model as a judge gives us an objective quality score.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Judges carry position, verbosity and self-preference biases, and drift with model versions. They must be calibrated against human labels before their scores mean anything.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner score 30 outputs by hand, score the same outputs with a judge, compute agreement, and then swap the order of candidates to expose position bias.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The answers are bad, so we need a better model.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: In a retrieval-augmented system the majority of bad answers are retrieval failures. Evaluation must be staged so blame is attributed to the stage that caused it, or you will spend money upgrading a component that was never the problem.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give the learner ten failing answers and require them to classify each as retrieval or generation failure using the retrieved context, before proposing any fix.

competencies.title: Agent and Workflow Orchestration
competencies.description: Use orchestration frameworks such as LangChain and LangGraph to compose chains, tools, routing, memory and multi-step agent loops with explicit state, termination conditions, human-in-the-loop checkpoints and failure handling — and judge when a plain function call is the better design.

desiredOutcomes.description: Implement an orchestrated multi-step system and justify each use of autonomy against a deterministic alternative.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Shows the graph or chain structure, maps at least one abstraction to the underlying API calls it wraps, and states the variance, cost and debuggability argument for each autonomous step.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Agents are more capable than workflows, so we should use agents.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Autonomy adds variance, latency, cost and debugging difficulty. Deterministic workflows are correct for most tasks, and agency is justified only when the path genuinely cannot be enumerated in advance.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner implement the same task as a fixed chain and as an agent loop, then compare accuracy, cost, latency and time spent debugging each.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: You need LangChain to build anything serious with LLMs.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Frameworks buy integrations and abstractions at the price of indirection. Understanding the underlying HTTP calls is what makes framework use, or deliberate rejection, an informed choice rather than a default.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner implement one chain with the framework and the identical behaviour with direct API calls, then articulate what the framework actually bought them.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: More specialised agents working together will give better results.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Multi-agent setups compound error rates and cost unless each agent has a crisply bounded role and verified handoffs. Two agents at 90 percent reliability chained without verification are worse than one.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner compute the compound reliability of a three-agent chain from per-agent accuracy, then add a verification step between handoffs and recompute.

competencies.title: Agent Loop Design
competencies.description: Design the iterative cycle an agent runs in — goal specification, context and state carried between turns, external validation versus self-assessment, termination and budget conditions, escalation to human — and select the loop architecture that fits a task's structure.

desiredOutcomes.description: Design and run a bounded agent loop with an external validator, an explicit budget and a defined escalation condition, and report cost per completed task.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: States the goal as a checkable condition, names the external validator, sets iteration and token budgets enforced outside the agent, and reports a real cost-per-task figure.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The loop is just whatever the framework or tool does by default.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Every agent already runs a loop; quality comes from designing it deliberately. Loop design, not model choice, is usually the dominant variable in agent performance.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner run the same task with a default agent and with a designed loop specifying goal, tools, validator, budget and escalation, and compare cost, wall time and outcome.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The agent can judge when it has finished the task.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Self-assessed completion is the source of runaway cost and false confidence. Robust loops validate against something external — a test suite, a separate checker, a schema — because the agent's self-assessment is not honest evidence.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner run a loop with self-assessed completion on a task with a hidden defect, observe it declaring success, then re-run with a failing test as the validator.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If the loop hasn't succeeded yet, let it keep trying.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Retrying an identical approach is the most common loop failure. A loop needs logic to vary strategy between attempts, and an escalation rule that detects repeated identical failure rather than simply spending more budget.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner implement an escalation rule that triggers on three identical consecutive failures, and compare total spend against an unbounded retry loop on the same task.

competencies.title: Model Adaptation and Customization
competencies.description: Decide among prompting, retrieval, fine-tuning — full versus parameter-efficient — and distillation for a given requirement; prepare datasets; run a small adaptation; and measure the result against a baseline.

desiredOutcomes.description: Recommend an adaptation strategy for a stated requirement and support it with a measured comparison against a prompt-only baseline.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Distinguishes behaviour and format goals from knowledge goals, reports a shared evaluation set for both arms, and states the ongoing maintenance cost of the adapted option.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Fine-tune it on our documents so it knows our data.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Fine-tuning teaches form, style and task behaviour far more reliably than it injects retrievable facts. Facts learned in weights cannot be updated, cited or permission-filtered, which is exactly what business knowledge requires.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner attempt fact recall from a small fine-tune and compare against retrieval on the same questions, including a question whose answer changed after training.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Fine-tuning needs a huge dataset and a GPU cluster, so it's out of reach.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA on a small model work with a few hundred well-curated examples and run on a single GPU or a capable laptop. Data quality dominates volume by a wide margin.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner run a LoRA adaptation on roughly 300 curated examples and measure the improvement, then deliberately degrade the data quality and re-measure.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Fine-tuning is a one-way upgrade — the model just gets better at our task.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It can degrade general capability, locks you to a base model version, and adds a retraining pipeline with permanent maintenance cost. The improvement is real but so is the ongoing liability.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner evaluate their adapted model on out-of-domain tasks alongside the target task, and write the retraining plan that would be required when the base model is deprecated.

competencies.title: AI Security, Safety, and Governance
competencies.description: Identify and mitigate LLM-specific risks — prompt injection, data exfiltration through tools, insecure output handling, PII exposure, over-permissioned agents — and apply guardrails, access controls, licensing and IP checks, and relevant regulatory obligations.

desiredOutcomes.description: Conduct a threat review of an AI system covering injection, exfiltration, insecure output handling and PII, and specify architectural mitigations rather than instruction-based ones.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Identifies at least one untrusted-input path through retrieved or tool-returned content, and proposes least-privilege or validation controls rather than prompt instructions.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: We can stop prompt injection by telling the model to ignore malicious instructions.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Instructions and data share a single channel, so the model cannot reliably distinguish them. Defence is architectural: least privilege, sandboxed tools, output validation and human approval on consequential actions.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner attack their own agent by planting an instruction inside a retrieved document, watch the instruction defence fail, then implement a permission-based control that holds.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Content from our own document store is trusted content.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Any ingested document, web page, ticket or email is untrusted input capable of carrying instructions to your model. Ownership of the store says nothing about who authored the contents.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner trace every path by which text enters their context window and label each as trusted or untrusted, then justify why any path is labelled trusted.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Compliance and data governance are legal's problem, not mine.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Data residency, retention, PII redaction and audit logging are implementation decisions made in code, usually early and often irreversibly. By the time legal reviews it, the architecture has already decided the answer.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner identify which three governance decisions their capstone architecture has already silently made, and what it would cost to reverse each one now versus at ingestion time.

competencies.title: Deployment and MLOps for AI Systems
competencies.description: Package and ship AI services — Docker images, dependency and model-artifact management, API service design, Kubernetes deployment and scaling, GPU versus CPU workloads, CI/CD including evaluation gates, configuration and secrets, and environment promotion.

desiredOutcomes.description: Containerise and deploy an AI service with health checks, resource limits, secret management and a CI pipeline that gates release on an evaluation suite.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Produces a running deployment with an eval gate that can actually block a release, and justifies the deployment target against the workload's characteristics.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: It's just a Python app — deploy it the way we deploy everything else.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Multi-gigabyte images, model artifacts, cold starts, long-lived streaming requests and GPU scheduling all break assumptions built into ordinary web-service deployment, from health-check timeouts to autoscaling signals.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner deploy naively, observe the cold-start and timeout failures under a streaming load test, then fix each with the specific mechanism that addresses it.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Serious AI deployment means Kubernetes.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Serverless and managed container platforms serve most early AI workloads better and cheaper. Kubernetes is justified by scale, GPU pooling or existing organisational standards, not by the presence of a model in the stack.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner cost and justify three deployment targets against their own workload's request pattern, then defend the choice against the two they rejected.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Once it's deployed, the project is done.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: With a non-deterministic system and drifting upstream models, deployment starts the work. Evaluation, observability and cost control are ongoing obligations, and providers will deprecate or silently update the model underneath you.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner write the operating plan — what is monitored, what thresholds page someone, who re-runs the eval suite and when — as a required deliverable alongside the deployment.

competencies.title: Observability, Cost, and Operations
competencies.description: Instrument LLM systems with tracing, structured logging and quality, latency and cost telemetry; apply caching, batching, routing and prompt compression to control spend; detect drift and regressions; and build user-feedback loops.

desiredOutcomes.description: Instrument a full request path with tracing and cost telemetry, then apply a targeted optimisation and quantify the saving.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Traces prompts, retrieved context and tool calls rather than only HTTP outcomes, identifies which side of the token ledger dominates, and reports a measured before-and-after cost per request.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Our existing APM and logging already cover this service.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A 200 OK carrying a wrong, ungrounded or unsafe answer is invisible to conventional monitoring. You must trace prompts, retrieved context, tool calls and quality signals, none of which appear in standard request metrics.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner deliberately break retrieval so answers become ungrounded, confirm that latency and error-rate dashboards stay green, then add the trace fields that would have caught it.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Token costs are small enough not to worry about.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Cost scales with context length multiplied by request volume multiplied by retries, and retrieval plus agent loops multiply all three. Unit economics need modelling before launch, not after the first invoice.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner project monthly cost at ten times current volume including retries and agent iterations, then identify which single change reduces it most.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: We haven't changed anything, so the system is stable.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Providers deprecate and silently update models, and your data and user behaviour drift. Stability is a property you continuously verify, not one you inherit from an absence of deploys.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner schedule the evaluation suite to run against production on a timer with no code change, and design the alert that fires when scores move beyond a threshold.

competencies.title: AI Project Delivery and Professional Communication
competencies.description: Scope AI work for an organisation — feasibility and build-versus-buy assessment, success criteria, risk and cost estimation, proof-of-concept to production staging, stakeholder expectation management — and package delivered work into portfolio artifacts and interview narratives that evidence engineering judgement.

desiredOutcomes.description: Assess a proposed AI initiative and produce a staged plan with success criteria, cost estimate and kill criteria; and package delivered work to a defined portfolio rubric.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: States measurable acceptance thresholds for a non-deterministic system before implementation, includes explicit kill criteria, and produces artifacts meeting the six portfolio rubric criteria.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The demo works, so we're most of the way there.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A demo is roughly the first ten percent. Evaluation, edge cases, security, cost and operations are the remaining work, and underestimating them is the primary cause of stalled AI initiatives.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner list every remaining work item between their own working capstone demo and a production release, then estimate each, and compare the total against the time the demo took.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Any AI problem can be solved with enough prompt iteration.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Some requirements — guaranteed correctness, strict determinism, deep private reasoning, legally accountable decisions — are outside current capability. Recognising and saying so early is a senior skill and prevents committed roadmaps built on impossibilities.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Give the learner three proposals, one genuinely infeasible, and require a proceed, reshape or decline recommendation with reasoning for each.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: My portfolio project should showcase the most advanced architecture I can build.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Reviewers weight problem framing, evaluation evidence, tradeoff reasoning and operational maturity above novelty. A well-evaluated simple system consistently outperforms an unevaluated multi-agent one in a hiring conversation.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Have the learner review two anonymised portfolio projects — one simple and measured, one elaborate and unmeasured — against the six-criterion rubric, and observe which scores higher and why.

assessments.title: Placing a Problem in the AI Landscape

questions.prompt: A vineyard wants to predict harvest yield per block from eight years of structured records: soil sensor readings, rainfall, canopy measurements and past yields. Which technique family fits best?
options: A large language model prompted with each block's readings
Gradient-boosted trees trained on the historical block-level table
A retrieval-augmented system over the vineyard's agronomy notes
A multimodal model analysing satellite imagery of the blocks

optionFeedback.feedback: This converts a tabular regression problem into a language problem, losing accuracy and explainability while multiplying cost per prediction.
Correct. Structured inputs and a continuous numeric output are the canonical fit for classical machine learning, and feature importances give the agronomist something actionable.
Retrieval answers questions from documents; it does not produce a calibrated numeric prediction from sensor history.
Imagery could supplement the features, but the request describes structured records and the vision pipeline adds cost without addressing the prediction task itself.

successCriteria: Identifies tabular input and numeric output as the deciding features
questions.reviewPromptOverride: For a numeric prediction from years of structured tabular records, which technique family fits best, and why?

errorPatterns.description: Learner reaches for a language model for any problem framed as 'AI', regardless of input and output shape.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-run the three classification questions on this scenario, then compare cost per prediction and explainability for a tree model versus an LLM at the stated volume.

questions.prompt: A colleague argues that because neural networks are modelled on the brain, the assistant will build up an understanding of the company over repeated use. Which response is most accurate?
options: Correct in principle, but it needs more usage before the understanding forms
Correct, provided the conversations are long enough for the model to consolidate them
The brain analogy is historical branding; the model has no persistence between calls and forms no understanding of the company from use
Only true for models with very large parameter counts

optionFeedback.feedback: Repetition changes nothing, because nothing is retained between requests to accumulate.
There is no consolidation step at inference; longer conversations only mean more tokens resent.
Correct. The analogy predicts nothing about behaviour, and expecting accumulated understanding leads directly to architectural mistakes.
Parameter count does not create persistence; this substitutes one unfounded expectation for another.

successCriteria: Rejects the biological analogy as predictive
Identifies statelessness as the operative fact
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why does the 'neural networks work like brains' analogy lead to bad engineering predictions?

errorPatterns.description: Learner uses the biological metaphor to predict system behaviour, expecting memory or accumulated understanding.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner list three behaviours predicted by the brain analogy and three predicted by the token-prediction mechanism, then test both sets against a live model.

questions.prompt: A national library must tag 2.4 million scanned catalogue cards into 30 subject categories. A team member proposes using the largest available frontier model for every card, arguing it will be the most accurate. Write a recommendation of 150 to 250 words. Address the volume constraint explicitly, name what you would build instead, and say what role a frontier model could still usefully play.
successCriteria: Identifies volume as the constraint that changes the answer
Proposes a small fine-tuned or embedding-based classifier for the bulk of the work
Assigns the frontier model a bootstrapping or long-tail role rather than the primary one
Does not appeal to model size as evidence of fitness

rubric.excellent: Names volume as decisive, computes or estimates the cost gap, proposes a small classifier for the bulk with a frontier model used to generate training labels or handle the ambiguous tail, and notes that at low volume the recommendation would reverse.
rubric.adequate: Recommends a smaller specialised model on cost grounds and gives the frontier model a limited role, but without quantifying the gap or acknowledging that the answer is volume-dependent.
rubric.weak: Endorses the frontier model on capability grounds, or rejects it without reference to volume, cost or task fit.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats model size as the primary quality signal and does not let workload constraints drive the recommendation.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner rank four approaches at 40 items per day and again at 40,000, and articulate why the ordering inverts.

questions.prompt: A museum's assistant is asked for the accession number of an artefact. The museum's catalogue was never in training data. The model returns a plausibly formatted number that does not exist. What is the mechanism?
options: The model searched its training corpus and returned the closest match
The model produced the most plausible continuation, and a well-formed accession number is exactly what plausibility looks like here
The output was corrupted by a high temperature setting
The catalogue needs to be added to the model's index

optionFeedback.feedback: There is no search step; generation runs over weights, and nothing is being matched or looked up.
Correct. Fabrication and recall are the same operation, and format plausibility is precisely what the mechanism optimises for.
At temperature zero the model would produce a fabricated number just as confidently, only more consistently.
Models have no index to add documents to; supplying the catalogue requires building a retrieval system.

successCriteria: Attributes the output to next-token prediction under an underconstrained distribution
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Explain, using the generation mechanism, why a model invents plausible identifiers for data it has never seen.

errorPatterns.description: Learner models inference as retrieval from an internal store rather than as prediction over weights.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Re-trace the six steps from input string to sampled token, then have the learner predict what happens at each step when the required fact is absent from training data.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly attributes each behaviour to its training stage?
options: Reversing a correct answer under user pressure comes from pretraining; not knowing your internal tooling comes from preference optimization
Both behaviours come from supervised fine-tuning
Reversing a correct answer under user pressure comes from preference optimization; not knowing your internal tooling is a pretraining data limit
Both are sampling artefacts controlled by temperature

optionFeedback.feedback: The attributions are inverted; sycophancy is a preference-optimization artefact and missing knowledge is a data-coverage limit.
Supervised fine-tuning installs the assistant format, but neither behaviour originates there.
Correct, and the distinction is practical: the first is sometimes addressable by prompting, the second never is.
Neither behaviour is a sampling effect; expecting a settings change to fix them wastes real time.

successCriteria: Attributes sycophancy to preference optimization
Attributes missing private knowledge to pretraining coverage
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Which training stage explains sycophancy, and which explains a model not knowing your internal tooling?

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats behavioural limits as transient defects awaiting a provider fix rather than as consequences of mechanism and training data.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner rank five hallucination mitigations and articulate why instruction-based mitigation ranks last.

questions.prompt: A support team reports that their assistant 'forgets what the customer said earlier' in long chats, and separately that their monthly bill grew far faster than their conversation volume. In 150 to 250 words, explain how a single property of the API accounts for both observations, and state what your application must do about it.
successCriteria: Identifies statelessness as the shared cause
Explains that apparent memory is the prior transcript being resent
Explains that resending prior turns makes cost grow faster than linearly with conversation length
Names a concrete context-budget strategy such as summarisation, windowing or selective retention

rubric.excellent: Names statelessness explicitly, derives both the forgetting and the cost curve from it, notes that forgetting is an application bug rather than a model limitation, and specifies a context budget with a concrete strategy at the ceiling.
rubric.adequate: Correctly identifies that history is resent and links it to at least one of the two observations, with a general remedy but no specific budgeting strategy.
rubric.weak: Attributes forgetting to model memory limits or context decay, or treats the two observations as unrelated problems.

errorPatterns.description: Learner attributes conversational continuity to model memory and therefore looks for the forgetting bug in the wrong system.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner plot cumulative tokens across twenty turns with no context management, then locate the truncation logic in their own client code.

assessments.title: Defending a Model and Hosting Choice

questions.prompt: A translation agency must process client contracts that are contractually barred from being used for model training. Two candidate models differ by four points on a public reasoning benchmark. Which consideration should decide the choice?
options: The benchmark gap, since it is the only objective measure available
Whichever provider offers the larger context window
Whether the provider offers a contractually backed zero-retention, no-training tier, evaluated against a task-specific test set
Whichever model is cheapest per million tokens

optionFeedback.feedback: Benchmark gaps are aggregated over tasks unlike yours and say nothing about the binding contractual constraint.
Context window matters for long contracts but does not address the constraint that actually eliminates candidates.
Correct. A hard contractual constraint filters the candidate set first; task-specific evaluation then decides among survivors.
Price is rarely decisive at agency volumes and cannot override a contractual prohibition.

successCriteria: Recognises the non-cost constraint as the filter applied first
questions.reviewPromptOverride: When a workload carries a hard contractual data constraint, what should decide model selection?

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats benchmark rank as the primary selection evidence and ignores binding non-capability constraints.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner re-solve the scenario with the benchmark scores hidden, and observe that the correct answer is unchanged.

questions.prompt: A team processes 900,000 input tokens per day and proposes self-hosting an open-weights model to save money. What is the strongest objection?
options: Open-weights models are not capable enough for production use
At that volume, API cost is small relative to the GPU capacity, engineering time and on-call burden self-hosting adds
Self-hosting is prohibited by most open-weights licences
Latency will always be worse when self-hosting

optionFeedback.feedback: Capability is not the issue; many open-weights models are entirely production-capable for ordinary tasks.
Correct. Self-hosting shifts cost rather than removing it, and below a crossover throughput the shifted cost is larger.
Most open-weights licences permit self-hosting; licence terms vary but are not the general objection.
Self-hosting can reduce latency with dedicated capacity; the objection is economic, not architectural.

successCriteria: Identifies the shifted-cost argument
Frames the decision around a throughput crossover
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why is 'open-weights models are cheaper because there is no per-token fee' usually wrong at moderate volume?

errorPatterns.description: Learner equates absence of per-token billing with lower total cost and omits infrastructure and staffing.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner compute fully-loaded monthly cost for both options including idle GPU capacity and on-call time, and find the crossover throughput.

questions.prompt: Eighteen months ago your team chose a model and wired its SDK directly into 30 call sites. Prices have since fallen by roughly 60 percent and three credible alternatives now exist. In 200 to 300 words, explain what this situation costs the organisation, what design decision would have prevented it, and how you would justify the remediation work to a manager who considers it refactoring with no user-visible benefit.
successCriteria: Frames the model as a swappable dependency rather than a settled choice
Names provider abstraction as the preventive design
Quantifies or estimates the overpayment to make the business case concrete
Notes that inability to switch causes teams to stop evaluating at all

rubric.excellent: Estimates the ongoing overpayment in currency, identifies the abstraction as ordinary dependency inversion, notes the second-order harm that unswitchable teams stop re-evaluating and drift further behind, and frames the manager pitch around recurring saving and optionality rather than code cleanliness.
rubric.adequate: Identifies lock-in and recommends an abstraction layer with a general cost argument, but without quantification or the second-order point.
rubric.weak: Treats the original choice as reasonable and settled, or proposes re-evaluation without addressing why substitution is currently impossible.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats model selection as a one-time architectural decision rather than a recurring evaluation enabled by cheap substitution.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require the provider abstraction in the section 5 build and exercise it in section 10 by routing part of the traffic to a cheaper model, then measure the saving.

questions.prompt: A prompt extracting fields from ferry timetables produces correct values but invents its own category labels, differently on each run. Which fix targets this failure specifically?
options: Add a closed enumeration of permitted category values to the prompt
Ask the model to be more consistent and precise
Raise the number of few-shot exemplars to ten
Lower the temperature to zero

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Taxonomy drift is an unconstrained degree of freedom, and enumeration closes it outright rather than reducing its frequency.
This adds no information, constraint or demonstration; it is phrasing rather than engineering.
Exemplars demonstrate a mapping but cannot enumerate a category set as reliably as stating it, and they cost tokens on every call.
This makes label choice consistent within a run but does not prevent an invented taxonomy from being used consistently.

successCriteria: Matches taxonomy drift to enumeration rather than to general advice
questions.reviewPromptOverride: A model invents its own category labels on each run. Which prompt technique targets that failure, and why not the alternatives?

errorPatterns.description: Learner responds to a structural failure with a wording change rather than a constraint.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner measure a phrasing-only change and a constraint-adding change against the same regression set and compare pass rates.

questions.prompt: You changed a prompt and it now handles three previously failing cases. What must you establish before shipping it?
options: That the three cases now pass consistently across repeated runs
That overall pass rate across the full regression set improved and no previously passing subset regressed
That the new prompt is not longer than the old one
That a colleague agrees the outputs read better

optionFeedback.feedback: Necessary but insufficient; a change that fixes three cases while breaking eight is still a regression.
Correct. The full-set comparison is what distinguishes a genuine improvement from a redistribution of failures.
Length affects cost and should be tracked, but it is not evidence of correctness.
Colleague impression is single-sample judgement in a second pair of eyes, and carries the same epistemic weakness.

successCriteria: Requires a full-set comparison rather than targeted-case verification
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Before shipping a prompt change that fixes three known failures, what must you establish?

errorPatterns.description: Learner accepts targeted or single-sample evidence as sufficient grounds for a prompt change.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner ship a change that fixes their known failures, then measure the full regression set and confront the regressed subset.

questions.prompt: A colleague proposes pasting an entire 90-page policy manual into every request so the assistant 'has full context'. In 150 to 250 words, give three independent arguments against this and state what you would do instead.
successCriteria: Names distraction from irrelevant material as an accuracy cost
Names position effects or middle-of-context degradation
Names cost and latency, ideally with reference to input tokens dominating the bill
Proposes retrieval of relevant sections as the alternative

rubric.excellent: Gives all three arguments with a mechanism for each, quantifies the token cost per request at a realistic volume, proposes retrieval with an ordering rule placing instructions first and the question last, and notes that curation typically beats any rewording.
rubric.adequate: Gives two of the three arguments and proposes retrieval, without quantification or ordering guidance.
rubric.weak: Objects only on cost grounds, or accepts the proposal on the basis that the context window is large enough to hold the manual.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats available context capacity as a reason to fill it, ignoring accuracy degradation.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner measure accuracy with two relevant documents versus ten documents containing the same two, and observe the drop directly.

assessments.title: Delegation and Verification in Daily Engineering

questions.prompt: Which task is the strongest candidate for full agentic delegation?
options: Deciding whether to split the monolith into services this quarter
Drafting the post-mortem for last week's outage
Applying a consistent, well-specified change across 20 call sites already covered by tests
Choosing which payments vendor to integrate

optionFeedback.feedback: Vague specification and organisational context make this undelegatable; the output would be confident and context-free.
Verification requires knowing what actually happened, and a plausible but wrong narrative is expensive to correct.
Correct. Both delegation conditions hold: the task specifies tightly and existing tests verify it cheaply.
A commercial judgement with tradeoffs the agent cannot weigh, not a specifiable engineering task.

successCriteria: Applies both the specificity and verification-cost conditions
questions.reviewPromptOverride: What two properties of a task determine whether it is safe to delegate to a coding agent?

errorPatterns.description: Learner selects tasks for delegation by size or tedium rather than by specification clarity and verification cost.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner time a proper review of a 400-line generated diff, compare against writing the change, then repeat with a failing test as the contract.

questions.prompt: A developer is told not to paste any company code into an assistant. They reply that their tool is the same product the company approved, so it must be fine. What is the flaw?
options: There is no flaw; approval of the product covers all its uses
Retention and training-use terms differ by tier and configuration, so the approved tier may not be the one they are using
The concern only applies to code containing credentials
Assistants cannot retain code, so the policy is unnecessary

optionFeedback.feedback: Approval is normally tier-specific and configuration-specific; the product name is not the unit of approval.
Correct. The same product's consumer and enterprise tiers frequently differ materially in retention and training use.
Proprietary logic and third-party licensed code carry obligations independent of credentials.
Retention depends entirely on the tier's terms, and assuming otherwise is exactly the error.

successCriteria: Identifies tier and configuration as the unit of the data-handling guarantee
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why is 'the company approved this assistant product' insufficient grounds for pasting proprietary code into it?

errorPatterns.description: Learner assumes data-handling guarantees follow the product rather than the specific tier and configuration in use.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require the learner to locate the actual terms for their own tier, configure exclusions, and verify the exclusions take effect.

questions.prompt: A senior engineer refuses to use coding assistants, arguing that reliance will erode their debugging ability and that of their juniors. In 200 to 300 words, give the strongest version of their concern, state where it is right and where it is wrong, and describe a team practice that captures the benefit while addressing the legitimate risk.
successCriteria: States the concern charitably rather than dismissing it
Concedes that uncritical acceptance genuinely does erode debugging skill
Identifies specification, decomposition and verification as skills exercised more under assisted workflows
Proposes a concrete practice such as test-first delegation, scoped diffs or risk-weighted review

rubric.excellent: Presents the concern as a real skill-formation argument grounded in learning through struggle, distinguishes sharply between uncritical acceptance and disciplined delegation, and proposes a specific practice with a reason it preserves the learning mechanism, ideally differentiating advice for juniors from advice for seniors.
rubric.adequate: Acknowledges both sides and proposes a verification practice, but treats the concern as broadly mistaken rather than partly correct.
rubric.weak: Dismisses the concern as resistance to change, or endorses abstinence without engaging with the productivity argument.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats the skill-erosion concern as either wholly right or wholly wrong instead of separating uncritical acceptance from disciplined delegation.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner log a week of assisted and unassisted tasks and identify which specific skills each mode exercised.

assessments.title: Building a Service Around a Model API

questions.prompt: A ticketing service parses JSON from model responses and fails roughly once in 40 calls on markdown fences and preambles. Which fix is strongest?
options: Strip fences and leading prose with a regex before parsing
Use provider-side schema-constrained decoding, validate, and allow one bounded repair attempt
Instruct the model more firmly to return only JSON
Retry until the response parses

optionFeedback.feedback: This handles the failures you have seen and not the ones you have not; truncation and nested fences will still break it.
Correct. Constrained decoding makes invalid output impossible rather than merely rarer, and the bounded repair covers provider gaps without unbounded spend.
Instruction reduces malformed output but cannot eliminate it, which is exactly the one-in-40 you are seeing.
An unbounded retry loop can spin indefinitely on a systematically failing input and is a known cost-runaway pattern.

successCriteria: Prefers a mechanism that makes the failure impossible over one that reduces frequency
questions.reviewPromptOverride: What is the strongest way to guarantee parseable structured output from a model API?

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats malformed structured output as an edge case handled by string cleanup rather than by constrained decoding and validation.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner run 200 requests under a prompt-only JSON instruction, count failures, then repeat with schema enforcement and compare.

questions.prompt: Your assistant's call to a tool that issues a refund times out. What is the correct handling?
options: Retry immediately, since timeouts are transient
Report failure to the user, since the call did not complete
Retry with backoff using an idempotency key so a duplicate refund cannot occur
Return the timeout to the model and let it decide whether to retry

optionFeedback.feedback: The first request may have succeeded; retrying without protection may issue a second refund.
You do not know it failed, and telling the user so may prompt a duplicate request through another channel.
Correct. Idempotency keys are what make retries safe for mutating operations, which is where naive retry logic causes real financial damage.
Autonomous retry of a mutating action is precisely the case requiring a human decision, not a model one.

successCriteria: Distinguishes retry safety for mutating versus read-only operations
questions.reviewPromptOverride: A mutating tool call times out. What makes retrying it safe?

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats the model's tool request as an authorised, executable instruction rather than an untrusted proposal evaluated by application code.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner write the handler for a tool call requesting another user's record, making explicit that identity comes from the session.

questions.prompt: A colleague states that setting temperature to zero makes your assistant deterministic, and that this is what will satisfy the auditor reviewing your loan-decision support tool. In 200 to 300 words, correct both claims and describe what would actually satisfy an auditor.
successCriteria: States that low temperature reduces variance without guaranteeing reproducibility across versions, batching or hardware
Separates determinism from auditability as distinct properties
Specifies logging of inputs, retrieved context, outputs, model version and parameters
Notes that a consequential decision should not rest solely on generative output

rubric.excellent: Corrects both claims precisely, explains why a deterministic system could still be unauditable and an auditable one need not be deterministic, specifies a concrete evidence trail with model and prompt versioning, and observes that the loan decision itself belongs in deterministic, testable code with the model confined to a supporting role.
rubric.adequate: Corrects the determinism claim and lists logging requirements, but does not clearly separate determinism from auditability.
rubric.weak: Accepts that temperature zero yields determinism, or addresses only audit logging without correcting the underlying claim.

errorPatterns.description: Learner equates a low sampling temperature with determinism, and determinism with auditability.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner run one zero-temperature prompt 50 times across a model version change, inspect the variation, then design the evidence trail an auditor would accept.

questions.prompt: A hardware retailer's semantic search handles 'something to stop a door slamming' well but fails on exact SKUs like `BX-4471-B`. Why?
options: Embeddings represent rare alphanumeric identifiers weakly, because such strings carry no semantic content
The chunks are too large for the identifiers to be found
The embedding model requires fine-tuning on the catalogue
The similarity metric should be Euclidean rather than cosine

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. This is the canonical case for hybrid retrieval, where lexical matching handles what dense retrieval structurally cannot.
Chunk size affects context and dilution, not the ability to match an exact string.
Adaptation cannot make an arbitrary identifier semantically meaningful; the technique is the mismatch.
The metric choice does not create semantic content where none exists.

successCriteria: Identifies the structural limitation of dense retrieval on exact identifiers
