questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why does dense retrieval fail on exact identifiers such as SKUs, and what fixes it?

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats dense retrieval as universally superior and does not reach for lexical or hybrid search.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner run a mixed query set through dense-only retrieval, inspect which queries fail, then add lexical fusion and re-measure recall.

questions.prompt: A team already operating Postgres needs retrieval over 800,000 chunks at modest query volume. Which recommendation is best supported?
options: A managed vector database, because purpose-built stores are always better for vectors
pgvector, because it adds no operational surface and integrates with their existing relational data
Whichever store ranks highest on published approximate-nearest-neighbour benchmarks
An in-process embedded store such as FAISS

optionFeedback.feedback: A vector store is an index over vectors, not a different species of database; managed services earn their cost at scale or when operations capacity is scarce.
Correct. At this scale and throughput it is comfortably sufficient, and one fewer system to operate is often the decisive factor.
Those benchmarks measure query performance under conditions unlike theirs and ignore operational cost entirely.
Workable for prototyping, but it complicates persistence, updates and multi-instance deployment for a production service.

successCriteria: Weights existing operational surface above benchmark position
questions.reviewPromptOverride: What is the first question to ask when choosing a vector store, and why is benchmark rank rarely decisive?

errorPatterns.description: Learner assumes AI workloads require a dedicated vector database regardless of scale or existing stack.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner implement identical retrieval on an embedded store and on pgvector, then state the specific throughput or operational condition that would justify a managed service.

questions.prompt: recall@5 on a corpus of building regulations is 0.55. The team's first instinct is to switch embedding models. In 200 to 300 words, describe the diagnostic process you would run first, name the two interventions most likely to matter on a corpus of this type, and explain why the embedding-model swap is usually the wrong first move.
successCriteria: Prescribes reading and categorising the failing queries before any change
Names structure-aware chunking as a likely dominant intervention on regulatory documents
Names hybrid retrieval for clause numbers and exact references
Explains that an embedding swap requires full re-indexing and rarely addresses the actual failure category

rubric.excellent: Leads with failure inspection and categorisation, ties each proposed intervention to a specific category found, notes that chunk boundaries determine what can ever be retrieved together and that no downstream fix recovers separated information, and identifies the embedding swap as the highest-cost lowest-evidence first move.
rubric.adequate: Proposes chunking and hybrid retrieval improvements with a general rationale, but treats diagnosis as optional or implicit.
rubric.weak: Proposes interventions in a list without diagnosis, or endorses the embedding-model swap as the natural starting point.

errorPatterns.description: Learner tunes downstream components while chunk boundaries remain the binding constraint on what can be retrieved.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner measure recall with fixed-size chunking on a corpus containing tables, inspect the failures, then re-chunk structure-aware and compare the improvement against any prompt change.

assessments.title: Building and Debugging a RAG Pipeline

questions.prompt: After adding retrieval, a museum archive assistant still occasionally states facts absent from the retrieved passages. What does this indicate?
options: Retrieval is not working and should be rebuilt
Grounding constrains generation but does not prevent the model falling back on priors, so citation requirements and an abstention path must be engineered
The retrieved passages are too short
The model needs fine-tuning on the archive

optionFeedback.feedback: Possible but not established; the described symptom occurs even with good retrieval and must be diagnosed at the generation stage.
Correct. Retrieval reduces fabrication without eliminating it, which is why abstention and citation are deliberate engineering rather than emergent behaviour.
Passage length affects sufficiency but does not explain assertions unsupported by any retrieved text.
Adaptation does not make a model refuse to exceed its evidence; that is a constraint and abstention design problem.

successCriteria: Locates the failure at generation rather than assuming retrieval
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why does adding retrieval reduce but not eliminate fabrication, and what must be engineered as a result?

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats retrieval as a complete solution to fabrication and omits citation and abstention design.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner query their own system for something genuinely absent from the corpus, observe the confident answer, then implement and re-test an abstention path.

questions.prompt: A team's RAG system embeds documents, takes the top five results and inserts them into the prompt. Quality has plateaued at mediocre. Which set of stages is most likely missing?
options: Query transformation and reranking, plus structure-aware parsing at ingestion
A larger model and a longer context window
More documents in the corpus
A conversational memory layer

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Naive top-k is the demo shape; the quality difference lives in parsing, query rewriting, reranking and filtering.
Scaling the model cannot compensate for retrieving the wrong passages in the first place.
More documents worsens precision unless retrieval quality is addressed first.
Memory affects multi-turn continuity, not single-query grounding quality.

successCriteria: Identifies the missing pipeline stages rather than proposing scale
questions.reviewPromptOverride: A naive embed-and-top-k RAG system has plateaued. Which pipeline stages are most likely missing?

errorPatterns.description: Learner equates RAG with embedding plus top-k retrieval and omits the stages where production quality is actually earned.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner measure the naive pipeline, then add query rewriting and reranking as separately measured steps so each stage's contribution appears as a number.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder argues that with a very long context window you can drop retrieval and paste the whole 300-document corpus into every request. In 200 to 300 words, give the strongest case for their position, then the four independent arguments against, and state the one requirement that makes stuffing structurally impossible rather than merely inefficient.
successCriteria: Fairly states the simplicity and recall advantages of the stuffing approach
Argues cost, latency, precision degradation over long context, and freshness or update cost
Identifies per-document access control as the structural blocker
Frames long context as changing the tradeoff rather than removing it

rubric.excellent: Presents the steelman honestly, gives four distinct arguments with mechanisms rather than assertions, correctly identifies permission filtering as structurally impossible under stuffing because unauthorised content is already in context, and concludes that the tradeoff has shifted rather than disappeared.
rubric.adequate: Gives two or three arguments against and identifies a practical blocker, without clearly distinguishing structural impossibility from inefficiency.
rubric.weak: Either accepts that long context obsoletes retrieval, or rejects the position on cost alone without engaging the strongest case for it.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats context capacity as a substitute for retrieval and overlooks precision, freshness and access control.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner compare accuracy and cost for stuffing versus retrieval on the same question set, including one permission-filtered query that stuffing cannot satisfy at all.

questions.prompt: A charity's grant-summarisation tool is about to ship. The team has reviewed roughly 20 outputs by hand and is satisfied. What is the core problem?
options: Twenty outputs is too small; they should review a hundred
Manual review cannot detect regressions on future changes or support a comparison between versions
They should have used a model as a judge instead
Nothing, provided the reviewers are domain experts

optionFeedback.feedback: Sample size is secondary; the missing element is a repeatable labelled set that can be re-run after every change.
Correct. Without a fixed golden set and a measured score there is no baseline, so no future change can be evaluated at all.
A judge without calibration against human labels substitutes an unvalidated scorer for an unvalidated impression.
Expertise should design the test set; it does not substitute for running one repeatedly.

successCriteria: Identifies the absence of a repeatable baseline as the core gap
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why is hand-reviewing a sample of outputs insufficient before shipping a generative feature?

errorPatterns.description: Learner substitutes manual inspection for a repeatable measured baseline.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner make a change they are confident improves quality, measure it against a golden set, and confront the subset that regressed while the average rose.

questions.prompt: Ten answers from a retrieval-augmented system are wrong. What must you determine before proposing any fix?
options: Whether a more capable model would have answered correctly
Whether the retrieved context actually contained the answer, separating retrieval failures from generation failures
Whether the prompt was clear enough
Whether users phrased their questions well

optionFeedback.feedback: This assumes the model is at fault before establishing it, and upgrading fixes nothing if the passages were never retrieved.
Correct. Staged attribution is what prevents spending money and effort on the component that was not responsible.
Prompt clarity matters only for the subset where correct context was retrieved and misused.
Query phrasing is a real factor, addressed by query transformation, but it is not the first attribution question.

successCriteria: Requires stage attribution before remediation
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Given ten wrong answers from a RAG system, what must you determine before proposing a fix?

errorPatterns.description: Learner attributes poor answers to model capability without checking whether retrieval supplied the necessary evidence.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Give the learner ten failing answers with their retrieved context and require classification as retrieval or generation failure before any fix is proposed.

questions.prompt: Your team wants to use a model as a judge to score answer quality nightly, and treat its scores as objective. In 200 to 300 words, describe the biases such a judge carries, the procedure that would make its scores trustworthy, and what you would still need human review for.
successCriteria: Names at least two of position, verbosity and self-preference bias
Prescribes calibration against human labels with an agreement measure
Notes that judge behaviour drifts with model versions and requires re-calibration
Reserves human review for high-stakes, ambiguous or novel categories

rubric.excellent: Names specific biases with the mechanism behind each, prescribes a calibration procedure with an explicit agreement statistic and a re-calibration trigger tied to model version changes, distinguishes what the judge can be trusted to track from what it cannot, and notes that a drifting judge silently invalidates historical score comparisons.
rubric.adequate: Identifies bias and recommends calibration against human labels, without specifying an agreement measure or a re-calibration trigger.
rubric.weak: Treats judge scores as objective, or rejects the technique outright without describing how calibration would make it usable.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats model-generated scores as objective ground truth without calibration against human labels.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner hand-score 30 outputs, score the same set with a judge, compute agreement, then swap candidate order to expose position bias.

questions.prompt: A publisher needs to classify a manuscript, extract metadata and generate a summary — always in that order, always the same three steps. What is the right design?
options: An autonomous agent with the three capabilities as tools
A deterministic chain of three calls with validation between steps
Three cooperating agents, one per step
One agent that plans its own approach for each manuscript

optionFeedback.feedback: Autonomy adds variance, latency and cost for a path that is fully known in advance.
Correct. When the path is enumerable, a deterministic workflow is cheaper, faster, testable and far easier to debug.
Multiple agents compound error rates and cost without adding capability to a fixed sequence.
Planning is wasted work when the plan is identical every time, and introduces variance into a stable process.

successCriteria: Prefers determinism when the path is fully enumerable
questions.reviewPromptOverride: When is a deterministic workflow the right choice over an autonomous agent?

errorPatterns.description: Learner reaches for autonomy on tasks whose steps are known in advance.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner implement the same task as a fixed chain and as an agent loop, then compare accuracy, cost, latency and debugging time.

questions.prompt: A proposed pipeline chains four specialised agents, each roughly 90 percent reliable, with no verification between handoffs. What is the strongest objection?
options: Four agents will be slower than one
Errors compound across unverified handoffs, so end-to-end reliability falls to roughly 65 percent
Frameworks do not support four-agent pipelines
Specialised agents are less capable than a single general one

optionFeedback.feedback: True but minor next to the correctness argument, and latency alone would not disqualify the design.
Correct. Compounding is the core reason multi-agent designs need bounded roles and verified handoffs to be viable at all.
Frameworks support this readily; the constraint is statistical, not technical.
Specialisation often helps per-step accuracy; the problem is the unverified composition, not the specialisation.

successCriteria: Reasons about compound reliability across handoffs
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why does chaining four 90-percent-reliable agents without verification produce a much weaker system?

errorPatterns.description: Learner adds agents to improve quality without bounding roles or verifying handoffs.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner compute compound reliability for a three-agent chain, then insert verification between handoffs and recompute.

questions.prompt: A teammate insists that any serious LLM application must be built on an orchestration framework. In 150 to 250 words, give a balanced assessment: what such frameworks genuinely provide, what they cost, and what a developer should understand before adopting one.
successCriteria: Names concrete benefits such as integrations, state management, tracing and graph structures with cycles
Names indirection, debugging difficulty and version churn as costs
States that understanding the underlying API calls is prerequisite to informed adoption
Avoids both uncritical endorsement and reflexive rejection

rubric.excellent: Gives specific benefits tied to real needs such as cyclic graphs that plain chains cannot express, names concrete costs including debugging through abstraction layers, argues that framework choice is only informed once the raw calls are understood, and identifies conditions under which direct API calls are the better engineering decision.
rubric.adequate: Lists benefits and costs in balance and mentions understanding the underlying calls, without specifics on either side.
rubric.weak: Endorses or rejects frameworks categorically without engaging the tradeoff.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats an orchestration framework as a prerequisite for LLM development rather than as an abstraction with costs and benefits.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner implement one chain with the framework and identical behaviour with direct API calls, then articulate precisely what the framework bought.

questions.prompt: An agent tasked with fixing a failing data import has run 30 iterations, each time reporting that it is making progress. What is the most likely design flaw?
options: No external validator and no budget, so the agent judges its own progress with nothing to stop it
The prompt describing the task was insufficiently detailed
The model is not capable enough for the task
The agent needs access to more tools

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Self-assessed progress with no enforced budget is the standard cause of loops that run long while achieving nothing.
Prompt detail helps, but without a validator a well-described task still has no reliable stopping condition.
A stronger model in an undesigned loop fails the same way, more expensively.
More tools widen the action space without supplying the missing success signal.

successCriteria: Identifies the missing external validator and budget
questions.reviewPromptOverride: An agent runs 30 iterations reporting progress without finishing. What is the likely design flaw?

errorPatterns.description: Learner accepts the tool's default loop rather than designing goal, validator, budget and escalation.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner run the same task with a default agent and with a fully designed loop, comparing cost, wall time and outcome.

questions.prompt: You are designing a loop to improve a project's onboarding documentation, where no automated test can judge quality. Which architecture fits best?
options: Retry, running until the output stops changing
A single agent instructed to write the docs then carefully check its own work
Generator-critic, with a separate critic evaluating against explicit written criteria
Explore-narrow, surveying the codebase before writing

optionFeedback.feedback: Retry requires a crisp pass or fail signal, which is exactly what this task lacks.
Self-review reliably ratifies rather than challenges; the separation of roles is the mechanism that makes critique work.
Correct. When no mechanical validator exists, separating production from evaluation is the strongest available substitute.
That architecture suits diagnosis across an unknown search space, not generation against quality criteria.

successCriteria: Selects generator-critic and identifies role separation as the mechanism
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Which loop architecture fits a task with no automated quality test, and what makes it work?

errorPatterns.description: Learner relies on the agent to evaluate its own output instead of separating generation from evaluation.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner run a self-assessed loop on a task with a hidden defect, watch it declare success, then re-run with a separate critic or failing test.

questions.prompt: Design a loop for this task: a nightly ETL job in a fisheries monitoring system fails roughly twice a week for varied reasons. Specify, in 250 to 350 words, the goal as a checkable condition, the tools and their boundaries, the external validator, the budget, and the escalation condition. Explain which failure categories must never be auto-remediated and state the principle behind that split.
successCriteria: States the goal as a machine-checkable condition rather than a description
Specifies an external validator constructed from existing signals such as a canary run, exit codes or row-count assertions
Sets iteration, time and token budgets enforced outside the agent
Defines an escalation rule that detects repeated identical failure rather than only budget exhaustion
Restricts auto-remediation to failures that are both recoverable and detectable

rubric.excellent: Specifies all five loop elements concretely, constructs a validator from signals that already exist rather than assuming a test suite, includes an escalation rule triggering on repeated identical failure, and articulates the principle that auto-remediation is acceptable only where failure is recoverable and detectable, with silent data corruption as the paradigm exclusion.
rubric.adequate: Specifies goal, validator and budget with a workable escalation rule, but treats the auto-remediation boundary as a list rather than a principle.
rubric.weak: Describes the task without a checkable goal, or relies on the agent to decide when it has finished.

errorPatterns.description: Learner allows repeated identical attempts and treats budget exhaustion as the only stopping condition.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner implement an escalation rule triggering on three identical consecutive failures and compare total spend against an unbounded retry loop on the same task.

assessments.title: Choosing and Measuring an Adaptation Strategy

questions.prompt: A shipping line wants the assistant to know its current port tariffs, which change monthly. Which approach fits?
options: Fine-tune monthly on the updated tariff documents
Retrieval over the tariff documents, with the model generating from retrieved passages
Include all tariffs in the system prompt permanently
Distil a smaller model from a larger one that has seen the tariffs

optionFeedback.feedback: Facts in weights cannot be cited, updated selectively or permission-filtered, and monthly retraining is a costly way to achieve what indexing does immediately.
Correct. Volatile, citable, permission-sensitive facts belong in retrieval, which is precisely the case retrieval was built for.
This burns context on every request and degrades as tariffs grow, while still requiring manual updates.
Distillation transfers behaviour, and inherits the same staleness problem for volatile facts.

successCriteria: Separates volatile knowledge from behaviour and routes it to retrieval
questions.reviewPromptOverride: For facts that change monthly and must be citable, which adaptation approach fits and why?

errorPatterns.description: Learner proposes fine-tuning to install factual knowledge that requires currency, citation or permission filtering.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner test fact recall from a small fine-tune against retrieval on the same questions, including one whose answer changed after training.

questions.prompt: A small team wants the model to reliably produce their house style of structured incident reports. They have 400 well-written past reports and one GPU. What is the best assessment?
options: This is out of reach; fine-tuning needs tens of thousands of examples and a cluster
This is a good fit for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, since format and style are exactly what adaptation teaches well
They should use retrieval over the 400 reports instead
They should prompt with all 400 reports as exemplars

optionFeedback.feedback: LoRA on a small model works with a few hundred curated examples on a single GPU; data quality dominates volume.
Correct. Consistent form and style is the strongest use case for adaptation, and the dataset size is appropriate for a parameter-efficient method.
Retrieval supplies facts, not a consistent output form; it is the wrong tool for a style requirement.
This is unaffordable per request and exceeds practical context budgets, per the context-engineering constraints.

successCriteria: Matches a style and format goal to adaptation
Rejects the scale barrier
questions.reviewPromptOverride: With 400 curated examples and one GPU, is fine-tuning for house style feasible, and why?

errorPatterns.description: Learner rules out adaptation on assumed data and compute requirements rather than evaluating the actual method.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner run a LoRA adaptation on roughly 300 curated examples, measure the gain, then degrade data quality and re-measure to see what actually drives the result.

questions.prompt: Your fine-tuned model beats the prompt-only baseline by 11 points on the target task. A manager proposes adopting it immediately across all features. In 200 to 300 words, describe what you would measure before agreeing, and the ongoing obligations adoption creates.
successCriteria: Requires out-of-domain evaluation to detect general capability degradation
Notes version lock to a specific base model and the deprecation risk
Names the retraining pipeline as a permanent maintenance cost
Recommends scoping adoption to the task measured rather than all features

rubric.excellent: Requires evaluation on tasks outside the training distribution before adoption, quantifies the maintenance obligation including retraining triggers and base-model deprecation, argues for scoping to the measured task, and notes that the 11-point gain is evidence about one task rather than about the model generally.
rubric.adequate: Raises capability regression and maintenance concerns and recommends narrower adoption, without specifying what would be measured.
rubric.weak: Accepts the target-task gain as sufficient evidence for broad adoption, or objects without naming a measurable check.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats a fine-tune as a permanent upgrade and omits capability regression and retraining obligations.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner evaluate the adapted model on out-of-domain tasks alongside the target task, then write the retraining plan required when the base model is deprecated.

assessments.title: Threat Review of an AI System

questions.prompt: An assistant summarises inbound supplier emails and can call a tool to update payment details. A supplier email contains text instructing the assistant to change bank details to a new account. Which defence actually holds?
options: A system prompt instructing the model to ignore instructions found inside emails
Removing the payment-update tool from the assistant, and requiring the change through an authenticated human workflow
Asking the model to flag suspicious instructions before acting
Filtering emails for suspicious keywords before processing

optionFeedback.feedback: Instructions and data share one channel, so this defence fails against any phrasing you did not anticipate.
Correct. Removing the capability is architectural and holds regardless of what the injected text says.
This delegates the security decision to the component under attack, which is the error the scenario is testing.
Keyword filtering is trivially evaded by rephrasing and gives false assurance.

successCriteria: Selects an architectural control over an instruction-based one
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why can't prompt injection be defended by instructing the model to ignore malicious instructions?

errorPatterns.description: Learner defends against injection with prompt instructions rather than least privilege and validation.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner plant an instruction inside a retrieved document, watch the instruction defence fail, then implement a permission-based control and re-test.

questions.prompt: A team argues that content from their own internal wiki is trusted, so retrieved passages need no special handling. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, provided the wiki is behind authentication
Anyone who can write to the wiki can place instructions into the model's context, so ownership of the store says nothing about authorship of its contents
The concern applies only to content fetched from the public internet
Internal content is safe once it has been embedded

optionFeedback.feedback: Authentication controls who may write, not what they write; a contractor, a compromised account or a well-meaning colleague all become injection vectors.
Correct. Every path by which text enters the context window is an untrusted input path until proven otherwise.
Tickets, emails, wikis and uploaded documents are all authored by someone and all carry the same risk.
Embedding is a representation step and confers no safety property whatsoever.

successCriteria: Treats all ingested content as untrusted input
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why is content from your own internal document store still untrusted input to a model?

errorPatterns.description: Learner conflates ownership of a data store with trustworthiness of its contents.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner enumerate every path by which text enters their context window, label each trusted or untrusted, and justify any trusted label.

questions.prompt: You are six weeks into building a citizen-facing benefits assistant. Nobody has raised governance yet, and the position is that legal will review before launch. In 250 to 350 words, identify three governance decisions your architecture has probably already made implicitly, explain what each would cost to reverse now versus at launch, and state what you would do this week.
successCriteria: Identifies implicit decisions such as data residency, retention of prompts and logs, PII in context, or audit trail coverage
Explains that reversal cost rises steeply because ingestion and logging decisions propagate
Proposes concrete near-term action rather than deferring to legal review
Notes that eligibility or entitlement determinations should not rest on generative output

rubric.excellent: Names three specific implicit decisions with the code-level place each was made, contrasts reversal cost now against re-ingestion and log purging later, proposes concrete action this week such as PII redaction at ingestion and audit fields in traces, and flags that benefit determinations require deterministic, contestable logic with a human decision-maker.
rubric.adequate: Identifies two or three implicit decisions and proposes some near-term action, without a clear cost-of-reversal argument.
rubric.weak: Defers to legal review, or treats governance as documentation to be produced before launch rather than architecture already committed.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats governance as a review gate rather than a set of architectural decisions already embedded in the build.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner audit their own capstone for three governance decisions already made implicitly, and cost the reversal of each at the current stage versus at launch.

questions.prompt: A streaming RAG service is deployed using the team's standard web-app template. Health checks fail intermittently and long responses are cut off. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model provider is rate-limiting the service
Default timeouts and health-check settings assume short request lifetimes, which streaming responses violate
The container image is too large
The service needs more replicas

optionFeedback.feedback: Rate limiting produces explicit errors rather than truncation at a consistent duration.
Correct. Long-lived streaming requests break assumptions baked into standard web-service templates, from proxy timeouts to readiness probes.
Image size affects cold start and deploy time, not mid-response truncation.
Replicas address throughput; they do not change per-request timeout behaviour.

successCriteria: Identifies the mismatch between streaming lifetimes and standard service defaults
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Which standard web-deployment assumptions break for a streaming AI service?

errorPatterns.description: Learner deploys an AI service on unmodified web-application defaults without accounting for streaming, cold starts or artifact size.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner deploy naively, run a streaming load test to reproduce the timeout and cold-start failures, then fix each with the specific mechanism that addresses it.

questions.prompt: A four-person team is deploying their first AI service: bursty traffic, no GPU requirement, no existing Kubernetes. What is the best-supported recommendation?
options: Adopt Kubernetes now, since AI workloads will require it eventually
A managed container or serverless platform, since the workload has no property that justifies the operational cost of Kubernetes
Run it on a single virtual machine with no orchestration
Whichever platform offers the most AI-specific features

optionFeedback.feedback: Kubernetes is justified by scale, GPU pooling or existing standards, none of which are present here.
Correct. Bursty CPU-only traffic with a small team is the archetypal case for a managed platform.
This leaves them without scaling or health management for genuinely bursty traffic.
Feature lists do not address the operational fit that actually decides this.

successCriteria: Matches deployment target to workload characteristics rather than to category
questions.reviewPromptOverride: What conditions actually justify Kubernetes for an AI service?

errorPatterns.description: Learner selects Kubernetes by default rather than justifying it against workload characteristics.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner cost and justify three deployment targets against their own workload's request pattern and defend the choice against the two rejected.

questions.prompt: Your capstone is deployed and working. In 250 to 350 words, write the operating plan: what is monitored, what thresholds trigger action, who re-runs the evaluation suite and on what trigger, and what you would do the day your provider announces the deprecation of the model you depend on.
successCriteria: Specifies quality, latency and cost signals rather than only availability
Defines concrete thresholds and an owner for each
Ties evaluation re-runs to triggers including scheduled runs and provider model changes
Gives a concrete deprecation response leveraging the provider abstraction and eval suite

rubric.excellent: Specifies monitored signals across quality, latency and cost with named thresholds and owners, schedules evaluation runs on a timer independent of deploys as well as on provider change, and describes a deprecation response in which the abstraction allows substitution and the eval suite provides the evidence that the substitute is acceptable.
rubric.adequate: Covers monitoring and evaluation re-runs with some thresholds, and gives a general deprecation response without connecting it to abstraction and evaluation.
rubric.weak: Treats deployment as completion, or lists monitoring signals without thresholds, owners or triggers.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats deployment as project completion and omits the ongoing evaluation and operations obligations.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Require an operating plan as a deliverable alongside the deployment, specifying monitored signals, thresholds, owners and evaluation triggers.

assessments.title: Operating and Costing an AI System

questions.prompt: A recipe-recommendation service's retrieval index silently fails to update for three weeks. Dashboards stay green throughout. Why?
options: The monitoring system was misconfigured
Conventional monitoring reports availability and latency; a fluent but ungrounded answer returns 200 OK and looks identical to a good one
Three weeks is too short for such a failure to appear
Retrieval failures always surface as errors eventually

optionFeedback.feedback: The monitoring worked exactly as designed; it was measuring the wrong things for this class of system.
Correct. Quality failures in generative systems are invisible to request-level metrics, which is why prompt, context and quality tracing are required.
Duration is irrelevant; the failure mode is undetectable by these signals at any timescale.
Ungrounded answers do not raise errors, which is precisely the danger.

successCriteria: Identifies the gap between request-level metrics and answer quality
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Why can an AI system be seriously broken while conventional monitoring stays green?

errorPatterns.description: Learner relies on conventional application monitoring and does not instrument prompts, retrieved context or quality signals.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner break retrieval deliberately, confirm dashboards stay green, then add the trace fields that would have caught it.

questions.prompt: A service sends 40,000 input tokens and receives 500 output tokens per request, at $3 per million input and $15 per million output. Where should optimisation effort go?
options: Output, since the per-token price is five times higher
Input, which dominates cost by roughly 16 to 1, making context reduction the highest-leverage change
Both equally, since costs are broadly balanced
Neither; token costs at this scale are negligible

optionFeedback.feedback: Unit price is higher but volume is 80 times lower, so output is a small fraction of the total.
Correct. Twelve cents of input against three quarters of a cent of output per request tells you exactly where to work.
Splitting effort evenly across a 16-to-1 imbalance wastes most of it.
Cost scales with context length times volume times retries, and dismissing it before modelling volume is how surprise invoices happen.

successCriteria: Computes the ratio rather than reasoning from unit price
questions.reviewPromptOverride: Given 40,000 input and 500 output tokens per request at $3 and $15 per million, where does optimisation effort belong?

errorPatterns.description: Learner reasons from unit prices rather than from total spend, or dismisses token cost without modelling volume and retries.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner project monthly cost at ten times current volume including retries and agent iterations, then identify the single change that reduces it most.

questions.prompt: A team says their assistant is stable because they have not deployed in four months. In 150 to 250 words, explain why that reasoning does not hold for this class of system, and describe the minimum practice that would let them make the claim honestly.
successCriteria: Names provider-side model updates or deprecation as a source of change without deploys
Names data drift or changing user behaviour as a second source
Prescribes scheduled evaluation runs against production independent of code changes
Specifies an alert threshold on score movement

rubric.excellent: Identifies at least two independent sources of change that require no deploy, explains that absence of deploys is evidence about the codebase rather than the system, prescribes timer-driven evaluation with a defined alert threshold, and notes that without a baseline they could not detect drift even if it had already occurred.
rubric.adequate: Names one or two sources of change and recommends periodic evaluation, without specifying thresholds or alerting.
rubric.weak: Accepts the stability claim, or objects generally without naming a mechanism by which the system changes.

errorPatterns.description: Learner infers system stability from absence of code changes, ignoring provider updates and data drift.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner schedule the evaluation suite against production on a timer with no code change, and design the alert that fires when scores move beyond a threshold.

assessments.title: Scoping, Delivering and Presenting AI Work

questions.prompt: A two-week prototype of a legal-document assistant impressed the partners, who now expect launch within a month. What is the most accurate assessment to give them?
options: A month is realistic, since the hard part is done
The prototype represents a small fraction of total effort; evaluation, security review, cost control and operations remain, and they are the larger share
It depends mainly on how quickly infrastructure can be provisioned
A month is realistic if more engineers are added

optionFeedback.feedback: The demo is roughly the first tenth of the work, and this expectation is the leading cause of stalled AI initiatives.
Correct, and stating it early is far cheaper than discovering it in month three of a committed timeline.
Infrastructure is rarely the constraint; evaluation and edge-case handling usually are.
Adding people does not compress evaluation work that has not yet been defined.

successCriteria: Identifies the remaining work categories and their relative weight
questions.reviewPromptOverride: A working AI demo exists. Roughly what share of the work is done, and what remains?

errorPatterns.description: Learner equates a working demo with near-complete delivery and underestimates evaluation, security, cost and operations work.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner enumerate and estimate every item between their own working capstone demo and a production release, then compare the total against the demo's build time.

questions.prompt: Two candidates present portfolios. Candidate A built a multi-agent research system with no evaluation. Candidate B built a single-retrieval assistant with a golden set, staged metrics, a cost analysis and a decision log. Which is stronger evidence of engineering judgement, and why?
options: Candidate A, because the architecture is more advanced
Candidate B, because evaluation evidence and documented tradeoffs demonstrate judgement that architectural novelty alone does not
Neither; portfolios are weak evidence in general
Candidate A, provided the system runs

optionFeedback.feedback: Novelty without measurement leaves a reviewer unable to tell whether the system works at all.
Correct. Reviewers weight problem framing, evidence and tradeoff reasoning above architectural ambition.
Portfolios are among the strongest available signals when they contain evidence rather than assertions.
Running is a low bar; it says nothing about whether the outputs are any good.

successCriteria: Weights evidence and judgement above architectural novelty
questions.reviewPromptOverride: What do portfolio reviewers weight above architectural novelty, and why?

errorPatterns.description: Learner optimises portfolio work for architectural ambition rather than for demonstrable judgement and evidence.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Have the learner score two anonymised portfolio projects against the six-criterion rubric and observe which scores higher and on which criteria.

questions.prompt: A hospital trust asks for an assistant that will answer clinicians' medication questions with guaranteed accuracy, and states that liability requires it never be wrong. In 250 to 350 words, give your recommendation: proceed, reshape or decline. Include measurable success criteria for whatever you propose, and explain how you would communicate the limitation without either overpromising or dismissing the underlying need.
successCriteria: Identifies guaranteed accuracy as outside current capability rather than an engineering effort problem
Reshapes rather than simply declining, proposing a supporting role with human decision-making retained
States measurable acceptance criteria including an abstention rate and groundedness threshold
Communicates the limitation in terms the requester's actual need can absorb

rubric.excellent: Declines the requirement as stated with a clear reason grounded in the generation mechanism, reshapes to a retrieval-and-citation assistant that surfaces source passages while the clinician decides, specifies acceptance criteria including groundedness, citation validity and abstention behaviour with numeric thresholds, and frames the conversation around what the trust actually needs rather than around what the model cannot do.
rubric.adequate: Recognises the requirement as infeasible and proposes a narrower scope with some success criteria, but without numeric thresholds or a clear stakeholder framing.
rubric.weak: Accepts the requirement as achievable with sufficient engineering effort, or declines flatly without proposing a reshaped alternative.

errorPatterns.description: Learner treats infeasible requirements as solvable through further iteration rather than recognising a capability boundary.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Give the learner three proposals, one genuinely infeasible, and require a proceed, reshape or decline recommendation with reasoning for each.

retrievalSystem.algorithm: Expanding-interval spaced retrieval with per-item schedule blocks and confidence-modulated scheduling. Each retrievalItem carries its own initialReviewDays and subsequentReviewDays; the scheduler advances an item on success and resets it toward initialReviewDays on failure. Correct answers given below 40 percent confidence are re-queued at the initial interval rather than advancing; incorrect answers given above 80 percent confidence are flagged miscalibrated and surfaced with the misconception text that best matches the error. Evidence weight halves every 30 days, so an item unreviewed past its window contributes progressively less to mastery.

glossary.definition: Algorithms that learn patterns from structured, tabular data — linear and logistic regression, decision trees, gradient-boosted trees, clustering. Usually trained on your own data in minutes.
Neural networks with many layers that learn their own feature representations from raw input such as pixels, audio or text, rather than from hand-engineered columns.
A model that maps an input to a label or score. The output space is small and defined in advance, which makes accuracy metrics straightforward.
A model that produces new content in the same space as its input. The output space is effectively unbounded, which is why evaluation requires deliberate design.
A large neural network trained to predict the next token in text, which as a side effect acquires broad language and reasoning ability.
Training on labelled examples, where each input is paired with the correct answer.
Training where labels come from the data itself, such as predicting a hidden next word, which is why language models can train on raw text with no human labelling.
A model that accepts or produces more than one kind of data, such as image in and text out.
Running a trained model to produce an output. Distinct from training, and the activity that almost all application development involves.
The unit a model reads and writes, roughly a word fragment. Billing, context limits and latency are all measured in tokens rather than words.
The deterministic, model-specific algorithm that splits text into tokens.
The maximum number of tokens, input plus output, the model can process in a single request. A hard architectural limit.
The mechanism that lets a model weigh how much each earlier token matters when predicting the next one. The core innovation of the transformer.
The raw scores a model produces for every possible next token, before they are converted into probabilities.
A sampling parameter. Low values concentrate probability on top candidates; higher values flatten the distribution and produce more varied output.
Nucleus sampling: restricting selection to the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities sum to p, cutting off the unlikely tail.
The first and most expensive training stage, predicting the next token across an enormous corpus. Produces raw capability rather than helpfulness.
Training on curated instruction and response pairs so the model follows instructions and adopts an assistant format.
Training on human comparisons of candidate responses, shaping tone, refusals and perceived helpfulness. The origin of sycophancy.
Fluent, confident output that is not true. Not a separate mode but the same mechanism as correct generation, operating where the training distribution underconstrains the answer.
The property that a model retains nothing between API calls. Apparent memory is the prior transcript being resent as input tokens.
Instructions supplied separately from user input, setting persistent role and constraints for a request.
A worked input and output pair included in a prompt to demonstrate the desired mapping. Zero-shot means none are supplied.
Splitting one complex request into several simpler chained requests, each independently checkable.
Instructing a model to work through intermediate steps before answering, which improves multi-step accuracy.
Requiring output to conform to a declared structure, ideally enforced by the API through constrained decoding rather than requested in prose.
The deliberate allocation of a token limit across instructions, examples, retrieved data and conversation history.
The tendency for material at the very start and end of a long input to influence output more than material buried in the middle.
A fixed collection of inputs with expected properties, run against every change to detect breakage.
A reference answer, or a set of required properties, for a given test input.
A checked-in file stating project conventions, architecture and constraints, loaded automatically into a coding assistant's context.
The repeating cycle of reason, act and observe that an agentic tool runs. Sometimes called the reason-act-observe cycle.
A pass or fail judgement produced by something other than the model — tests, compiler, linter, type checker — which is what makes autonomous loops safe.
Hard limits on iterations, wall-clock time and token spend, enforced by the harness rather than left to the agent's discretion.
The predefined state in which a loop stops and hands control back to a human, along with the information it hands over.
Work inside an existing codebase with existing conventions, constraints and history. The opposite of greenfield.
Receiving output tokens as they are generated rather than waiting for completion. Improves perceived latency but complicates validation.
A bounded fallback that attempts to fix or re-request output which failed validation.
The model emits a structured request naming a function and its arguments. It does not execute anything; your code decides whether to honour the request.
The property that performing an operation twice has the same effect as performing it once. Essential wherever retries exist.
A retry strategy where waits grow multiplicatively and are randomised, preventing synchronised retry storms.
Serving a reduced but useful response when the ideal path fails, rather than returning an error.
An internal interface your code calls, with provider-specific adapters behind it, enabling model substitution without touching call sites.
A fixed-length vector representing the meaning of a piece of content, positioned so that similar content sits nearby.
Similarity measured as the angle between two vectors, ignoring magnitude. The usual default for text retrieval.
Search by vector similarity, which matches meaning rather than exact words.
Search by term overlap, such as BM25 or keyword matching, which matches exact words including identifiers.
Combining dense and lexical results into a single ranking. The strong default for real corpora.
A unit of text embedded and stored as one retrievable item. Chunk boundaries determine what can ever be retrieved together.
Repeating text between adjacent chunks so that material spanning a boundary is not lost.
Index structures such as HNSW or IVF that trade exactness for speed when searching large vector collections.
Restricting search by structured attributes such as date, author, department or permission, before or during similarity search.
The proportion of queries for which a correct document appears in the top k results. The core retrieval metric.
A second-stage model that reorders retrieved candidates by relevance. It can only reorder what retrieval already found.
Rewriting or expanding a user's question before retrieval, to bridge the gap between how people ask and how documents are written.
The degree to which an answer's claims are supported by the retrieved passages provided to the model.
Designed behaviour where the system declines to answer when retrieved evidence is insufficient, converting a fabrication into a visible gap.
Using a model to score outputs. Carries position, verbosity and self-preference biases and requires calibration against human labels.
A fixed set of real inputs with labelled correct answers or required properties, used as the baseline for every evaluation run.
A CI step that blocks a release when the evaluation suite falls below a defined threshold.
A fixed sequence of calls where the path is known in advance. Cheaper, faster and more testable than an agent when the steps are enumerable.
A system where the model chooses its own next action within a loop, rather than following a predetermined path.
A loop architecture separating production from evaluation, with a distinct critic assessing output against explicit criteria.
A loop architecture that plans steps, executes them, then verifies against the goal. Suited to multi-file changes where ordering matters.
A loop architecture that surveys broadly before committing and going deep. Suited to debugging and unfamiliar codebases.
A design where the loop pauses at defined checkpoints for human approval. Mandatory for irreversible actions.
Low-rank adaptation: a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains a small number of additional weights rather than the whole model.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: the family of methods, including LoRA, that adapt a model by training a small fraction of its parameters.
Training a smaller model to reproduce the behaviour of a larger one, usually to reduce cost and latency.
An attack where instructions embedded in data reach the model and alter its behaviour. Defended architecturally, since instructions and data share one channel.
Granting a component only the permissions it needs. The primary architectural defence for tool-using agents.
Treating model output as trusted input to another system, allowing generated content to trigger unintended execution or queries.
The delay when a new instance must load dependencies and model artifacts before serving. A common surprise in AI deployment.
Recording the full path of a request including prompts, retrieved context, tool calls and outputs, so a failure can be localised to a step.
Gradual change in data, user behaviour or upstream model behaviour that degrades system quality without any code change.
Directing requests to different models by difficulty or type, to reduce cost while preserving quality on the cases that need it.
A record of significant choices, alternatives considered and what was traded away. The highest-signal portfolio artifact and distinct from a changelog.
Conditions defined in advance under which a project will be stopped, agreed before work begins rather than argued afterwards.

sections.title: The Modern AI Landscape for Engineers
sections.description: Map the territory of modern AI, establish where language models do and do not belong, and set up the toolchain used for the rest of the course. The skill this section teaches is refusal: knowing which problems not to point a language model at.

learningObjectives.description: Classify a given problem statement into the AI technique family most likely to solve it (classical ML, deep learning, generative, embedding-based, or no-AI) and justify the classification.
Distinguish generative from discriminative approaches and describe the input/output contract of each, including the evaluation consequence that follows from choosing generative.
Identify at least three problems commonly mis-assigned to language models and name a more appropriate technique for each.
Configure a working local environment (Python environment, API keys, secrets handling, notebook or CLI) and execute a first successful model call.

motivationHooks.prompt:
Within the next year — possibly the next month — you will be in a meeting where someone says *"can we use AI for this?"* and everyone turns to you.

What happens next decides whether your team spends six weeks and a large budget building something a fifty-line script would have done better, or whether you ship something that works. The most expensive mistakes in corporate AI are not made in code. They are made in the first twenty minutes of the first meeting, when someone picks the wrong family of technique. That choice then gets ratified by a prototype, a budget and a roadmap, and by the time anyone notices, changing course is politically impossible.

An agricultural equipment dealership sends four requests to your desk in one week:

1. Predict which leased machines will need servicing in the next 90 days, from telemetry you already collect.
2. When a technician uploads a photo of a damaged part, tell them the part number.
3. Make 4,000 pages of service manuals answerable in plain language.
4. Draft the follow-up emails sales reps send after a demo.

**Before reading on, commit to an answer: how many of these four are language-model problems?** Write your number down. You will check it at the end of the section.

**Two.** Requests 3 and 4.

Request 1 is classical machine learning — structured telemetry in, a probability out. A gradient-boosted tree beats a language model on accuracy, cost and explainability, and tells you *why* it predicted what it did. Request 2 is image classification: a specialised vision model, not a language model. Request 3 needs both generation and embeddings, because the model has never seen those manuals — that combination is retrieval-augmented generation, and it is the spine of this course. Request 4 is the only clean, purely generative fit.

If you answered three or four, you have just found the most expensive habit in applied AI, and you have found it in week one rather than in month four of a committed roadmap.

sectionSummary.content:
You should now believe the following about problems that arrive labelled "AI":

The word *AI* tells you almost nothing about which technique a problem needs. Three questions do the work: **what shape is the output**, **what shape is the input**, and **where does the required knowledge live**. Output shape resolves most cases on its own — a fixed set of labels or a number means discriminative, and free-form content that could be phrased infinitely many ways means generative.

Choosing generative is a commitment, not a default. The output space is unbounded, so no accuracy metric works out of the box, and you have accepted an evaluation burden that a classification problem would never have imposed. Make that trade deliberately.

A pretrained model has no access to your private data and never will. Any sentence of the form "the model will know our business" is describing infrastructure that somebody has to build.

And frequently the honest answer to a request containing the word AI is: *AI for fifteen percent of this, and boring reliable code for the rest.* Recognising which fifteen percent is the whole skill.
keyTakeaways: Run the three classification questions before proposing any technique.
Output shape is the highest-yield single question: closed set means discriminative, unbounded means generative.
Choosing generative means accepting an evaluation burden — plan for it now, not later.
A pretrained model cannot know your private data; closing that gap is engineering work with its own failure modes.
Model size and leaderboard rank predict very little about fitness for your specific task.
'Not AI' is a legitimate and often correct recommendation.
