learningExperiences.title: Four Requests, Four Techniques

contentBlocks.content:
## What you will be able to do

By the end of this experience you will be able to:

- **`s01-o1`** — classify a problem statement into the AI technique family most likely to solve it, and justify the classification
- **`s01-o3`** — name at least three problems commonly mis-assigned to language models, and a better technique for each

This is the only part of the course with no building in it. The skill here is refusal.

terms.definition: Algorithms that learn patterns from structured, tabular data — regression, decision trees, gradient-boosted trees, clustering. Typically trained on your own data, in minutes, on a laptop.
Neural networks with many layers that learn their own feature representations from raw input such as pixels, audio or text, rather than from hand-engineered columns.
A model that maps an input to a label or score. It answers *which category is this?* or *how much?* The output space is small and defined in advance.
A model that produces new content in the same space as its input. The output space is effectively unbounded.
A fixed-length list of numbers representing the meaning of a piece of content, positioned so that similar content sits close together in that numeric space.
Running a trained model to get an output. Distinct from training. Almost everything you do in this course is inference.

contentBlocks.content:
## Start concrete: four requests from one company

You work at a mid-sized agricultural equipment dealership. In one week, four requests land on your desk.

**Request 1** — *Predict which of our 12,000 leased machines will need servicing in the next 90 days, from the telemetry we already collect.*

**Request 2** — *When a technician uploads a photo of a damaged part, tell them the part number.*

**Request 3** — *Our service manuals are 4,000 pages. Technicians can't find anything. Let them ask questions in plain language.*

**Request 4** — *Draft the follow-up emails our sales reps send after a demo.*

Every one of these is "AI". Only two of them are language models. Getting this right is the entire skill.

### Working through them

**Request 1 is classical machine learning.** You have structured, tabular data — hours run, fault codes, ambient temperature, part age — and a well-defined output: a probability. This is what gradient-boosted trees do better than anything else on earth. A language model would be slower, more expensive, less accurate, and unable to tell you *why* it predicted what it did. A junior data scientist with XGBoost solves this in a week.

**Request 2 is deep learning, specifically computer vision.** Input is raw pixels; output is one label from a known set of part numbers. This is a discriminative task — image classification. You would fine-tune an existing vision model on photos of your parts catalogue. A vision-capable language model might do surprisingly well as a prototype, but at production volume a small specialised classifier will be faster, cheaper and more accurate.

**Request 3 is generative *and* embedding-based.** The output is free-form language, so you need a generative model. But the model has never seen your service manuals, so you must find the relevant pages first — that is what embeddings are for. This combination is retrieval-augmented generation, and it is the spine of this course.

**Request 4 is purely generative.** Free-form text out, no external facts strictly required, tolerance for variation, a human reviews before sending. The cleanest language-model fit of the four.

## Now abstract: how to classify anything

Ask three questions, in this order.

### Question 1 — What shape is the output?

If the output is one of a fixed set of labels, or a number, you are in discriminative territory: classical ML or a specialised deep model. If the output is free-form content that could be phrased infinitely many ways, you are in generative territory.

This single question resolves most cases. *"Which of these five categories does this support ticket belong to?"* is classification, even though it involves text. You **can** do it with a language model, and at low volume that may be the pragmatic choice. But at 50,000 tickets a day, a fine-tuned small classifier costs a rounding error compared to API calls.

### Question 2 — What shape is the input?

Structured rows and columns point strongly toward classical ML. Raw perceptual data — images, audio, video — points toward deep learning. Free text points toward language models or embeddings.

### Question 3 — Where does the required knowledge live?

If the knowledge needed is *in the data you already have*, you train or retrieve. If it is general world knowledge and language competence, a pretrained model already has it. If it is private and specific — your manuals, your policies, your codebase — **the model does not have it and never will.**

That gap is why retrieval exists, and it is the single most common source of failed AI projects: teams assume the model somehow knows their business.

contentBlocks.title: The sentence that should always make you stop
contentBlocks.content:
*"We'll point the model at our wiki so it knows our procedures."*

Providing documents is the right idea. But phrasing it as the model "knowing" the wiki conceals an entire retrieval system that has to be built, measured and maintained — with its own failure modes. That concealment is how a six-week estimate becomes a six-month project.

contentBlocks.caption: Two beliefs worth dismantling in week one
rows: More parameters is better
Capability comes from training data quality, training compute, post-training and fit to *your* task. Leaderboard position predicts almost nothing about your use case.
A 7B model fine-tuned on your invoices beats a frontier model on your invoices, at a fraction of the cost.
Neural networks work like the brain

The analogy is 1950s branding that survived because it is evocative. It predicts nothing about behaviour and makes people expect memory, understanding and consistent reasoning the architecture does not provide.
Drop the metaphor. Reason from the mechanism instead — you will make better predictions, as section 2 will show.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before reading the analysis: of the four dealership requests, **how many are genuinely language-model problems?** Commit to a number and one sentence of reasoning.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The answer is two — requests 3 and 4. Most people answer three or four on a first pass, because the word *AI* pulls everything toward the most visible technology. If that was you, this section is doing its job: you have just found the habit in a low-stakes setting rather than in month four of a committed roadmap.
feedback.correctiveFeedback: Requests 1 and 2 are prediction from structured data and image classification respectively. Neither involves language, and neither benefits from a language model.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in that count?

interactionSequence.prompt: A logistics company wants to predict, from twelve months of structured shipment records, which deliveries will arrive late. Which approach fits best?
options: Gradient-boosted trees trained on the historical shipment table
A language model prompted with each shipment's details
A frontier language model, because it has the most parameters and therefore the best reasoning
An embedding model that stores shipments as vectors and finds similar past shipments

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Structured tabular input with a closed numeric output is the canonical strength of classical machine learning — more accurate, far cheaper, and it gives you feature importances the business can act on.
This treats a tabular prediction problem as a language problem. It costs orders of magnitude more per prediction and will lose to a tree model on accuracy.
Parameter count does not transfer to tabular prediction. Task fit dominates raw scale, and this option pays the most for the least.
Nearest-neighbour retrieval is a weaker, less calibrated way to do what supervised learning does directly here, and it gives you no explanation of the prediction.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Run the three questions and this falls out immediately. Output shape: a probability — closed, numeric, discriminative. Input shape: structured rows. Knowledge location: entirely in data you already hold. Three signals, all pointing the same way.
hints: Start with question 1: what shape is the output?
A probability is a number, not free-form content. What does that tell you about the technique family?

interactionSequence.prompt: A team says: *"We'll point the model at our internal wiki so it knows our deployment procedures."* What is wrong with this sentence **as stated**?
options: Nothing — providing documents at inference time is exactly how this works
A pretrained model has no access to private data unless you build a mechanism to put that data into the request
The wiki would need to be much larger before the model could use it
The model would need to be retrained on the wiki, which is the only way to give it that knowledge

optionFeedback.feedback: Providing documents *is* the right idea, but the sentence describes the model "knowing" the wiki, which hides the retrieval system that has to be built, measured and maintained.
Correct. The knowledge gap is structural. Closing it is engineering work with its own failure modes — not a configuration setting.
Corpus size is irrelevant to the access question. A one-page wiki is equally invisible to a pretrained model.
Retraining is neither necessary nor effective here — fine-tuning teaches form and behaviour far more reliably than it injects retrievable facts. Knowledge belongs in retrieval.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is question 3 of the framework — where does the required knowledge live? — and it is the question that quietly kills the most projects. Sections 6 and 7 build the mechanism this sentence assumes already exists.

interactionSequence.prompt: A colleague argues that because neural networks are modelled on the brain, the assistant will gradually build up an understanding of your company through repeated use. Which response is most accurate?
options: Correct in principle, but it needs more usage before the understanding forms
The brain analogy is historical branding; it predicts nothing about behaviour, and the model forms no understanding of your company from use
Correct, provided the conversations are long enough for the model to consolidate them
Only true for models with very large parameter counts

optionFeedback.feedback: Repetition changes nothing, because nothing is retained between requests to accumulate.
Correct. The analogy is evocative but predicts nothing, and expecting accumulated understanding leads directly to architectural mistakes.
There is no consolidation step — longer conversations only mean more tokens resent, as section 2 will show in detail.
Parameter count does not create persistence; this substitutes one unfounded expectation for another.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The practical cost of this metaphor is that it makes people expect memory, understanding and consistent reasoning that the architecture does not provide — and then design systems around those expectations. Section 2 replaces the metaphor with the actual mechanism.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: think of one system you have worked on where someone proposed an AI feature, or where you can imagine one being proposed. **Run the three questions on it.** Where does the knowledge live, and what would that mean for what you would actually have to build?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The most useful answers usually discover that a request splits — part of it is genuinely generative, part of it is a lookup or a calculation that belongs in ordinary code. That split is the shape of most real AI features, and noticing it early is what keeps a project honest.

workedExamples.problem: A hospital procurement team says: *"We get about 300 supplier invoices a week as PDFs. We need to know, for each one, the supplier, the total, the due date, and whether the line items match our purchase order."* Classify this request and recommend an architecture.
steps: **Step 1 — What shape is the output?** Two different outputs are hiding inside one request. Supplier, total and due date are *extraction*: pulling defined fields into a defined schema, which is closed-output. The purchase-order match is a *comparison* producing a yes/no plus an explanation — the yes/no is closed, the explanation is generative.
**Step 2 — What shape is the input?** PDFs. Semi-structured, visually formatted, inconsistent across suppliers, possibly scanned. This is the hard part of the request and nobody mentioned it.
**Step 3 — Where does the required knowledge live?** Entirely in the documents plus the purchase-order database. No general world knowledge is required at all.

**Step 4 — Check whether AI is needed for all of it.** If all 300 invoices come from twelve suppliers in stable formats, template-based extraction is more accurate, cheaper and auditable — and finance functions need auditability. AI earns its place only in the long tail of irregular formats.

**Step 5 — Assign each part to the right tool.** Template extraction for known suppliers. A vision-capable model with schema-constrained output for the irregular tail. The line-item comparison against the purchase-order database in ordinary deterministic code.
workedExamples.conclusion:
The recommendation is a hybrid, and the reasoning that matters is step 5: **the model does not do the matching arithmetic — code does.** Never let a language model do arithmetic you could do in Python.

More generally: the correct answer to a request containing the word *AI* is frequently "AI for fifteen percent of it, and boring reliable code for the rest." Recognising which fifteen percent is the skill this section teaches, and you will apply it again in section 5 when deciding what a tool call may and may not do.

retrievalPractice.prompt: State the three classification questions, in order, and say what each one tells you.
Name three problems commonly assigned to language models that would be better served by another technique, and name the better technique for each.
A colleague says the frontier model at the top of the leaderboard is the safest default choice for a new project. Give two reasons that is weak evidence for your specific use case.

learningExperiences.title: The Generative Contract and What It Costs You

contentBlocks.content:
## What you will be able to do

- **`s01-o2`** — distinguish generative from discriminative approaches, describe the input/output contract of each, and state the evaluation consequence of choosing generative

This is short, and it is the idea the rest of the course leans on hardest.

## Two contracts

Be precise about the interface, because it determines everything downstream.

**The discriminative contract:** input → one of N outputs, plus a confidence score. The output space is *closed*. You can enumerate every possible answer in advance. That means you can evaluate with accuracy, precision and recall — settled, well-understood metrics. Testing is straightforward, and a regression is a number that moved.

**The generative contract:** input → an unbounded sequence of tokens. The output space is *infinite*. You cannot enumerate correct answers. Two entirely correct answers may share almost no words, so exact-match scoring punishes valid output and rewards memorised phrasing. There is no accuracy metric that works out of the box.

contentBlocks.title: Choosing generative means accepting an evaluation burden
contentBlocks.content:
This is not a minor inconvenience. It is the reason an entire section of this course is devoted to evaluation, and the reason so many teams get a great demo and then stall for six months — unable to say whether any change they make is an improvement.

Make the trade deliberately, not by default. Sometimes the right move is to reshape a request so that part of it becomes a closed-output problem you can actually measure.

contentBlocks.caption: The two contracts side by side
rows: Output space
Closed — enumerable in advance
Unbounded
Typical metrics
Accuracy, precision, recall, F1
None available out of the box
Testing
Straightforward; a regression is a number
Requires a golden set and designed metrics
Cost per item
Usually very low
Scales with input and output tokens
Explainability
Feature importances, confidence scores
Requires citations and grounding to be engineered

interactionSequence.prompt: Which statement about the generative output contract is accurate?
options: The output space is unbounded, so standard accuracy metrics do not apply out of the box
The output space is unbounded, but accuracy can be measured normally by comparing the output to a reference answer
The output is drawn from a fixed set of labels with a confidence score
Output variation disappears once you set the temperature to zero

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. This is exactly why generative systems carry an evaluation burden that classification does not, and why measurement gets its own dedicated section later.
Two correct answers can share almost no words, so exact comparison to a reference punishes valid output and rewards memorised phrasing.
That describes the discriminative contract — the one you are choosing *against* when you pick a generative approach.
Zero temperature reduces variance but does not guarantee reproducibility across model versions, batching or hardware — and it does nothing about the unbounded output space.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Hold onto this. When you reach the evaluation section and are asked to build a golden set by hand, this is the reason: nobody handed you a metric, so you have to construct one.

interactionSequence.prompt: A retailer wants to route **40,000 customer emails per day** into eight support categories. Rank these approaches from best to worst *for this specific requirement*.
options: Fine-tuned small text classifier
Embedding-based nearest-centroid classification
Frontier language model with a well-designed classification prompt
Fine-tuning a frontier model for classification

optionFeedback.feedback: First. Closed output space, enormous volume, cost and latency dominate — this is the textbook fit.
Second. Cheap, fast, no training loop, slightly less accurate. A strong pragmatic choice when you want results this week.
Third. Accurate and quick to build, but at 40,000 a day the cost and latency are hard to defend. Best used to generate training labels that bootstrap option one.
Last. The highest cost and maintenance burden for a task a small model solves — paying frontier prices for a closed-output problem.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The decisive variable is **volume**. At 40 emails a day this ranking inverts: option 3 becomes the right answer and option 1 is over-engineering. The technique has no fixed rank — the constraints determine it. That is the habit worth taking from this exercise, and you will use it again for vector stores, adaptation strategies and deployment targets.
hints: Which constraint in this scenario is doing the most work? It is not accuracy.
Ask what changes if the volume were 40 per day instead of 40,000.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this ordering?

retrievalPractice.prompt: Describe the discriminative and generative output contracts, and state the single most important consequence that follows from choosing generative.

transferExercises.context: Municipal transport — a domain deliberately different from the agricultural and hospital examples used in the lecture.
transferExercises.scenario:
A city transit authority brings you five requests:

1. Predict bus bunching on route 14 twenty minutes before it happens, from live GPS and passenger-count feeds.
2. Automatically generate the plain-language accessibility description read aloud at each stop, from the stop's structured attributes.
3. Answer resident questions about fare policy, drawn from 200 pages of published tariff regulations.
4. Detect graffiti in depot CCTV stills.
5. Decide whether a specific concession-fare application is approved, given the applicant's submitted documents and the eligibility rules.
transferExercises.task:
For each request: **classify the technique family**, **state the output contract**, and **name the single biggest risk** in your chosen approach.

Where the honest answer is *"this shouldn't use AI"*, say so and name what should be used instead. At least one of these five is a trap.
successCriteria: Identifies request 1 as classical machine learning on time-series telemetry, with a closed numeric output
Identifies request 2 as template or rules-based — the output is fully determined by structured attributes, so a generative model adds variance and risk for no benefit
Identifies request 3 as retrieval-augmented generation, and notes that the model has no access to the tariff regulations without it
Identifies request 4 as computer-vision classification rather than a language-model task

Recognises request 5 as the trap: an eligibility decision affecting a person's benefits should not be made by a generative model. Field extraction with AI is acceptable; the rules must be applied in deterministic code, logged, with a human in the loop
Names a risk specific to each choice rather than a generic caveat about accuracy

learningExperiences.title: Environment Setup and Your First Call

contentBlocks.content:
## What you will be able to do

- **`s01-o4`** — configure a working environment with proper secrets handling, and execute a first successful model call

Everything you build for the next ten sections runs from here, so it is worth doing properly once.

## The setup

1. Create an isolated Python environment (`venv` or `uv`), Python 3.10 or later.
2. Install one model provider SDK and `python-dotenv`.
3. Create a `.env` file for your API key. **Add `.env` to `.gitignore` *before* you put the key in it.**
4. Write `first_call.py` that loads the key from the environment — never a literal in source — sends one prompt, and prints the response.
5. Run it **three times with the same prompt.** Record whether the outputs are identical.
6. Print the token usage from the response metadata and note it in a file called `cost-log.md`.

You will keep adding to `cost-log.md` for the whole course.

contentBlocks.caption: Verify the ignore rule actually matched — an untested .gitignore is not a control
contentBlocks.content:
# Should print the matching rule and the filename.
# Silence means the file is NOT ignored and your key is one commit from public.
git check-ignore -v .env

contentBlocks.title: Do this before the key exists, not after
contentBlocks.content:
Adding `.gitignore` after committing a key does not remove the key from history. Rotating a leaked key is quick; discovering the leak six months later in a public repository is not.

This is the first of several places in the course where a governance decision is made in code, early, and is expensive to reverse.

## One more file: `decision-log.md`

Create it now, in a personal repository, even though it will be nearly empty.

Every self-guided exercise in this course appends to it. In the final section it becomes a **graded portfolio artifact** — and it is the single highest-signal item a hiring reviewer looks at, because it shows judgement rather than completion.

Starting it now rather than reconstructing it at the end is the difference between a real record and an obviously invented one. Real decision logs contain reversals. Invented ones do not.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before you run it three times: **will the three outputs be identical?** Commit to yes or no, and give your reasoning in one sentence.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Whatever you observed, hold the question open. You now have an observation without an explanation — which is the ideal state in which to start the next section, where you will trace exactly where the variation enters and why turning the temperature to zero does not fully remove it.
hints: Consider whether anything in the process involves a choice among several plausible options.

interactionSequence.prompt: Record your first token count and what that single call would cost at 10,000 calls a day. What surprised you — the number itself, or how little you had previously thought about it?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Most developers have never costed a single API call before building on one. In section 2 you will do this arithmetic properly for a realistic workload, and discover that input tokens usually dominate the bill by a wide margin — which determines where every later optimisation should go.

selfGuidedExercise.objective: Apply the three classification questions to a real request from someone who is not you, and record the result as the first entry in your decision log.
selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: A genuine "could we use AI for this?" conversation happening outside the course — at work, in an open-source project, in a community group you belong to, or in a public forum thread.
instructions: Over the next two weeks, find one real conversation where someone proposes an AI solution to a problem.
Write down the request **in the requester's own words**, before you start analysing it. The original phrasing usually contains the assumption worth examining.
Run the three classification questions on it: output shape, input shape, knowledge location.
Write a one-paragraph recommendation — including, explicitly, the parts that should **not** use AI.
Share it with the requester if that is appropriate, and record how they responded. Their reaction is data about how this reasoning lands with non-specialists.
Save the whole thing as the first entry in `decision-log.md`.
materialsOrPrerequisites: A personal git repository containing `decision-log.md`
Access to any forum, workplace or community where AI proposals actually get made
reflectionPrompts: Which of the three questions was hardest to answer for this particular request, and why?
Did the request split into an AI part and a non-AI part? What proportion was actually AI?
If you shared it: what did the requester find most surprising or least convincing?
Would you have given the same recommendation before this section? If not, what changed?

verification.mode: self-assessment against criteria, with the decision-log entry as the artifact
selfAssessmentCriteria: The request is recorded verbatim before any analysis
All three classification questions are answered explicitly, not implied
The recommendation names at least one component that should not use AI
The reasoning appeals to output shape, input shape or knowledge location — not to which model is best
The entry is honest about uncertainty where you had some

sections.title: Inside LLMs: From Tokens to Trained Models
sections.description: Build an accurate mental model of what happens between a prompt and a response, and why language models fail the way they do. This is the only theory-heavy section in the course, and it is here because every difficult bug in the next nine sections has its explanation in it.

learningObjectives.description: Trace an input string through tokenization, embedding, attention and next-token sampling, and explain the effect of temperature and top-p on output.
Describe the pretraining → supervised fine-tuning → preference-optimization pipeline and attribute specific observed model behaviours (refusals, sycophancy, formatting habits) to specific stages.
Explain hallucination as a consequence of the generation mechanism and predict which prompt conditions raise its likelihood.
Compare candidate models across capability, context window, latency, cost per million tokens, licensing and privacy posture, and recommend one for a stated requirement set.
Calculate token counts and projected cost for a realistic request pattern.

motivationHooks.prompt:
In a few weeks you will ship a system, and a colleague will report that it is *"randomly making things up about our refund policy."* Someone will ask you whether it can be fixed.

Your answer depends entirely on whether you understand what the model is doing. If you think it looks things up, you will file a bug and wait for a provider fix that is never coming. If you understand that it is predicting tokens, you will know immediately that the fix is architectural — constrain the input, ground the output, verify before display — and you will start building the right thing that afternoon.

That is the whole reason this section exists. Learn the mechanism once, deeply, and you stop being surprised.

At the end of the last section you ran the same prompt three times and recorded whether the outputs were identical.

**Now commit to an explanation.** Where in the process does the variation come from — and if you set the temperature to zero to remove it, would the system then be fully deterministic?

Write down your answer to both parts. You will check it against the mechanism at the end of this section, and the second half is the one most people get wrong.

**Where it comes from:** step 5, sampling. The model produces a score for every possible next token, those scores become probabilities, and then one token is *chosen*. That choice is where non-determinism enters — not in attention, not in the weights, which are fixed.

**And the second half:** no. Temperature zero makes the model take the highest-scoring token nearly every time, which removes most variation. It does not guarantee reproducibility across model versions, request batching or hardware. If you predicted full determinism, you are in good company — it is the single most common wrong assumption developers carry into production, and in section 5 you will see a team try to satisfy an auditor with it.

sectionSummary.content:
You should now believe the following about how these systems behave:

**Generation is prediction, one token at a time, with no plan.** Each token is chosen given everything before it, and the model is committed to whatever it has already said. It cannot backspace — which is why a model that starts an answer wrongly will often construct a plausible continuation rather than reverse.

**Fabrication and recall are the same operation.** The model has no internal flag distinguishing *I am recalling* from *I am constructing*. Where the training distribution is underconstrained — private data, recent events, specific identifiers — plausible-looking output is exactly what the mechanism produces. This is not a defect awaiting a patch.

**Behaviours trace to training stages, and the distinction is practical.** Sycophancy comes from preference optimization and is sometimes addressable by prompting. Not knowing your internal tooling is a pretraining data limit and never is.

**The API is stateless.** Apparent memory is your code resending the transcript, which is why conversation cost grows faster than linearly and why "the model forgot" is a bug in your application.

**Requirements select models; leaderboards do not.** Confidentiality, context length, latency and licensing routinely eliminate candidates that benchmark higher.
keyTakeaways: Trace: tokenize → embed → attend → logits → sample → repeat. Non-determinism enters at sampling.
Hallucination is the generation mechanism operating where the distribution underconstrains the answer.
Five conditions raise fabrication risk: private or post-cutoff information, requested identifiers, presupposed facts, rare topics, pressure toward confidence.
Pretraining gives knowledge; SFT gives the assistant format; preference optimization gives tone, refusals and sycophancy.
Statelessness explains both apparent forgetting and super-linear conversation cost.
Input tokens usually dominate the bill — check the ledger before optimising anything.

learningExperiences.title: One Sentence, Six Steps

contentBlocks.content:
## What you will be able to do

- **`s02-o1`** — trace an input string through tokenization, embedding, attention and sampling, and explain what temperature and top-p change
- **`s02-o3`** — explain hallucination as a consequence of the mechanism, and predict which prompt conditions raise its likelihood

This is the densest twenty minutes in the course. It pays for itself in section 7.

terms.definition: The unit a model reads and writes — roughly a word fragment. Billing, context limits and latency are all measured in tokens, not words.
The deterministic, model-specific algorithm that splits text into tokens.
The mechanism letting the model weigh how much each earlier token matters when predicting the next one. The core innovation of the transformer.
Raw scores the model produces for every possible next token, before they are turned into probabilities.
A sampling parameter. Low values concentrate probability on the top candidates; high values flatten the distribution, producing more varied output.
Nucleus sampling: restricting selection to the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities sum to *p*, cutting off the unlikely tail.
Fluent, confident output that is not true. Not a distinct mode — the same mechanism as correct generation, operating where the training distribution underconstrains the answer.
The property that a model retains nothing between API calls. Apparent memory is the prior transcript being resent.

contentBlocks.content:
## Watch one sentence become a prediction

Take the input:

> `The publisher rejected the manuscript because it was too`

**Step 1 — Tokenization.** The string is split into tokens. Common words are single tokens; unusual ones fragment. This is why a prompt full of product SKUs, UUIDs or non-English text costs more than an English paragraph of the same character count. Whitespace and punctuation are tokens too.

**Step 2 — Embedding.** Each token becomes a vector — a long list of numbers. Position information is added, because otherwise the model would have no notion of order.

**Step 3 — Attention, repeated.** Through dozens of layers, each token's representation is updated by attending to the others. By the end, the representation at the final position encodes a great deal about the whole sentence: that a publisher is the actor, that a rejection happened, that the word after *too* should be an adjective describing a manuscript from a publisher's point of view.

**Step 4 — Logits.** The model outputs a score for every token in its vocabulary — perhaps 100,000 of them. After *too*, `long` scores high, `derivative` scores well, `purple` scores low, `the` scores very low.

**Step 5 — Sampling.** Scores become probabilities. Then one token is **chosen**. This is the step people forget, and it is where non-determinism enters. At temperature 0 the model takes the highest-scoring token nearly every time. At temperature 1.0 it samples proportionally, so a token with 8% probability gets picked roughly 8% of the time.

**Step 6 — Repeat.** The chosen token is appended and the entire process runs again, from the beginning, for the next token.

contentBlocks.title: There is no plan
contentBlocks.content:
No sentence is drafted in advance. Each token is chosen given everything before it, and the model is committed to whatever it has already said.

This explains a behaviour you will see constantly: a model that starts an answer confidently and then, rather than reversing, constructs a plausible continuation of a claim it should never have made. **It cannot backspace.**

## Why this makes hallucination structural

Here is the key insight, and it is worth reading twice.

**The model uses exactly the same mechanism to produce a true statement and a false one.**

Ask which year the Treaty of Westphalia was signed and the training distribution concentrates strongly on 1648 — the highest-probability continuation is correct. Ask for the section number of your company's remote-work policy and the training distribution contains nothing about your company. The model still produces the most plausible-looking continuation, because producing a plausible continuation is the only thing it does. `Section 4.2` looks exactly like a policy section number. It is fluent, well-formed and invented.

The model has no internal flag distinguishing *I am recalling* from *I am constructing*. Both are the same operation.

**Therefore:** hallucination is not a defect awaiting a patch. It is the generation mechanism operating where the distribution is underconstrained. You mitigate it by changing the conditions — supplying the true information in the prompt, constraining the output format, requiring citations, permitting abstention. You do not mitigate it by asking the model to be more accurate.

contentBlocks.caption: Five conditions that raise fabrication risk — treat this as a practical checklist
rows: Private or post-cutoff information
Nothing in the distribution constrains the answer
Your internal API, last week's incident, a client's contract terms
Specific identifiers requested
Format plausibility is easy to produce; correctness is not
Clause numbers, citations, URLs, part numbers, dates
The prompt presupposes a fact
The format implies an answer exists, so one is produced
*"What does section 7 say about overtime?"* when there is no section 7
Rare topic in training data
The distribution is thin and diffuse
Obscure local regulations, niche tooling, minority-language content
Phrasing pressures confidence
Hedging is penalised by the framing
*"Just give me the number, no caveats"*

contentBlocks.content:
## The three training stages, and the behaviour each explains

**Pretraining** — predict the next token over an enormous corpus. This produces knowledge, grammar, reasoning ability and coding skill. It also produces something not directly useful: a base model *completes* text rather than answering questions. Ask a base model a question and it may generate more questions, because that is what a list of questions looks like.

**Supervised fine-tuning** — training on curated instruction/response pairs. This installs the assistant format: you ask, it answers. Formatting habits come largely from here — the tendency toward headed sections and bulleted lists reflects what annotators wrote.

**Preference optimization** — humans compare candidate responses; the model is trained toward the preferred ones. This shapes tone, refusal behaviour and hedging. It also produces **sycophancy**: if human raters slightly preferred agreeable answers, the model learned that agreement scores well. When you push back on a correct answer and the model caves, you are seeing preference optimization, not reasoning.

Attributing behaviours to stages is practically useful. A model that will not answer a legitimate security question is exhibiting preference-optimization behaviour — often fixable by clarifying context. A model that does not know your internal API is exhibiting a pretraining data limit — **never** fixable by prompting.

## Statelessness, and why your bill grows

The API is stateless. It remembers nothing. A twenty-turn conversation is not the model recalling turn one; it is **your code resending all twenty turns as input**.

The cost consequence is stark: conversation cost grows roughly quadratically with turns, because turn *n* resends everything before it. A chat that feels free at turn three is expensive at turn thirty.

Managing context is therefore a cost and correctness discipline, not a user-experience detail. You will design a context budget in section 3 and implement one in section 5.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before reading the trace: at **which of the six steps** does the same prompt start producing different outputs on different runs? Name the step and say why.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The answer is step 5, sampling. The weights are fixed and attention is deterministic; the variation comes from *choosing* among candidate tokens once scores become probabilities. If you guessed attention or the weights, that is a very common and reasonable guess — and correcting it is the difference between chasing the wrong fix and reaching for the right one.
hints: Which step involves a choice rather than a calculation?

interactionSequence.prompt: A museum's assistant is asked for the accession number of an artefact. The museum's catalogue was never in training data. The model returns a plausibly formatted number that does not exist. What is the mechanism?
options: The model searched its training corpus and returned the closest match
The model produced the most plausible continuation, and a well-formed accession number is exactly what plausibility looks like here
The output was corrupted by a high temperature setting
The catalogue needs to be added to the model's index

optionFeedback.feedback: There is no search step at inference. Generation runs over learned weights, and nothing is being matched or looked up.
Correct. Fabrication and recall are the same operation, and format plausibility is precisely what the mechanism optimises for.
At temperature zero the model would produce a fabricated number just as confidently — only the same one every time.
Models have no index to add documents to. Supplying the catalogue requires building a retrieval system, which is sections 6 and 7.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Notice which conditions from the risk checklist are stacked here: private information the model has never seen, *and* a specific identifier requested. Both raise fabrication likelihood, and together they make it close to certain.

interactionSequence.prompt: A user complains that the assistant *"forgot"* what they said eight messages ago. What is actually happening?
options: The model's memory decays as the conversation lengthens
Your application is not resending the earlier turns, or is truncating them to fit the context window
The provider caps how many turns a single conversation may contain
The model needs fine-tuning on the conversation to retain it

optionFeedback.feedback: There is no memory to decay — nothing persists between calls at all.
Correct. Apparent memory is entirely a function of what your code puts in the request, which makes "forgetting" a context-management bug in your application.
The constraint is the token limit of a single request, which your code controls — not a turn count imposed by the provider.
Fine-tuning shapes behaviour and form, not per-conversation recall.

feedback.correctiveFeedback: The practical consequence: when a user reports forgetting, look in your own client code, not at the model. In section 5 you will implement the context budget that decides what gets kept, summarised or dropped.

interactionSequence.prompt: Which observed behaviour is best attributed to **preference optimization** rather than pretraining?
options: The model does not know your company's internal deployment tool
The model reverses a correct answer when the user insists it is wrong
The model can write working Python
The model splits rare words into several tokens

optionFeedback.feedback: That is a pretraining data limitation, and no amount of prompting fixes it — only supplying the information at request time will.
Correct. Sycophancy is learned from human raters mildly preferring agreeable responses. It is a preference-optimization artefact, not a reasoning failure.
Coding ability is acquired during pretraining on large code corpora.
That is tokenizer behaviour, fixed before any training stage begins.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The distinction is practical, not academic. Preference-optimization behaviours are sometimes addressable by clarifying context in your prompt. Pretraining data limits never are — and knowing which you are facing saves days of pointless prompt iteration.

interactionSequence.prompt: Rank these mitigations by how effectively they reduce **fabricated facts** in answers about a private document set, most to least effective.
options: Retrieve the relevant passages and require the answer to cite them
Require the model to answer "not found in the provided documents" when the passages don't support an answer
Constrain output to a schema with a required source-quote field
Lower the temperature
Instruct the model: "do not hallucinate; only state true facts"

optionFeedback.feedback: First. It supplies the missing distribution — the only intervention that gives the model the information it lacked — and makes claims checkable.
Second. Abstention converts a fabrication into a visible gap, which is a far better failure mode.
Third. Structure forces grounding and makes violations machine-detectable in code, with no human or judge needed.
Fourth. This reduces variation, not fabrication. The confident wrong answer simply becomes consistent.
Last. The model has no internal signal distinguishing recall from construction, so the instruction cannot be followed even in principle.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: One principle produces this whole ordering: mitigations that change the **information available** beat mitigations that change the **sampling**, which beat mitigations that merely **ask**. You will see the same ordering principle again for tool authorisation in section 5 and injection defence in section 8.
hints: Ask of each option: does this give the model something it did not have, or does it just request better behaviour?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this ordering?

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words, and in two sentences: explain to a non-technical colleague why the assistant confidently invented a policy clause number. Use no jargon — no *tokens*, no *distribution*, no *weights*.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
One version that works: *"It writes the most likely next words rather than looking anything up. When it has never seen our handbook, the most likely-looking thing to write is something shaped like a clause number — so that's what it writes, just as confidently as when it's right."*

You will need this explanation more often than you expect. In section 11 it becomes a stakeholder-communication skill, and being able to deliver it in ninety seconds reframes every later conversation about what the system can promise.

workedExamples.problem: A legal team's assistant is asked: *"Under section 12 of our standard supplier agreement, what is the notice period for termination for convenience?"* The assistant has no access to the agreement. Predict what it will do, and identify every risk condition present.
steps: **Step 1 — Check the risk checklist against the prompt.** Private information: yes, the agreement was never in training data. Specific identifier requested: yes, a notice period, which is a number. Presupposed fact: yes — the question assumes a section 12 exists and that it covers termination for convenience.
**Step 2 — Count the conditions.** Three of the five conditions are present simultaneously. That is not a marginal risk case; it is close to a guaranteed fabrication.

**Step 3 — Predict the specific failure.** The model will produce a well-formed, professional-sounding answer such as *"Section 12 provides for a 30-day notice period for termination for convenience."* Thirty days is the most common notice period in commercial agreements, so it is the highest-probability continuation. It is fluent, plausible and unrelated to this contract.

**Step 4 — Note the presupposition trap specifically.** Even if the agreement had been supplied and contained no section 12, the phrasing implies an answer exists. The format pressures the model to produce one. This is why an explicit abstention branch matters more than it appears to.

**Step 5 — Identify what would actually change the outcome.** Only supplying the agreement text changes the information available. Instructing the model to be careful does not. Lowering the temperature does not — it makes the fabricated answer reproducible.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**The conclusion is a habit, not a fact:** before shipping any feature, run the prompt pattern against the five risk conditions. Three or more present means you need grounding, citations and an abstention path *by design* — not as a later improvement.

This worked example is also a preview of the entire arc from here: section 3 constrains the output, section 6 finds the right passage, and section 7 requires the answer to cite it.

fadedVariant.problem: A recruitment platform's assistant is asked by a candidate: *"What was the average time-to-hire for engineering roles at TechCorp last quarter?"* The assistant has access to general web knowledge but no access to TechCorp's internal hiring data. Work through the same analysis.
givenSteps: **Step 1 — Check the risk checklist.** Private information: yes — internal hiring metrics are not published. Specific identifier requested: yes — a numeric metric. Recency: 'last quarter' is likely at or beyond the training cutoff.
**Step 2 — Count the conditions.** At least three conditions are present, putting this firmly in high-risk territory.
blankedStepPrompts: **Step 3 —** Predict the specific failure. What kind of answer will the model produce, and why is that particular value the likely one?
**Step 4 —** Identify what the phrasing presupposes, and why that raises risk further.
**Step 5 —** Name the one intervention that would actually change the outcome, and one that would not.
blankedStepAnswers: It will produce a plausible industry-typical figure — something like *"approximately 45 days"* — stated with the same fluency as a correct answer. That range is the highest-probability continuation because it reflects commonly published industry averages in the training data, which have nothing to do with TechCorp.

The question presupposes that this metric exists, is tracked, and is knowable. The format implies an answer is expected, and the model has no easy low-status way to decline unless one has been designed. Under that pressure it produces something rather than nothing.

**Would work:** supplying TechCorp's actual hiring data at request time, with a required citation and an abstention path when the data is absent. **Would not work:** instructing the model to only state verified facts — it has no internal signal separating recall from construction, so the instruction is unfollowable.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Trace the six steps from input string to next token. At which step does non-determinism enter, and why?
In one sentence using the word *distribution*, explain why hallucination is structural rather than a bug awaiting a fix.

List the five conditions that raise fabrication likelihood. Then apply them to this prompt and count how many are present: *"What's the escalation threshold in our incident response runbook for a sev-2?"*
Name the three training stages and one observed model behaviour that each explains. Then state why the distinction matters when you are deciding whether to attempt a prompt fix.
Carry-forward from section 1: state the three classification questions in order, and say which one the phrase *"the model will know our business data"* fails.

transferExercises.context: Emergency dispatch software — deliberately different from the publishing and legal examples used in the lecture.
transferExercises.scenario: A 911 dispatch software vendor wants a language model to summarise live caller transcripts into a structured incident card for responders. Calls are distressed, disfluent and full of place names, unit numbers and addresses. The vendor proposes a 40-turn conversation in which the model retains the whole call.
transferExercises.task:
Work through five questions.

1. Using the five risk conditions, list every condition present in this workload that raises fabrication likelihood.
2. For each, state one **architectural** mitigation — not a change of prompt wording.
3. Estimate the token growth pattern across the proposed 40 turns, and state the operational risk **beyond cost**.
4. The vendor's lead engineer says: *"We'll set temperature to 0 so it's deterministic and therefore auditable for legal review."* Write a two-sentence correction.
5. Name one requirement in this domain that should disqualify a purely generative approach for at least part of the pipeline, and say which part.
successCriteria: Identifies at least four risk conditions: private and real-time information, specific identifiers (addresses, unit numbers), pressure toward confident output, rare or disfluent vocabulary

Proposes architectural mitigations — retrieval against an address gazetteer, schema-constrained extraction, a mandatory abstention field, human confirmation on dispatch-critical fields — rather than prompt-wording changes
Recognises super-linear token growth from statelessness, and identifies latency as the operational risk that matters most in this domain, since latency is a safety risk here

Corrects the determinism claim: low temperature reduces variance without guaranteeing reproducibility across versions, batching or hardware, and auditability comes from logging inputs, outputs and versions
Identifies that the dispatch decision and address resolution must not be generative

learningExperiences.title: Token Math on a Real Workload

contentBlocks.content:
## What you will be able to do

- **`s02-o5`** — calculate token counts and projected cost for a realistic request pattern, and identify which side of the ledger dominates

This is arithmetic, and it is the arithmetic that decides where every optimisation in section 10 should go.

terms.definition: The maximum number of tokens, input plus output, the model can process in a single request. A hard architectural limit.
The standard pricing unit, quoted separately for input and output. Output is typically several times more expensive per token — which is not the same as being the larger share of your bill.

contentBlocks.content:
## Tokens are not words

English prose runs at roughly **1.3 tokens per word**. That ratio moves a great deal by content type:

- English prose: efficient, close to the baseline
- JSON and structured data: worse — braces, quotes and field names are all tokens
- Code: worse again — indentation, punctuation and identifiers fragment heavily
- Product SKUs, UUIDs, non-English text: worst — rare strings split into many small tokens

This matters more than it sounds. A prompt full of identifiers can cost several times what a prose paragraph of the same character count costs, and the difference shows up on every single request forever.

contentBlocks.title: Read the ledger before optimising anything
contentBlocks.content:
Output tokens usually carry a higher unit price. Input tokens usually carry vastly higher volume.

In most real workloads input dominates total spend by somewhere between 5:1 and 20:1 — which means effort spent shortening outputs is effort spent on the small side of the ledger. Compute the ratio first. It takes two minutes and it redirects everything that follows.

interactionSequence.prompt:
A workload sends **40,000 input tokens** and receives **500 output tokens** per request. Input costs $3 per million; output costs $15 per million.

Before calculating: **which side do you expect to dominate the bill, and by roughly what ratio?**

feedback.elaborativeFeedback:
Input, by about 16:1. The arithmetic: input is 0.040 × $3 = **$0.12**; output is 0.0005 × $15 = **$0.0075**. The 5× higher unit price on output is completely swamped by 80× the volume on input.

Many people expect output to dominate because the per-token price is the number they remember. This is why you compute rather than recall.

interactionSequence.prompt: Given that same workload — 40,000 input and 500 output tokens per request at $3/M and $15/M — which conclusion is best supported?
options: Output cost dominates, because the output price is five times higher
Input cost dominates by roughly 16:1, so context reduction is the highest-leverage optimisation
Costs are broadly balanced, so optimise both equally
Self-hosting is clearly justified at these prices

optionFeedback.feedback: Unit price is higher but volume is 80× lower: $0.12 of input against $0.0075 of output per request.
Correct. Trimming retrieved context or routing cheaply attacks the real cost driver — which is exactly the optimisation you will run in section 10.
Splitting effort evenly across a 16:1 imbalance wastes most of the effort.
Nothing here establishes sustained throughput high enough to beat API pricing once GPU capacity and operations time are counted.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Carry this forward. In section 10 you will cut a service's cost by 71% without losing quality, and almost every step will be on the input side — because that is where the money was.

interactionSequence.prompt: Think of a workload from your own job that could plausibly use a model. Estimate its input and output tokens per request and its daily volume. Which side dominates, and does that surprise you?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Two patterns recur. Document-heavy workloads — summarisation, extraction, retrieval-augmented answering — are overwhelmingly input-dominated. Generation-heavy workloads such as long-form drafting are the rare exception where output matters. Knowing which you have determines whether context trimming or output constraints are worth your time.

workedExamples.problem: A publishing house wants a tool that reads submitted manuscripts (average 90,000 words) and produces a two-page structured assessment. Roughly 200 submissions per month. Manuscripts are confidential and unpublished; contracts require they not be used for model training. A 24-hour turnaround is acceptable. Estimate the cost and recommend a selection approach.
steps: **Step 1 — Token estimate.** English runs about 1.3 tokens per word, so 90,000 words ≈ **117,000 input tokens**. Add a 700-token instruction. Output: two pages ≈ 1,000 words ≈ **1,300 tokens**. Per manuscript: ~117,700 in, ~1,300 out.
**Step 2 — Monthly volume.** 200 × 117,700 ≈ **23.5M input tokens**. 200 × 1,300 = **260,000 output tokens**.
**Step 3 — Cost at illustrative prices** of $3.00 per million input and $15.00 per million output. Input: 23.5 × $3.00 ≈ **$70.50**. Output: 0.26 × $15.00 ≈ **$3.90**. Total ≈ **$74 per month**.

**Step 4 — Interpret the total.** The cost is trivial. Any instinct to self-host to save money is wrong at this volume — the engineering time to run your own inference would exceed a decade of API fees.

**Step 5 — Interpret the ratio, which matters more.** Input dominates by roughly **18:1**. If a cheaper first pass could identify the 30% of manuscripts warranting full analysis, cost drops proportionally. That is the routing pattern you will implement in section 10.

**Step 6 — Apply the non-cost constraints.** Confidentiality and the contractual no-training term are decisive here, not price. The selection question becomes: which providers offer a zero-retention, no-training tier with contractual backing? That eliminates some options regardless of benchmark score. Context window matters too — 117,000 tokens in one request rules out short-context models, though chunked processing is an alternative.
workedExamples.conclusion:
**The winning model here is chosen on privacy posture and context window, with cost as a rounding error and benchmark rank barely relevant.**

Requirements select models. Leaderboards do not. Note also that the two most useful outputs of this analysis — that self-hosting is wrong and that routing is the lever — both came from arithmetic that took five minutes.

fadedVariant.problem: A property management company wants to extract structured data from tenancy agreements: average 6,000 words each, 4,000 agreements to process in a one-off backfill, then about 150 per month ongoing. Output is a 400-token JSON record. Agreements contain tenant personal data subject to data-protection obligations. Same illustrative prices: $3.00/M input, $15.00/M output.
givenSteps: **Step 1 — Token estimate.** 6,000 words × 1.3 ≈ 7,800 input tokens, plus a 500-token instruction ≈ **8,300 input tokens**. Output: **400 tokens**.
**Step 2 — Volume.** Backfill: 4,000 × 8,300 = **33.2M input tokens** and 4,000 × 400 = **1.6M output tokens**. Ongoing: 150 × 8,300 ≈ **1.25M input tokens** per month.
blankedStepPrompts: **Step 3 —** Compute the backfill cost and the ongoing monthly cost.
**Step 4 —** State the input-to-output cost ratio and what it implies about where optimisation effort belongs.
**Step 5 —** Identify the non-cost constraint that should actually drive model selection here, and what it rules out.
blankedStepAnswers: Input dominates by roughly **4:1** on the backfill — a narrower ratio than the publishing case because outputs here are proportionally larger relative to inputs. Optimisation still belongs on the input side, but the gap is small enough that both sides are worth a look. The more important observation is that total cost is so low that **optimisation is not worth anyone's time at all** — engineering effort belongs on extraction accuracy instead.

**Tenant personal data under data-protection obligations.** This drives everything: it constrains which providers and tiers are permissible, may impose data-residency requirements on where the request is processed, and forces decisions about redaction before ingestion and about retention in logs. It can rule out consumer tiers entirely regardless of price or benchmark performance — and, as section 10 will show, these are architectural decisions that are expensive to reverse once made.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Explain why the cost of a long conversation grows faster than linearly with the number of turns, and name one strategy that bounds it.

selfGuidedExercise.objective: Find the point at which a model stops being reliable on a topic you know expertly, and observe whether its tone changes when it crosses that line.
selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: Your own area of genuine expertise — a hobby, your job's domain, a place you have lived, a community you belong to. Somewhere you can grade the answers without looking anything up.
instructions: Pick a topic you know expertly. You must be able to judge correctness yourself — that is the whole point.

Ask a model ten questions of increasing specificity, ending with ones requiring facts almost certainly absent from training data: obscure local details, private organisational specifics, very recent events.
Record where it stops being reliable. Then record — crucially — whether its **tone** changed when it crossed that line. Could you have told from the output alone?
Ask it for citations or specific numbers on the ones it got wrong. Check whether the fabrications are structurally plausible: do the invented citations look like real citations?
Write a paragraph in `decision-log.md` on what this implies for any system you build where users cannot verify the answers themselves.
materialsOrPrerequisites: Access to any general-purpose model interface
A topic you genuinely know well
Your `decision-log.md` from section 1
reflectionPrompts: At what point did answers stop being reliable, and was there any signal in the output that you had crossed that boundary?
Were the fabrications sloppy or well-formed? What does that imply about users who cannot check?
Which of the five risk conditions were present in the questions that produced fabrication?
How would you design a system so that a user without your expertise could tell a grounded answer from an invented one?

verification.mode: self-assessment against criteria, with the decision-log entry as the artifact
selfAssessmentCriteria: At least ten questions asked, with genuinely increasing specificity
The reliability boundary is identified explicitly rather than described vaguely
The observation about tone is recorded — specifically whether confidence changed at the boundary
At least one fabricated specific (citation, number, name) is captured verbatim as evidence
The write-up connects the observation to a design implication, not just an anecdote

learningExperiences.title: Choosing a Model on Requirements, Not Rank

contentBlocks.content:
## What you will be able to do

- **`s02-o4`** — compare candidate models across capability, context window, latency, cost, licensing and privacy posture, and recommend one for a stated requirement set

The skill is knowing which constraint is actually decisive. It is rarely the one on the leaderboard.

contentBlocks.caption: The six axes — and when each one is the deciding factor
rows: Capability on *your* task
Task is genuinely hard or unusual
A task-specific eval set built from your own inputs — never a public benchmark
Context window
Single requests carry large documents
Compute your actual maximum request size, including retrieved context
Latency
User-facing interactive features
Measure p95 on realistic prompt lengths, not on toy prompts
Cost per million tokens
High volume, thin margins
Project monthly spend at realistic volume including retries
Privacy posture
Confidential, regulated or contractually restricted data
Read the terms for **your specific tier**; check retention and training use
Licensing
Open-weights models, or output used commercially
Check the actual licence text and your organisation's stated position

contentBlocks.content:
## The order matters

Apply the axes as a filter, then a comparison:

1. **Filter on hard constraints first.** Privacy posture, licensing and context window are usually binary — a candidate either satisfies them or is eliminated. Applying these first often reduces a field of ten to a field of three, before any evaluation work.
2. **Then compare survivors on your own eval set.** Not a public benchmark. Your inputs, your task, your definition of correct.
3. **Then apply cost and latency** to choose among survivors that meet the quality bar.

Doing this in the wrong order — benchmarking first, then discovering the winner fails a contractual constraint — wastes the evaluation work entirely.

contentBlocks.title: Model choice is not a one-time decision
contentBlocks.content:
Prices fall, capabilities shift, and providers deprecate. A model is a **swappable dependency**, and teams that wire a provider SDK directly into thirty call sites stop being able to switch — so they stop re-evaluating, and quietly overpay for years.

In section 5 you will build a provider abstraction before you need one. This is why.

interactionSequence.prompt: A translation agency must process client contracts that are contractually barred from being used for model training. Two candidate models differ by four points on a public reasoning benchmark. Which consideration should decide the choice?
options: The benchmark gap, since it is the only objective measure available
Whichever provider offers the larger context window
Whether the provider offers a contractually backed zero-retention, no-training tier — then task-specific evaluation among those that qualify
Whichever model is cheapest per million tokens

optionFeedback.feedback: Benchmark gaps are aggregated over tasks unlike yours and say nothing about the constraint that actually binds here.
Context window matters for long contracts, but it does not address the constraint that eliminates candidates outright.
Correct. Hard constraints filter the candidate set first; evaluation then decides among the survivors.
Price is rarely decisive at agency volumes, and it cannot override a contractual prohibition.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A useful test: hide the benchmark scores and re-solve the problem. If the answer does not change, the benchmark was never the deciding factor — which is more often than most engineers expect.

interactionSequence.prompt: A team processes 900,000 input tokens per day and proposes self-hosting an open-weights model to save money. What is the strongest objection?
options: Open-weights models are not capable enough for production use
At that volume, API cost is small relative to the GPU capacity, engineering time and on-call burden self-hosting adds
Self-hosting is prohibited by most open-weights licences
Latency will always be worse when self-hosting

optionFeedback.feedback: Capability is not the issue — many open-weights models are entirely production-capable for ordinary tasks.
Correct. Self-hosting shifts cost rather than removing it, and below a crossover throughput the shifted cost is larger.
Most open-weights licences permit self-hosting. Terms vary, but this is not the general objection.
Dedicated capacity can reduce latency. The objection here is economic, not architectural.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The right framing is a **crossover throughput**: below it, APIs win; above it, self-hosting does. Find the crossover rather than arguing from principle — and remember to include idle GPU capacity and on-call time, which are the costs people omit.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: your manager asks why you are not simply using the model that tops the current leaderboard. Answer in three sentences, without dismissing the leaderboard as worthless.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The strongest version concedes something real: leaderboards are a reasonable prior about general capability. Then it names what they cannot tell you — performance on *your* task, cost at *your* volume, and whether the provider's terms permit *your* data. Concede, then redirect to the constraint that actually binds. That structure works in most technical disagreements, not just this one.

transferExercises.context: Legal e-discovery — deliberately different from the publishing and translation examples used in the lecture.
transferExercises.scenario:
A litigation support firm must review roughly 2.4 million documents for a single case: emails, attachments, scanned correspondence and chat exports. For each document they need a relevance classification against the case's issue list, plus a short justification for any document marked relevant.

Constraints: documents are subject to legal privilege and a protective order barring disclosure to third parties; the review must complete within six weeks; the firm must be able to explain and defend its methodology in court; and opposing counsel may challenge the process. Average document length is 900 words.
transferExercises.task:
Produce a model and hosting recommendation.

1. Identify which of the six axes are **hard constraints** that filter the candidate set, and which are comparison criteria. Justify the split.
2. Estimate token volume and cost across the full review at $3/M input and $15/M output. Show your arithmetic.
3. This volume is unusual for this course. Determine whether it crosses the self-hosting threshold, and state what additional information you would need to be confident.
4. The relevance classification is a closed-output task and the justification is generative. Explain why that distinction should change your architecture, and what you would do differently for each part.
5. *"Defensible in court"* is a requirement this course has not covered directly. State what it implies about logging, reproducibility and human review — and explain why setting temperature to zero does not satisfy it.
6. Give your recommendation in a form you could hand to a partner: the choice, the two rejected alternatives, and the constraint that decided it.
successCriteria: Correctly identifies privilege and the protective order as hard filters applied before any evaluation, alongside licensing
Shows token arithmetic: roughly 1,170 tokens per document × 2.4M documents ≈ 2.8B input tokens, and reaches a total in the region of $8,000–9,000 at the stated input price plus output costs

Recognises that this volume plausibly crosses the self-hosting crossover, and identifies the missing information — sustained throughput required to hit six weeks, available GPU capacity, engineering time, and whether privilege permits any hosted option at all

Splits the architecture: a small fine-tuned or embedding-based classifier for relevance at this volume, with generative justification only for the subset marked relevant — reducing generative calls by an order of magnitude

Identifies that defensibility requires full logging of inputs, outputs, model versions and parameters, sampling-based human review with measured agreement, and a documented methodology — and explains that temperature zero does not guarantee reproducibility across versions, batching or hardware, so it is not an audit control
Delivers a recommendation naming the decisive constraint rather than the highest-scoring model

sections.title: Prompt and Context Engineering as an Engineering Discipline
sections.description: Treat prompts as versioned, testable specifications rather than incantations. Build the regression-testing habit and the harness that carries forward into evaluation and deployment gating later in the course.

learningObjectives.description: Construct prompts using explicit role, task, constraint and output-format specification for a defined task.
Apply decomposition, few-shot exemplars and reasoning-elicitation techniques, and identify which is appropriate for a given failure mode.
Enforce machine-parseable output through schema specification and validation, with a defined fallback path on violation.
Build a small prompt regression set and use it to compare two prompt variants on measured pass rate rather than impression.
Diagnose degradation caused by excessive or poorly ordered context and restructure the input to remedy it.

motivationHooks.prompt:
Most developers learn prompting by trial and error, land on something that works, ship it — and then three weeks later it silently breaks. A different model version, a slightly different input distribution, a colleague edits one word. Nobody can tell what changed or whether the "fix" made things worse.

The difference between a hobbyist and a professional here is not better wording. It is that the professional treats a prompt as a **versioned specification with a test suite** — exactly like any other piece of logic in the codebase. That is the whole of this section, and it is the earliest point in the course where you build something you keep: the regression harness you write today gets reused when you evaluate a full RAG pipeline, and again when you gate a deployment in CI.

Later in this section you will see two versions of the same extraction prompt. Version 4 adds two few-shot exemplars that Version 3 lacks, at a cost of 340 extra tokens on every single call — a real, permanent line item on the bill.

**Before you see the measurement: do you expect Version 4 to be worth its extra cost, across the whole workload?** Answer yes or no, and say what evidence would change your mind.

The honest answer is: **neither version is the right thing to ship everywhere.** Version 4's entire measured gain concentrates on one subset of inputs — the ones Version 3 already struggled with — and is roughly flat everywhere else. Paying the extra 340 tokens on every call, including the 80% of calls where it buys nothing, is a bad trade.

The real answer, invisible until you measured in subsets rather than in aggregate, is to **route**: cheap detection sends the hard subset to Version 4 and everything else to Version 3. If you answered a flat yes or no, you are in good company — the interesting finding here was never "which version is better," it was *where* the benefit was concentrated, and that only shows up when you measure by subset.

sectionSummary.content:
You should now believe the following about prompts:

**Three things make a prompt work, and nothing else does.** Information the model needs, constraints that close off wrong answers, and demonstrations where prose describes a mapping poorly. Every genuinely useful prompting technique supplies one of these three. If a technique supplies none of them, it is phrasing, not engineering.

**Diagnose the failure before choosing the fix.** Format drift wants a schema. Invented categories want an enumeration. Multi-step errors want decomposition or reasoning elicitation. Tone and edge-case misjudgement wants exemplars targeted at exactly those cases. Applying the wrong remedy wastes tokens and can make things worse.

**More context is not better context.** Distraction from irrelevant material, position effects that bury material in the middle of a long input, and straightforward cost and latency all argue for curation over accumulation.

**A prompt change is not evidence until it is measured against a regression set.** Single-sample impressions — "it looks better in the playground" — cannot tell you whether a change helped or what it silently broke. You now have a harness that answers that question, and you will extend it rather than rebuild it for the rest of the course.
keyTakeaways: Prompts work through information, constraint and demonstration — nothing else moves the needle.
Match the remedy to the diagnosed failure mode; there is no universal fix.
Design outputs so correctness is mechanically checkable wherever possible — a verbatim-quote requirement is worth more than it looks.
More context degrades accuracy through distraction and position effects, in addition to raising cost.
A regression set with a measured pass rate is what turns a prompt change from an impression into evidence.
Measuring in subsets, not just in aggregate, is often what reveals the real fix.

furtherReading.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
furtherReading.citation: Liu, N. F., Lin, K., Hewitt, J., Paranjape, A., Bevilacqua, M., Petroni, F., & Liang, P. (2023). Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts.
