furtherReading.rationaleNote: The empirical source for the position-effect claim in this section — accuracy on facts placed in the middle of a long context measurably drops relative to facts placed at the start or end. Read the figures if you want the evidence behind the ordering advice.

furtherReading.title: Anthropic Prompt Engineering Overview
furtherReading.citation: Anthropic. Prompt Engineering Overview. Claude Docs.
furtherReading.author: Anthropic
furtherReading.rationaleNote: A concrete, technique-by-technique reference for role framing, examples, output formatting and reasoning elicitation, organised the same way this section teaches them: by what problem each one solves.

learningExperiences.title: Specification Beats Phrasing

contentBlocks.content:
## What you will be able to do

- **`s03-o1`** — construct prompts using explicit role, task, constraint and output-format specification
- **`s03-o2`** — apply decomposition, few-shot exemplars and reasoning elicitation, matched to the failure mode that calls for each
- **`s03-o3`** — enforce machine-parseable output with a bounded fallback path

One prompt, four revisions. Watch *why* each change works, not just what changed.

terms.definition: Instructions supplied separately from user input, setting persistent role and constraints for the request.
A worked input/output pair included in the prompt to demonstrate the desired mapping. Zero-shot means none are given.
Splitting one complex request into several simpler chained requests, each independently checkable.
Instructing the model to work through intermediate steps before answering, which improves multi-step accuracy.
Requiring output to conform to a declared structure (e.g. JSON Schema), ideally enforced by the API rather than requested in prose.

contentBlocks.content:
## One prompt, four revisions

A restaurant group wants to turn free-text customer feedback into structured records.

**Version 1.** `Analyse this review: {review}`

Output is a paragraph of prose, differently shaped every time. Unparseable. The failure: no output contract was specified at all.

**Version 2.** `You are a customer experience analyst. Extract the sentiment, the issues mentioned, and whether the customer intends to return. Review: {review}`

Better — role and task are specified. But *issues* is undefined, so the model invents its own taxonomy, differently per review. Output is still prose.

contentBlocks.caption: Version 3 — constraints and a declared format
contentBlocks.content:
Extract structured data from a restaurant review.

Categories (use ONLY these): food_quality, service_speed, staff_attitude,
cleanliness, value, atmosphere, other

Return JSON:
{
  "sentiment": "positive" | "mixed" | "negative",
  "issues": [{"category": <one of the above>, "quote": "<exact text from review>"}],
  "return_intent": "yes" | "no" | "unclear"
}

Rules:
- "quote" must be text copied verbatim from the review.
- If the review does not indicate return intent, use "unclear". Do not infer.
- If no issues are raised, return an empty array.

Review: {review}

Three specific things happened, and each targets a distinct failure:

- **The closed category list** eliminates taxonomy drift. The model can no longer invent `portion_size` on review 400.
- **The verbatim quote requirement** makes fabrication detectable in code: you can assert the quote is a substring of the input. This is a general and underused technique — *require output that can be mechanically verified against the input.*
- **The explicit "unclear" branch and the empty-array case** remove the pressure to produce something. Unhandled edge cases are where models invent, because the format implies an answer is expected.

**Version 4.** Add two few-shot exemplars — one sarcastic review, one mentioning several issues at once — because those are the two cases Version 3 gets wrong.

That is the key discipline: **you add examples in response to observed failures, not preemptively.** Each exemplar costs tokens on every call forever. Examples are for demonstrating a mapping that prose describes poorly — tone judgements, edge-case handling, formatting subtleties.

contentBlocks.title: What actually makes prompts work
contentBlocks.content:
Strip away the folklore and three things determine reliability:

1. **Information.** Does the prompt contain what is needed to produce the answer?
2. **Constraint.** Have you closed off the wrong answers?
3. **Demonstration.** Where prose fails to convey the mapping, show it.

Notice what is absent: magic words. Techniques that survive contact with measurement do so because they add information, constraint or demonstration — not because of their wording. When you read a prompting tip, ask which of the three it supplies. If none, ignore it.

contentBlocks.caption: Diagnose first, then pick a technique — applying the wrong remedy wastes tokens
rows: Output shape varies between calls
Schema constraint, ideally API-enforced
Model invents categories or labels
Closed enumeration in the prompt
Correct on simple inputs, wrong on multi-step ones
Reasoning elicitation, or decomposition into chained calls
Correct in isolation, wrong in a long document
Context reduction and reordering
Misjudges tone, sarcasm, or edge cases
Few-shot exemplars covering exactly those cases
Fabricates specifics
Retrieval, verbatim-quote requirements, explicit abstention branch
Fine most of the time, occasionally catastrophic
You have an evaluation problem, not a prompt problem

contentBlocks.title: That last row matters more than it looks
contentBlocks.content: If you cannot say *how often* something fails, you cannot tell whether your change helped. This is the seed of a habit the rest of this section builds into a harness, and that section 7 turns into a full evaluation suite.

interactionSequence.prompt: A prompt extracting fields from ferry timetables produces correct values but invents its own category labels, differently on each run. Which fix targets this failure specifically?
options: Add a closed enumeration of permitted category values to the prompt
Ask the model to be more consistent and precise
Raise the number of few-shot exemplars to ten
Lower the temperature to zero

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Taxonomy drift is an unconstrained degree of freedom, and enumeration closes it outright rather than reducing its frequency.
This adds no information, constraint or demonstration — it is phrasing rather than engineering.
Exemplars demonstrate a mapping but cannot enumerate a category set as reliably as stating it, and they cost tokens on every call forever.
This makes label choice consistent within a run but does not prevent an invented taxonomy from being used consistently.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Run this through the three-thing test: enumeration supplies a **constraint**. Consistency instructions supply nothing checkable. That difference is the whole diagnosis.

interactionSequence.prompt: Which prompt design choice most directly enables **free, automatic** detection of fabricated content in an extraction task?
options: Requiring every extracted claim to include a verbatim quote from the source text
Instructing the model to be accurate and avoid making things up
Setting temperature to 0
Using a larger model

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. A substring assertion in code catches invention with no human review and no judge model — this is the technique from Version 3, generalised.
The model has no internal signal separating recall from construction, so it cannot comply with this instruction.
This makes output more consistent, which can make a fabrication reproducible rather than absent.
It may fabricate less often, but you still have no mechanical way to detect when it does.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Design your outputs so most of your evaluation is free. This one design decision — require verbatim quotes — will reappear in section 7's RAG pipeline and section 8's agent tool results doing exactly the same job.

interactionSequence.prompt: A classification prompt is correct on ordinary inputs but wrong on sarcastic ones. Which remedy fits the failure mode best — and why do the other three not fit?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Few-shot exemplars showing sarcastic inputs with their correct labels. Sarcasm is a mapping prose describes poorly — demonstration is exactly the tool for it. Reasoning elicitation helps multi-step failures, not a single tone judgement. A stricter schema fixes shape problems, and the shape here is already fine. More context about the business adds tokens and distraction without addressing the specific mapping being missed.
hints: Which of the three things — information, constraint or demonstration — does sarcasm detection actually need?

interactionSequence.prompt: Think of a prompt you have written, for this course or elsewhere, that did not work as expected. In your own words: which of the three things — information, constraint, demonstration — was missing, and how would Version 3's technique (a closed enumeration, a verbatim requirement, an explicit null branch) have caught it?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Most failures people report here turn out to be missing constraint — an unstated assumption about the output shape that the model had no way to know. That is the single most common gap, and it is also the cheapest to fix.

workedExamples.problem: A freight company wants delivery-exception emails converted into structured incident records: carrier, tracking number, exception type, and whether a claim should be filed. Design the prompt from Version 1 quality to Version 3 quality in one pass, and identify the specific failure each design choice prevents.
steps: **Step 1 — Start from the naive version and predict its failure.** `Extract the incident details from this email: {email}` will produce prose, differently shaped every time, for the same reason Version 1 failed the restaurant task: no output contract exists.

**Step 2 — Add role and task.** State that the reader is a claims analyst extracting structured incident data. This narrows tone and framing but still leaves *exception type* undefined — the model will invent its own categories across emails, exactly as *issues* did in Version 2.

**Step 3 — Close the categorical fields.** Enumerate exception types explicitly: `damaged`, `delayed`, `lost`, `wrong_address`, `refused`, `other`. This is a **constraint** and it eliminates taxonomy drift outright.

**Step 4 — Require verbatim evidence for the tracking number and carrier name.** These are exact identifiers, not judgements — require them quoted verbatim from the email, and assert the substring relationship in code after the call. This makes fabricated tracking numbers mechanically detectable, at zero ongoing cost.

**Step 5 — Add the null branches.** Some emails will not clearly state whether a claim should be filed. Add an explicit `"unclear"` value and instruct the model not to infer it. Without this branch, the format's implicit pressure to produce *something* will manufacture a yes or no.

**Step 6 — Decide what does NOT belong here yet.** No few-shot exemplars are added at this stage, because no specific failure has been observed to justify their token cost. That decision is deferred until measurement — the next experience — reveals whether one is needed.
workedExamples.conclusion: The design choices map one-to-one onto failure modes: role/task narrows framing, enumeration prevents taxonomy drift, verbatim requirements make fabrication checkable, and explicit null branches remove invented-answer pressure. **Nothing here was a phrasing improvement — every change added information, constraint, or a mechanically verifiable property.** That is the whole discipline, applied to a new domain.

fadedVariant.problem: An HR team wants exit-interview transcripts converted into structured records: department, primary reason for leaving, whether the departure was voluntary, and whether the employee would recommend the company. Apply the same design process.
givenSteps: **Step 1 — Predict the naive failure.** `Summarise the key points from this exit interview: {transcript}` will produce prose, unparseable and differently shaped every time — the Version 1 failure again.
blankedStepPrompts: **Step 2 —** Add role and task framing. What is still left undefined after this step, and what failure will it cause?
**Step 3 —** Which field(s) need a closed enumeration, and what specific values would you propose for *primary reason for leaving*?
**Step 4 —** Is there a field here that calls for a verbatim-quote requirement, the way tracking numbers did in the worked example? If yes, which, and why. If no, explain why not.
**Step 5 —** Which field needs an explicit null or unclear branch, and what invented-answer risk does it prevent?
**Step 6 —** Would few-shot exemplars be justified at this stage? Answer using the rule from the worked example, not a general impression.
blankedStepAnswers: Role and task narrow the framing, but *primary reason for leaving* is still open-ended free text, which means it will be phrased differently across every transcript — impossible to aggregate or report on later, the same taxonomy-drift failure as *issues* in the restaurant example.

*Primary reason for leaving* needs enumeration. Proposed values: `compensation`, `management`, `career_growth`, `relocation`, `work_life_balance`, `role_mismatch`, `other`. *Whether voluntary* and *would recommend* are already naturally closed (yes/no/unclear) and do not need a custom enumeration.

Yes — a quote supporting the classified *reason for leaving* should be required verbatim from the transcript. Unlike a tracking number this is not a pure identifier, but requiring the supporting quote still makes the classification checkable: you can verify the quote exists in the transcript, even though you cannot verify the classification itself is correct without a human label.

*Would recommend the company* needs an explicit `"unclear"` branch, because many transcripts will not directly address it. Without the branch, the model will infer a yes or no from tone, which is exactly the kind of invented answer the null branch exists to prevent.

No — not yet. Per the worked example's rule, exemplars are added in response to *observed* failures, not preemptively. At this stage no failure has been measured, so adding exemplars now would be paying token cost against a guess rather than evidence. That decision is made after running the design against real transcripts, which is what the next experience does.

retrievalPractice.prompt: State the three things that actually make prompts work. For a given prompting tip you read online, how do you decide whether it is real?
Reconstruct the failure-mode-to-remedy table from memory: give at least four distinct failure modes and the technique that targets each.
Carry-forward from section 1: describe the discriminative and generative output contracts, and state the evaluation consequence of choosing generative.

learningExperiences.title: Context Engineering: Why More Can Hurt

contentBlocks.content:
## What you will be able to do

- **`s03-o5`** — diagnose degradation caused by excessive or poorly ordered context, and restructure the input to remedy it

The intuition that a bigger context window means you should fill it is wrong, and expensively so.

terms.definition: The deliberate allocation of your token limit across instructions, examples, retrieved data and conversation history.
The tendency for material at the very start and very end of a long input to influence output more than material in the middle.

contentBlocks.content:
## Three costs accumulate

- **Distraction.** Irrelevant passages compete for attention. A model given ten documents where two are relevant does measurably worse than one given only the two.
- **Position effects.** Material buried mid-input has less influence than material at the beginning or end. A crucial constraint at token 40,000 of 60,000 may effectively not be there.
- **Cost and latency.** Recall from section 2: input tokens usually dominate the bill, and long inputs are slower — which users feel directly.

Practical rules: put instructions at the start, put the most important retrieved material closest to the question, put the actual question last. Cut aggressively — removing three irrelevant documents typically improves accuracy more than any rewording. Track your context budget explicitly rather than letting history accumulate.

contentBlocks.title: The context window is a capacity, not a target
contentBlocks.content: Having 200,000 tokens of room does not mean 200,000 tokens is the right amount to send. This is the same mistake as filling a truck to its maximum legal weight regardless of what you are actually shipping — capacity and correct usage are different questions entirely.

interactionSequence.prompt: A prompt works reliably on short documents but degrades on 30-page ones. Before reading further: what is your first hypothesis, and what would you try first?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The common first instinct is to move to a model with a larger context window. That treats the symptom as a capacity problem. But the document already fits — the problem is that irrelevant material degrades attention regardless of how much room is left. A bigger window makes this easier to worsen, not better.
hints: Does the document currently fit within the model's context window at all? If yes, is capacity really the constraint?

interactionSequence.prompt: A prompt works reliably on short documents but degrades badly on 30-page ones. What is the first thing to try?
options: Reduce and reorder the context — cut irrelevant sections, and place instructions first and the question last
Move to a model with a larger context window
Add "pay close attention to the whole document" to the prompt
Raise the temperature so the model considers more possibilities

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. This targets distraction and position effects directly, and reduces cost and latency at the same time.
The document already fits; the problem is that irrelevant material degrades attention, which a bigger window makes easier to worsen.
This adds no information, constraint or demonstration — it is phrasing, not engineering.
Temperature governs sampling variation and has no bearing on attention over long inputs.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This exact diagnosis reappears in section 6 as chunking, where the same principle — cut what is irrelevant before you tune anything else — turns out to be the highest-leverage fix in retrieval systems too.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: explain to a teammate why sending your entire 90-page policy manual in every request is a worse idea than it sounds, using at least two of the three costs from this section.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong version names distraction (most of the manual is irrelevant to any given question) and cost (paying to resend 90 pages on every call), and proposes retrieving only the relevant section instead — which is exactly what sections 6 and 7 build.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name three distinct reasons that adding more context to a prompt can reduce output quality.
Carry-forward from section 2: give the one-sentence structural explanation of hallucination, using the word 'distribution'.

learningExperiences.title: Measuring a Prompt Change

contentBlocks.content:
## What you will be able to do

- **`s03-o4`** — build a small prompt regression set and compare two variants on measured pass rate rather than impression

This experience builds the harness you will extend, not replace, in sections 7 and 10. Build it properly once.

terms.definition: A fixed collection of inputs with expected properties, run against every prompt change to detect breakage.
A reference answer or set of required properties for a given test input.

contentBlocks.content:
## From vibes to a measured decision

**Situation.** Version 3 and Version 4 of the restaurant prompt from the last experience. Version 4 costs 340 extra tokens per call. Is it worth it? At 8,000 reviews a day that is 2.7M extra tokens a day — a real bill. "It seems better" is not a defensible basis for that spend.

**Step 1 — Build the regression set from real reviews.** 40 real reviews, deliberately over-sampling hard cases: 8 sarcastic, 8 multi-issue, 6 non-English, 6 extremely short, 12 ordinary. Real inputs, not invented ones — invented test data shares your blind spots.

**Step 2 — Define pass criteria mechanically.** For each input, assert properties, not exact strings:
- Output parses as JSON and validates against the schema.
- Every `category` is in the allowed enumeration.
- Every `quote` is a verbatim substring of the input.
- `return_intent` is `unclear` unless the review contains explicit intent (human-labelled once, for these 40).
- Sentiment matches the human label.

Four of these five are checkable in code with no human and no judge model. **Design your outputs so most of your evaluation is free** — the payoff of Version 3's schema design, arriving right on schedule.

contentBlocks.caption: The harness skeleton — roughly 30 lines. Extend this in section 7; do not rebuild it.
Step 3 — run both variants, three times each, to see variance as well as means
rows: Schema valid
Quote verbatim
Sentiment correct
Sentiment correct, sarcastic subset
Return intent correct
Tokens/call

contentBlocks.title: These numbers are illustrative
contentBlocks.content:
The figures in this table are a worked example, not a benchmark. Your own pass rates will depend entirely on your task, your inputs and your model — a first measurement of 0.6 is not a sign something is broken.

What transfers is the **shape** of the finding: a change whose benefit concentrates in one subset, revealed only because the subset was measured separately.

**Step 4 — Interpret.** Nearly all of V4's gain is on the sarcastic subset — exactly what the exemplars targeted. Everything else moved slightly.

**Step 5 — Decide, and notice the third option.** The naive framing is "V3 vs V4, pick one." But sarcasm is 8 of 40 in the *test* set because it was deliberately over-sampled; in production it is perhaps 5% of reviews. The better design is a cheap classifier or a keyword-and-length heuristic routing only likely-sarcastic reviews to V4, and everything else to V3. Cost lands near V3's, accuracy near V4's.

contentBlocks.title: The measurement did more than pick a winner
contentBlocks.content:
It revealed *where* the benefit concentrated, which is what made the routing design visible in the first place. This is the general payoff of evaluation: you get architectural insight, not just a score.

You will do this again with retrieval in section 7 and with model routing in section 10 — same move, different system.

interactionSequence.prompt: A team ships a prompt change because "the outputs look better in the playground." What is the core problem?
options: Playground outputs use different model settings than production
Single-sample inspection of a probabilistic system cannot establish that a change helped, or reveal what it broke
Playground models are older versions
Nothing — for prompts, expert judgement is the accepted standard

optionFeedback.feedback: A real risk, but secondary — the reasoning error would remain even with identical settings.
Correct. Without a regression set and a pass rate there is no basis for the claim and no way to detect the subset that regressed.
Sometimes true, but this is not the reasoning flaw being demonstrated here.
Expert judgement designs the test set; it does not substitute for running one.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is also the seed of `ai-system-evaluation`, taught in full in section 7. Notice that the same underlying mistake — trusting an impression instead of a measured pass rate — is what `eval-m1-eyeball-the-outputs` names directly.

interactionSequence.prompt: Rank these by how much they typically improve reliability on a structured-extraction task, most to least.
options: API-enforced output schema
Closed enumerations for every categorical field
Explicit null/unknown branches for every field
Few-shot exemplars targeting measured failure cases
Politeness, emphasis, or role flourishes in the instruction wording

optionFeedback.feedback: First. Removes an entire failure class rather than reducing its frequency.
Second. Eliminates taxonomy drift across large runs.
Third. Removes the pressure to invent when data is absent.
Fourth. Effective but narrow, and costs tokens on every call — which is exactly why you measured before deciding to keep it.
Last. Supplies no information, constraint or demonstration.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The ordering follows one rule — mechanisms that make a failure *impossible* outrank those that make it *less likely*, which outrank those that merely *request* better behaviour. You will see this exact ordering principle again for tool-calling authorisation in section 5.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this ordering?

interactionSequence.prompt: The routing solution split cost and accuracy in a way neither pure V3 nor pure V4 achieved alone. What made this visible was measuring by subset rather than in aggregate. Where else in software engineering have you seen an aggregate metric hide the real answer?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A common answer: average latency hiding a p99 problem affecting a specific user segment. The pattern is the same — an aggregate number is a summary that can erase exactly the detail that matters for the decision you are trying to make.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Explain why "require a verbatim quote from the input" is a disproportionately powerful design choice, and name one other field type where the same technique would apply.

transferExercises.context: Veterinary clinic records — deliberately different from the restaurant feedback used in the lecture.
transferExercises.scenario: A veterinary group wants to convert free-text visit notes into structured records: species, presenting complaint, diagnosis, medications prescribed with dose, and follow-up interval. Vets abbreviate heavily and inconsistently — "q12h PO", "SID", "BAR" — and notation varies by clinic.
transferExercises.task:
1. Write the prompt, specifying role, task, constraints, schema, and every null/edge branch you can identify. State which fields must come from a closed enumeration and which cannot.

2. Identify the field where fabrication would be most dangerous, and design a mechanical check that catches it without a human or a judge model.

3. Which technique addresses the abbreviation problem, and why is it the right one rather than the alternatives?

4. Your regression set is 30 notes from one clinic. Name the specific way this set will mislead you, and how you would fix it.

5. A colleague proposes pasting the clinic's entire 60-page drug formulary into every request "so it knows the drugs." Give the three-part argument against, and state what to do instead.
successCriteria: Specifies species, medication route/frequency codes, and follow-up interval as candidates for closed enumeration where the value set is genuinely bounded, while presenting complaint and diagnosis are left as constrained free text with a verbatim-quote requirement

Identifies medication dose as the highest-risk fabrication field, and proposes requiring the dose as a verbatim quote from the note plus a range check against a drug table in code — never validated in the prompt itself
Selects few-shot exemplars as the technique for abbreviation handling, and justifies it as a mapping prose describes poorly rather than a constraint or information gap
Identifies that a single-clinic regression set will overfit to that clinic's shorthand and fail elsewhere, and proposes sourcing notes from multiple clinics
Argues against context-stuffing on distraction, position-effect and cost grounds, and proposes retrieval plus a deterministic dose-range check in code instead

selfGuidedExercise.objective: Find a prompt already in real use, put it under version control if it is not already, and measure it against a regression set built from real usage.
selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: A personal automation, a team's internal tool, or an open-source project's prompt file — something genuinely used by someone, not written for this exercise.
instructions: Find a prompt you or someone you know actually uses regularly.
Put it under version control if it isn't already.
Build a 15-case regression set for it from real usage, not invented inputs.
Measure the current pass rate. Record the number.
Make one improvement, re-measure, and record whether it actually helped — and whether it helped everywhere or only on a subset.
If it is someone else's prompt, offer them the harness and the numbers.
materialsOrPrerequisites: A real prompt in active use, yours or someone else's
The regression-harness pattern from this experience
Your `decision-log.md`
reflectionPrompts: What did the measured pass rate turn out to be before you changed anything? Was it higher or lower than your impression of the prompt?
Did your improvement help uniformly, or was the gain concentrated in a subset — and if so, does a routing design make sense here too?
If this was someone else's prompt: how did they react to seeing a measured number instead of an impression?
What is one case in your regression set that surprised you — an input you had not thought to test?

verification.mode: self-assessment against criteria, with the decision-log entry as the artifact
selfAssessmentCriteria: The prompt is a genuinely pre-existing one, not written for this exercise
The regression set has at least 15 real inputs with mechanically or explicitly defined pass criteria
A before-and-after pass rate is reported, not just a single measurement
The write-up states whether the improvement was uniform or concentrated in a subset
At least one case in the set was a genuine surprise, named explicitly

sections.title: AI in Your Daily Development Workflow
sections.description: Turn assistants and agentic coding tools into a measurable throughput gain without surrendering verification, and move from prompting agents to designing the loops that prompt them. Produces the course's only brownfield portfolio artifact.

learningObjectives.description: Select the appropriate mode of AI assistance (autocomplete, chat, agentic task, review) for a given engineering task and justify the choice.
Supply effective repository context (project rules/config files, file scoping, tests, conventions) to a coding assistant and demonstrate improved output quality.
Apply a verification protocol — tests, targeted review, static analysis — to AI-generated changes before merge.
Use AI tooling to comprehend an unfamiliar existing codebase and deliver a scoped, tested change to it, documenting the before/after.
Evaluate what may be shared with a given assistant under data-handling and licensing constraints, and configure exclusions accordingly.
Design and run a bounded loop that drives a coding agent against an external success signal (test suite, linter, build) without per-step human prompting.
Set iteration and cost budgets for an autonomous loop, quantify spend per completed task, and define the escalation condition that returns control to a human.

motivationHooks.prompt:
Two developers use the same coding assistant. One reports it saves an hour a day. The other reports it costs them time. The tooling is identical.

The difference is entirely in how they use it — what they delegate, what context they supply, and how they verify. There is also a second shift underway that separates current practice from a year ago: the highest-leverage skill is no longer writing a good prompt for an agent, but **designing the loop the agent runs in** — the goal, the tools, the validation signal, the stopping condition, the budget. You stop being the person who prompts the agent and become the person who designs the system that prompts it.

This section is also where you build your only brownfield portfolio artifact. Every other project in this course is greenfield — the easy case every candidate's portfolio already demonstrates. Integrating AI into code you did not write is the skill hiring managers most want evidence of and most rarely see.

Later in this section, a bounded agent loop is set loose on a real repository to add retry-with-backoff to 14 call sites of an external API, validated purely by a test suite and a type checker.

**Before you see what happens: if both the tests and the type checker pass at the end, does that mean the change is safe to merge?** Answer yes or no, and say what — if anything — a passing validator could still fail to catch.

**No.** In the run you are about to see, both tests and the type checker pass cleanly — and the agent has also applied retry logic to a `POST /permits/submit` endpoint that is **not idempotent**. Retrying a timed-out submission would double-file a permit. Nothing in the validator catches this, because nobody thought to encode it as a check.

The loop proved the validator passes. It did not prove the change is good. **No validator catches what you did not think to encode** — which is exactly why a designed loop reduces the verification burden, but never removes your judgement from it.

sectionSummary.content:
You should now believe the following about using AI in daily engineering work:

**Delegation works in proportion to two things:** how well you can specify the task, and how cheaply you can verify the result. Both high, delegate aggressively — ideally to a designed loop. Either low, do it yourself or narrow the scope until it isn't.

**"The AI writes it, I review it" collapses under volume.** Reviewing code you did not write is slower per line than writing it. The fix is not less assistance — it is cheaper verification: tight scope, tests as the contract, existing gates, and review weighted by risk rather than applied uniformly.

**Context is the whole game, and more is not better.** A checked-in repository context file, tight file scoping and a concrete example to imitate outperform a longer prose description every time — the same principle from section 3, in a new setting.

**A designed loop needs five things**, and one of them is load-bearing: a goal stated as a checkable condition, defined tools, an **external validator**, an enforced budget, and an escalation rule. Self-assessed completion is not evidence — it is where runaway cost and false confidence come from.

**A passing validator proves the validator passes.** It does not prove the change is good. No validator catches what nobody thought to encode, which is why your judgement stays in the loop even when your typing does not.
keyTakeaways: Delegate based on specification clarity and verification cost, not on task length or tedium.
Make verification cheap: scope tightly, use tests as the contract, lean on existing gates, review by risk.
The durable skills are specification, decomposition and verification — exercised more under disciplined delegation, not less.
A repository context file and a concrete example to imitate beat a longer prompt.
A designed loop has five elements; the external validator is the one that makes autonomy safe.
Budgets and escalation rules are enforced by your harness, never left to the agent's discretion.
A passing validator is not proof of a good change — only of a change that satisfies what you thought to check.
