learningExperiences.title: Delegation, Context and the Verification Trap

contentBlocks.content:
## What you will be able to do

- **`s04-o1`** — select the appropriate mode of assistance for a task, and justify the choice
- **`s04-o2`** — supply repository context that measurably improves output quality
- **`s04-o3`** — apply a verification protocol proportionate to risk, without re-reading every line
- **`s04-o5`** — evaluate what may be shared with an assistant under your actual data-handling terms

terms.definition: Inline suggestions as you type. Lowest latency, smallest scope, cheapest to reject.
Conversational assistance with explicit context you choose. You remain the executor.
The tool reads files, edits them, runs commands, and iterates toward a goal with limited human input.
A checked-in file stating project conventions, architecture and constraints, loaded automatically into the assistant's context.
Work inside an existing codebase with existing conventions, constraints and history. The opposite of greenfield.

contentBlocks.caption: Four tasks in a real codebase — a 180,000-line, five-year-old construction project-management application — and the mode each calls for
rows: Rename a variable across one file
Autocomplete or plain editor tooling
Delegating to an agent is slower and more expensive than doing it directly
Understand why invoicing rounds incorrectly on multi-currency projects
Chat, with relevant files attached
You want explanation, not edits — value is comprehension speed on unfamiliar code
Add retry-with-backoff to 14 call sites of an external API, consistent with existing patterns
Agentic
Mechanical, repetitive, well-specified, verifiable by tests — the sweet spot
Decide whether to introduce a queue between two services
None of the above
An architecture decision requiring team, operational and roadmap context; delegating it produces confident, context-free advice

contentBlocks.title: The pattern
contentBlocks.content: Delegation works in proportion to how well you can specify the task **and** how cheaply you can verify the result. Both high — delegate aggressively. Verification expensive or specification vague — do it yourself, or narrow the scope until it isn't.

## The verification trap

The seductive failure is: *the assistant writes the code, I review it.* This collapses under volume.

Reviewing code you did not write is slower per line than writing it. Generation is now nearly free while review remains bounded by your reading speed. Accept a 600-line diff and you either read it properly — spending more time than writing would have taken — or you skim it and ship unreviewed code. Most people skim, because the code looks plausible: fluent, idiomatic, correctly formatted. Exactly what a model optimises for.

The fix is not less assistance. It is making verification cheap:

- **Scope tightly.** Many small verifiable changes, not one large one.
- **Make tests the contract.** Write or generate the test first, confirm it fails, then have the agent make it pass. Correctness is now machine-checked.
- **Lean on your existing gates.** Type checkers, linters and static analysis catch a real fraction of AI-introduced errors for free.
- **Review by risk, not uniformly.** Read the security boundary, the money arithmetic, the data migration closely. Skim the boilerplate.

contentBlocks.title: On the skill-erosion worry
contentBlocks.content: The durable skills are specification, decomposition and verification — and disciplined delegation exercises those *more*, not less. But the worry is not baseless: uncritical acceptance genuinely does erode debugging ability, because debugging is learned by struggling. The mitigation is verification discipline, not abstinence.

## Context is the whole game

The single biggest quality difference between developers using identical tools is what context they provide — a direct application of section 3's principle that information beats phrasing.

What actually helps: a checked-in repository context file stating stack, conventions, architecture and explicit prohibitions (*"never call the billing service directly; use `BillingGateway`"*). Scoping to the specific files that matter, rather than letting the tool guess. Supplying the failing test. Pointing at an existing example of the pattern you want followed — *"do this the way `PermitSyncJob` does it"* transfers more than three paragraphs of description.

And section 3's lesson still applies unchanged: more context is not better. Twenty files where three matter produces distraction and cost.

## Data handling: the boring section that ends careers

Before pointing any assistant at any code, answer three questions.

**What tier are you on, and what does it do with your data?** Consumer, business and enterprise tiers of the same product often have materially different retention and training-use terms. Check the actual terms for your tier — not a blog post, not a colleague's recollection.

**What is in the repository that must never leave?** Credentials, customer data in fixtures, proprietary algorithms under contract, third-party code under restrictive licence. Configure exclusions and verify they work. An untested ignore file is not a control.

**What is the licence position on the output?** Policies vary by organisation and jurisdiction and are still moving. For anything shipped commercially, know your employer's stated position rather than inventing one.

interactionSequence.prompt: Which task is the strongest candidate for full agentic delegation?
options: Deciding whether to migrate the team's job queue from one technology to another
Applying a consistent, well-specified change across 20 call sites, covered by an existing test suite
Writing the first draft of the incident post-mortem for last week's outage
Choosing which of three vendors to use for the payment integration

optionFeedback.feedback: Specification is vague and verification requires organisational context an agent lacks.
Correct. Both delegation conditions hold: the task specifies tightly and the tests verify cheaply.
Verification requires knowing what actually happened — there is no cheap external signal, and the cost of a plausible-but-wrong narrative is high.
A commercial judgement with tradeoffs the agent cannot weigh, not a specifiable engineering task.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Notice that none of the wrong answers are wrong because the task is hard. They are wrong because specification is vague, verification is expensive, or both.

interactionSequence.prompt: A developer says AI assistance has doubled their output because they accept large multi-file diffs and review them at the end. What is the strongest concern?
options: Review effort scales with unverified volume, so either review time exceeds the time saved, or the code is not really being reviewed
Using AI heavily will erode their debugging skills
The cost per diff will be unsustainable
Large diffs are harder for the model to generate accurately

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. This is the central arithmetic of the verification trap, and skimming is the usual outcome because the code looks plausible.
A real long-term risk, but not the *strongest* concern here — the immediate problem is unreviewed code reaching production.
Token cost for coding assistance is generally small relative to developer time.
Partly true, but this describes a model limitation, not the workflow error being demonstrated.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The fix from this section's lecture applies directly: scope the diffs smaller, make tests the contract, and review the 600 lines by risk rather than uniformly.

interactionSequence.prompt: A developer is told not to paste company code into an assistant. They reply that their tool is the same product the company approved, so it must be fine. What is the flaw?
options: There is no flaw — approval of the product covers all its uses
Retention and training-use terms differ by tier and configuration, so the approved tier may not be the one they are using
The concern only applies to code containing credentials
Assistants cannot retain code, so the policy is unnecessary

optionFeedback.feedback: Approval is normally tier-specific and configuration-specific — the product name is not the unit of approval.
Correct. The same product's consumer and enterprise tiers frequently differ materially in retention and training use.
Proprietary logic and third-party licensed code carry obligations independent of credentials.
Retention depends entirely on the tier's terms, and assuming otherwise is exactly the error.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The action this implies: locate the actual terms for your own tier, configure exclusions, and then verify — with a real test — that the exclusions take effect. An untested `.aiignore` file is not a control.

interactionSequence.prompt: Rank these by how much they typically improve a coding agent's output on an unfamiliar repository, most to least.
options: Supplying a failing test that defines success
A checked-in repository context file with conventions, architecture and explicit prohibitions
Pointing at an existing file that exemplifies the pattern you want followed
Scoping to the three relevant files rather than the whole repository
A longer, more detailed prose description of what you want

optionFeedback.feedback: First. It converts an open-ended task into a checkable one, and is what enables autonomous iteration at all.
Second. Persistent, applies to every request, prevents whole classes of wrong-pattern output.
Third. Demonstration transfers conventions faster than description — the section 3 lesson, again.
Fourth. Reduces distraction and cost, per section 3's context-budget principle.
Last. Adds tokens and, past a point, distraction rather than constraint.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The top item outranks the rest because it changes the *kind* of loop available to you. With a validator you can run autonomously — which is exactly what the next experience builds on.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this ordering?

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: find the actual data-retention and training-use terms for the coding assistant tier you currently use — not what you assume, the actual published terms. Summarise them in two sentences.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Most people doing this exercise for the first time discover their assumption was wrong in one direction or the other — either more permissive or more restrictive than they believed. That gap between assumption and terms is exactly what `aug-m3` names, and it is worth having closed it once, deliberately, rather than carrying the assumption forward.

workedExamples.problem: A teammate asks the assistant, in chat mode with no repository context supplied, to "add caching to the pricing calculation." The result compiles, passes a quick manual check, and is merged. Two weeks later, pricing is occasionally wrong under concurrent requests. Diagnose what went wrong in the *workflow*, not just the code.
steps: **Step 1 — Identify the mode chosen and whether it fit the task.** Chat mode was used for a change with real correctness constraints (concurrency safety) and an existing codebase convention for how caching is done elsewhere. This task profile — well-specified once you know the codebase's caching pattern, cheaply verifiable by a concurrency test — was actually a strong candidate for **agentic mode with tests as the contract**, not a conversational one-off.

**Step 2 — Identify the missing context.** No repository context file, no pointer to an existing caching implementation elsewhere in the codebase, no mention of the project's concurrency conventions. The assistant had no way to know a thread-safety convention existed, so it produced a plausible generic cache with no such guarantee.

**Step 3 — Identify the missing verification.** "Passes a quick manual check" tested the happy path under no load. There was no concurrency test, and none was requested — the verification step people describe when they mean "read the diff and it looked fine."

**Step 4 — Reconstruct the workflow that would have caught this.** Point at the existing thread-safe cache implementation elsewhere in the codebase as the pattern to follow. Supply or generate a concurrency test *before* the change, confirm it fails against the naive implementation, then have the agent make it pass. The existing static-analysis gate, if one exists for concurrency primitives, runs for free.

**Step 5 — Note what would NOT have helped.** A longer prose description of "make sure it's thread-safe" is a request, not a constraint — it supplies no mechanically checkable property. The fix is a test that fails without thread-safety and passes with it, not a stronger-worded instruction.
workedExamples.conclusion: The bug was not really a model failure. It was a **workflow** failure: wrong mode for the risk profile, no context pointing at the codebase's own convention, and no verification beyond a happy-path glance. Every one of the concrete fixes here — a failing test, an example to imitate, a repository convention documented once — is unglamorous and is also the entire content of `ai-augmented-development` done well.

fadedVariant.problem: A teammate asks the assistant, in chat mode with no repository context, to "add input validation to the refund endpoint." The result compiles and looks reasonable. A month later, a refund for a negative amount is discovered in production — the validation silently allowed it because the endpoint's currency-handling convention (amounts always in minor units, always positive, checked against a central `Money` type) was never followed.
givenSteps: **Step 1 — Identify the mode chosen and whether it fit the task.** Chat mode, for a change with a real financial-correctness constraint and an existing codebase convention (the `Money` type) that the assistant was never shown.
blankedStepPrompts: **Step 2 —** What context was missing, specifically, and what would supplying it have looked like?
**Step 3 —** What verification step was skipped, and what would the right one have been?
**Step 4 —** Reconstruct the workflow that would have caught this before merge.
**Step 5 —** Name one intervention that sounds like it would help here but would not, and explain why.
blankedStepAnswers: The assistant was never told the `Money` type exists or that it is the required convention for handling amounts. Supplying it would mean pointing at an existing endpoint that correctly uses `Money`, and stating the prohibition explicitly in a repository context file: *"never accept raw numeric amounts; always validate through `Money`."*

There was no test asserting that a negative or non-minor-unit amount is rejected. The right verification is a test supplying a negative amount and asserting the endpoint raises a validation error, written and confirmed failing *before* the agent's change, then confirmed passing after.

Agentic mode, scoped to the single endpoint, with the failing validation test as the contract and the existing `Money`-using endpoint supplied as the pattern to imitate. The change is verified by the test passing, not by a manual glance at a diff.

A longer instruction telling the assistant to "be careful with money and validate inputs properly" sounds like it addresses this, but it supplies no mechanically checkable property and does not tell the assistant that a `Money` type exists to enforce. It is a request, not a constraint — exactly the distinction section 3 draws between phrasing and engineering.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What two properties of a task determine whether it is safe to delegate to an agent?
Name three ways to make verification of AI-generated code cheap, without reading every line yourself.
Name the three data-handling questions to answer before pointing an assistant at a repository.
Carry-forward from section 3: name three reasons that adding more context to a prompt can reduce output quality.

learningExperiences.title: Designing the Loop

contentBlocks.content:
## What you will be able to do

- **`s04-o6`** — design and run a bounded loop that drives a coding agent against an external success signal, without per-step prompting

Every agentic tool already runs a loop. Most people never design it — they just start it and watch.

terms.definition: The repeating cycle of reason, act and observe that an agentic tool runs. Sometimes called the reason-act-observe cycle.
A pass or fail judgement produced by something other than the model — tests, compiler, linter, type checker. What makes autonomous loops safe.
Hard limits on iterations, wall-clock time and token spend, enforced by your harness rather than the agent's discretion.
The predefined state in which a loop stops and hands control back to a human, along with the information it hands over.

contentBlocks.content:
## Five things a designed loop needs

1. **A goal stated as a checkable condition**, not a description. *"All tests in `test_permits.py` pass and `mypy` reports no new errors"* — not *"improve the permit module."*
2. **Tools** — what the agent may read, edit and execute, and what it may not touch.
3. **An external validator.** This is the load-bearing element. If the agent decides for itself whether it succeeded, it will eventually decide yes while wrong, confidently, repeatedly. Tests, compilers and type checkers are honest; the agent's self-assessment is not.
4. **Termination and budget.** Maximum iterations, maximum tokens, maximum wall clock — enforced by your harness. An agent will not stop itself.
5. **An escalation condition.** What state returns control to you, and what information it hands over.

contentBlocks.title: Element 3 is the one that matters most
contentBlocks.content: Every agentic tool already runs a loop; quality comes from designing it deliberately. That gap — starting the default loop instead of designing one — is where runaway cost and false progress come from.

contentBlocks.caption: Loop architectures — choose by task shape. Section 8 revisits these comparatively; here, you build one.
rows: Retry
Short atomic tasks, crisp pass/fail
Retrying an identical approach forever — needs strategy variation between attempts
Plan-execute-verify
Multi-step changes where ordering matters
A bad plan executed diligently
Generator-critic
Work with no mechanical test — docs, summaries, review
Critic and generator too similar; critic ratifies rather than challenges
Explore-narrow
Diagnosis over an unknown search space
Exploring forever; needs a narrowing trigger
Human-in-the-loop
Irreversible actions — mutations, deploys, payments
Checkpoint fatigue if used too often

interactionSequence.prompt: The task ahead — adding retry-with-backoff to 14 call sites, validated by an existing test suite and a type checker — which architecture from the table fits best, and why?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Retry (or a light plan-execute-verify, since 14 call sites benefit from some ordering) is the fit: the task is short, atomic per call site, and has a crisp pass/fail signal already available in the existing test suite. There is no ambiguity to explore and no absence of a mechanical check that would call for generator-critic.

interactionSequence.prompt: Which element of a designed loop is described as load-bearing, and why?
options: The tools the agent may use, because more tools mean more capability
The external validator, because without it the agent's self-assessment substitutes for real evidence of success
The budget, because it is the only element that limits cost
The goal statement, because a longer, more detailed goal always produces better results

optionFeedback.feedback: Tools define the action space, but more tools without a validator just means more ways to confidently produce a wrong result.
Correct. Every other element assumes something is checking the outcome; the external validator is that something.
Budget limits runaway cost, but it does not tell you whether the work produced within budget is any good.
A checkable condition matters far more than length — a vague goal stated at length is still not verifiable.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is the single idea to carry out of this experience. Every design decision in the worked example that follows traces back to this one element.

workedExamples.problem: In the construction project-management application, the permitting integration has no retry logic. Add retry-with-backoff to all 14 call sites, matching existing conventions, using a bounded, unattended agent loop.
steps: **Step 1 — Make the goal checkable before writing any loop.** Write a test asserting that a transient failure results in a retry and eventual success, for one call site. Confirm it fails. This test is now the validator. Without it there is no loop — only a chatbot with file access.

**Step 2 — Define the loop explicitly.** Validator: `pytest tests/test_permit_retry.py && mypy src/permits/`. Tools: read/edit under `src/permits/`, run the test command — no network access, no writes outside that directory. Budget: 12 iterations, 20 minutes, $4.00. Escalation: on budget exhaustion, or if the same test fails identically three times in a row, stop and emit the last diff plus the failure output.

**Step 3 — Note the escalation rule's purpose.** "Same failure three times" catches the retry-without-strategy-variation pattern named in the architecture table. If an approach is not working, more attempts will not help — a human needs to change the strategy, not spend more budget on it.

**Step 4 — Run it and observe.** Iterations 1–3: the agent adds a decorator, tests fail (wrong exception type caught). Iteration 4: broadens the exception, tests pass, `mypy` fails on a missing annotation. Iteration 5: fixes the annotation. Both pass. The loop exits on success. Cost: $1.15. Time: 4 minutes. Human involvement after setup: none.

**Step 5 — Verify anyway, because the validator only proved the validator passes.** Read the diff. Did it apply retries to all 14 sites, or just the one covered by the test? Did it retry any non-idempotent call — which would risk double-submitting a permit? Does it match the existing backoff convention used elsewhere in the codebase?

**Step 6 — Find what the validator missed.** In this run, the agent applied retries to `POST /permits/submit`, which is not idempotent. The tests passed. `mypy` passed. Nothing in the validator encoded idempotency, because nobody thought to check for it — this is the exact scenario from the section's opening prediction.
workedExamples.conclusion: **A designed loop with an external validator, a hard budget, and an escalation rule converts an unpredictable agent into a bounded, costed unit of work — but it does not remove your judgement, only relocate it.** The loop's $1.15 and 4 minutes bought a mechanically correct change and one production-shaped bug, found only because step 5 was not skipped. The design is the deliverable; the code the agent writes is a byproduct.

fadedVariant.problem: In the same codebase, add structured logging to all 9 call sites of the notification service, matching the existing logging convention used elsewhere in the application, using a bounded unattended loop.
givenSteps: **Step 1 — Make the goal checkable.** Write a test asserting that calling the notification service produces a log entry with the required structured fields (event type, recipient ID, timestamp), for one call site. Confirm it fails.
blankedStepPrompts: **Step 2 —** Define the loop: validator command, tool boundaries, budget, and an escalation rule. Be specific.
**Step 3 —** Explain what your escalation rule is designed to catch, referencing the architecture table's failure modes.
**Step 4 —** The loop reports success after 6 iterations, all tests and lint checks passing. What do you do next, and why is this step not optional?
**Step 5 —** Name one property this validator likely does NOT check, that could still make the change wrong. How would you check for it?
blankedStepAnswers: Validator: `pytest tests/test_notification_logging.py && ruff check src/notifications/`. Tools: read/edit under `src/notifications/` only, run the test and lint commands — no network, no writes elsewhere. Budget: 10 iterations, 15 minutes, $3.00. Escalation: on budget exhaustion, or three identical consecutive test failures, stop and surface the diff and failure output.

The three-identical-failures rule is designed to catch the retry architecture's named failure mode: retrying an identical approach with no strategy variation. If the same fix keeps failing the same way, more iterations will not help — only a human changing the approach will.

Read the diff regardless of the passing validator. The validator proved the validator passes, not that the change is good — this is the section's central finding. Specifically check: were all 9 call sites actually changed, or just the tested one? Does the logging format match the convention used elsewhere, or a plausible-looking approximation of it?

The validator likely does not check whether the logged fields contain sensitive data that should not appear in logs — for instance, a recipient's raw contact details rather than an internal ID. This is a governance property, not a functional one, and nothing in a pytest-and-lint validator would catch it. Checking it requires a manual read of what is actually being logged, or a dedicated assertion added specifically for it.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name the five elements a designed agent loop needs. Which one is load-bearing, and why?
Name the loop architectures introduced in this section and the task shape each fits.

learningExperiences.title: Budget, Escalation and the Economics of a Loop

contentBlocks.content:
## What you will be able to do

- **`s04-o7`** — set iteration and cost budgets for a loop, quantify spend per completed task, and define the escalation condition

The permit-retry loop cost $1.15. That number was not incidental — it is the argument you will make to a manager.

contentBlocks.title: Budgets belong to the harness, not the agent
contentBlocks.content: An agent will not stop itself. "It seemed to be making progress" is not a budget — it is the absence of one. Iteration count, wall-clock time and token spend are limits your code enforces from the outside, checked before every action, not requested politely in the prompt.

## Quantify cost per completed task

The permit-retry loop: **$1.15**, 4 minutes, zero human involvement mid-run, for a task that would take a competent developer roughly 40 minutes plus review time. That comparison — cost and time of the loop against cost and time of doing it yourself — is the number worth recording every time, because it is what turns "the agent worked" into a decision a manager can act on.

The comparison only means something if the *outcome* is comparable too. A loop that finishes fast and cheap but ships the non-idempotent bug from the previous experience has not actually saved 36 minutes — it has deferred a production incident. Cost-per-completed-task must be cost-per-**correctly**-completed-task, which is why step 5 of the loop-design process (verify anyway) is not optional overhead on top of the economics — it is part of what the economics actually measure.

contentBlocks.title: These cost figures are illustrative
contentBlocks.content:
The $1.15, the four minutes, the $7.25 across six flaky tests — these are a worked example of the arithmetic, not targets your own loops should hit. Costs vary enormously with model, task and how many iterations your validator actually requires.

What transfers is the **practice**: record cost-per-correctly-completed-task every time, and compare it against your own estimate of doing the work by hand. The number you produce is the one that matters.

## Designing the escalation rule

A good escalation rule detects two distinct conditions, and they call for different handling:

**Budget exhaustion.** The loop has spent its allotted iterations, time or money without meeting the goal. Escalate with the current state: what was tried, what the last failure was.

**Repeated identical failure.** The same check has failed the same way three times running. This is a stronger signal than budget exhaustion alone — it means the current *approach* is wrong, not merely incomplete, and burning the remaining budget on more identical attempts is close to guaranteed waste. Escalate immediately rather than waiting for the budget to exhaust.

interactionSequence.prompt: An agent has been running for 40 minutes on a refactoring task, reporting progress each iteration. Costs are climbing. What does this most likely indicate about the loop's design?
options: No external validator and no budget — the agent is assessing its own progress with nothing to stop it
The model is too small for the task and should be upgraded
The task should be split across multiple cooperating agents
This is normal for agentic work and requires patience

optionFeedback.feedback: Correct. Self-assessed progress with no budget is exactly the condition under which loops run long while achieving nothing.
A more capable model in an undesigned loop fails the same way, more expensively.
Adding agents compounds error rates and cost; it does not supply the missing validator or budget.
Treating the default loop as a given is the underlying error this section corrects.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: "Reporting progress" is doing a lot of work in that sentence — progress reported by the agent itself is not evidence, for the same reason a self-graded exam is not evidence. Only the external validator's verdict counts.

interactionSequence.prompt: A loop's validator has failed three times with an identical error. A teammate proposes raising the iteration budget from 12 to 30 so it has more chances to get there. What is the strongest objection?
options: Thirty iterations would exceed a reasonable wall-clock limit for an unattended task
Identical repeated failures mean the approach is wrong, not incomplete — more attempts at an unchanged strategy is close to guaranteed waste
The budget should never be changed once a loop has started running
A larger budget will cause the agent to attempt riskier edits

optionFeedback.feedback: A real secondary concern, but it addresses the symptom rather than the reason the extra iterations would not help.
Correct. A loop needs strategy variation between attempts; without it, budget is simply the ceiling on how much you spend failing the same way.
Budgets can legitimately be revised — the problem here is what the identical failures are telling you, not the act of changing a number.
Budget size does not change what the agent attempts, only how many times it may attempt it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is why the escalation rule checks for repeated identical failure *independently* of budget exhaustion. Budget answers "how much am I willing to spend?" — the identical-failure rule answers the different and more useful question, "is spending more going to help at all?"

interactionSequence.prompt: A loop fails its validator on attempt 1, then fails again on attempts 2 and 3 with the identical error message. Its budget allows 12 attempts. Should it continue to attempt 4, or escalate now? Justify your answer.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Escalate now, even though 9 attempts of budget remain. Three identical consecutive failures is the specific signal that the *approach* is wrong, not merely incomplete — spending the remaining budget on more identical attempts is close to guaranteed waste. This is the retry architecture's named failure mode from the previous experience, and it is why the escalation rule checks for repeated identical failure independently of whether the budget is exhausted.
hints: Does more budget help if the same fix keeps producing the same error?

workedExamples.problem: The same construction application's CI pipeline has 6 tests that fail intermittently — flaky, not broken. A bounded loop is proposed to diagnose and fix each one. Design the budget and escalation rule, and compute the cost-per-fixed-test economics.
steps: **Step 1 — Note that this task shape differs from the permit example.** Diagnosing *why* a test is flaky is closer to explore-narrow than retry: the cause is unknown at the start (timing dependency? shared state? external service call?) and must be searched for before a fix can even be attempted.
**Step 2 — Set the validator.** Run the specific flaky test 20 times in a row; the fix is validated only if it passes all 20, since a single pass proves nothing about a flaky test.

**Step 3 — Set the budget per test, not per run.** 8 iterations, 15 minutes, $2.50 **per flaky test** — six independent budgets, because a diagnosis that stalls on test 1 should not consume the allowance intended for tests 2 through 6.

**Step 4 — Set the escalation rule.** Three consecutive iterations proposing the same category of fix (for instance, three attempts all adding a `sleep()` call) without the 20-run validator passing — escalate. A `sleep()`-based fix is also a design smell worth flagging to the human regardless of whether it passes, since it treats a symptom rather than the underlying race condition.

**Step 5 — Run across all six tests and total the outcome.** Four of six resolved within budget, costing $1.80, $2.10, $0.95 and $2.40 — total $7.25. Two escalated: one after exhausting its budget with no working fix, one after the sleep-pattern rule triggered on iteration 3.

**Step 6 — Compute the comparable-outcome economics.** $7.25 and roughly 35 minutes of unattended time resolved four of six flaky tests that had been tolerated, unfixed, for months. The two escalations are not failures of the loop — they are exactly what the escalation rule is for, surfacing the two tests where automated attempts should stop and a human's judgement should start.
workedExamples.conclusion: **Budgets are set per unit of independent work, not per session, and an escalation is a correct outcome, not a failed one.** The real cost figure to report is not "$7.25 for six tests" — it is "$7.25 and 35 minutes to close four, plus a clear, evidenced handoff on the two that needed a human," which is a stronger and more honest number than a loop that silently ships a `sleep()` call to hit six-for-six.

fadedVariant.problem: The same pipeline has 10 outdated dependency-version pins that need bumping, each requiring the test suite to still pass afterward. Design the budget, escalation rule, and economics for a bounded loop handling this batch.
givenSteps: **Step 1 — Note the task shape.** This is closer to retry than explore-narrow: for each dependency, the fix (bump the version) is known in advance; what is uncertain is only whether the existing test suite still passes afterward.
blankedStepPrompts: **Step 2 —** Set the validator for a single dependency bump.
**Step 3 —** Set the budget. Per dependency, or for the whole batch? Justify your choice using the flaky-test example's reasoning.
**Step 4 —** Set an escalation rule appropriate to this task shape.

**Step 5 —** After running across all 10, 7 succeed and 3 escalate on a breaking API change in the same downstream library. Compute what you would report as the cost-per-completed-task figure, and state what the three escalations tell you that a 10-for-10 success would not.
blankedStepAnswers: Validator: bump the version pin, run the full test suite, pass only if the suite is green with no new failures.
Per dependency, for the same reason as the flaky-test loop: a bump that stalls on one library should not consume budget intended for the other nine independent bumps.

Escalate after 2 failed attempts at the same bump if the failure is identical both times — for a known, well-specified change like a version bump, more than two attempts at an unchanged approach is unlikely to help, tighter than the flaky-test loop's three-attempt threshold because the task is simpler and more mechanical.

Report cost-per-completed-task on the 7 successful bumps, not blended across all 10 — blending would understate the true cost of the ones that actually completed. Separately and explicitly report that 3 escalations shared a common cause: a breaking API change in one downstream library. That pattern — the SAME cause behind multiple escalations — is a stronger and more valuable finding than the raw success count, because it points at one specific piece of work for a human rather than three unrelated problems.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Carry-forward from section 2: name the three training stages and one observed model behaviour that each explains.

learningExperiences.title: P2: Brownfield Integration Case Study

contentBlocks.content:
## What you will be able to do

- **`s04-o4`** — use AI tooling to comprehend an unfamiliar existing codebase and deliver a scoped, tested change to it, documenting the before/after

This experience is the setup and instructions for a graded portfolio artifact. The build itself continues outside class.

contentBlocks.title: Why this is the only brownfield project in the course
contentBlocks.content:
Every other build in this course is greenfield — starting from nothing, on a corpus and architecture you chose. That is the easy case, and it is what every candidate's AI portfolio already shows.

Most real AI work in a normal engineering organisation is integration into something that already exists, and that is the thing hiring managers can least verify from a typical portfolio. This artifact exists specifically to close that gap.

## Building P2

Choose an existing codebase you did not write — an open-source project you use, or your employer's with permission.

**1. Comprehend.** Use chat mode to map the architecture. Produce a one-page written summary and a diagram. Note explicitly where the assistant was wrong about the codebase, and how you found out — a genuine wrong turn is more instructive than a clean narrative.

**2. Scope.** Pick one genuinely useful AI-related addition — semantic search over the project's issues, an automated changelog summariser, structured extraction from an existing text field. It must be small enough to finish and real enough to be useful.

**3. Set up context.** Write a repository context file with conventions, architecture notes and prohibitions. Record output quality before and after adding it — a measured comparison, in the spirit of section 3's regression harness, not an impression.

**4. Design a loop.** Goal-as-checkable-condition, tools, external validator, budget, escalation rule. Write it down *before* running anything.

**5. Run it.** Log every iteration: what it did, whether the validator passed, tokens spent.

**6. Verify.** Apply your risk-weighted verification protocol. Record what the validator missed and what you caught only by reading.

**7. Document.** Before/after, the loop design, cost per completed task, and what you would do differently. Include at least one failure honestly — the agent going in circles, or passing tests while doing something wrong. The failure you document is worth more to a reviewer than the success.

contentBlocks.title: This artifact is graded later, against a rubric you have not seen yet
contentBlocks.content:
In the final section of this course you will encounter a six-criterion portfolio rubric. P2 is assessed against four of its six criteria: problem framing, runnable in under ten minutes, architecture legibility, and a decision log recording genuine tradeoffs — including reversals.

You do not need the rubric's exact wording now. You do need to know that a tidy, failure-free write-up is a weaker artifact than an honest one, and that this is true today, not just at the end of the course.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before you start: what codebase will you use, and what is the one addition you are scoping? State why it is small enough to finish and real enough to matter — in one sentence each.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The most common failure at this stage is scoping something that requires understanding the whole codebase before any part of it can be built. If your one-sentence justification for "small enough to finish" required describing more than two subsystems, the scope is probably too large — narrow it before you start the loop design.

interactionSequence.prompt: In your own words: what is the difference between the verification protocol you would apply to a change in a codebase you wrote yourself, and one you would apply to a change in code you have never seen before? Be specific about what changes and why.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong answer notices that in your own code, you have implicit knowledge of the conventions and traps that never got written down anywhere — which is exactly the knowledge a repository context file has to supply explicitly when the codebase is not yours. Brownfield work makes visible how much tacit knowledge ordinarily substitutes for documentation.

transferExercises.context: A scientific data pipeline — deliberately not application development, unlike the construction project-management codebase used in the lecture.
transferExercises.scenario: A genomics lab runs a nightly pipeline of shell scripts and R code that fails roughly twice a week, always for a different reason: malformed input files, disk exhaustion, an upstream schema change, a flaky reference-data download. A postdoc, not a professional developer, maintains it.
transferExercises.task:
1. Which loop architecture fits *"diagnose why last night's run failed and propose a fix"*? Justify against at least two alternatives.

2. There is no test suite. Design an external validator anyway — what pass/fail signal can you construct from what already exists?

3. Which failure categories should escalate to a human immediately rather than being auto-remediated? State the principle behind your split, not just the list.

4. Set a budget. The pipeline processes patient-derived data under strict governance. What does that change about tools, logging, and which assistant tier may be used?

5. The postdoc proposes letting the agent auto-commit and re-run until the pipeline succeeds. Give the two strongest objections, one about correctness and one about cost.
successCriteria: Selects explore-narrow for diagnosis, since the failure cause is unknown and the search space is wide, then retry or plan-execute-verify for applying the fix — and rejects retry alone, since retry assumes the fix approach is already known
Constructs a validator from existing signals without a test suite: a canary run against a small fixed input with a known expected output, plus exit codes, row counts, and schema assertions on outputs

Distinguishes escalation on the principle that auto-remediation is acceptable only where the failure is both recoverable and detectable, and identifies that anything touching data integrity, reference data, or governance boundaries fails that test and must escalate
Recognises that patient-derived data likely forbids consumer assistant tiers entirely, requires redacted logs and no raw data in prompts, and may require local or specifically approved tooling

Gives a correctness objection (a pipeline that 'succeeds' after the agent relaxes a validation threshold is worse than one that fails loudly) and a cost objection (an unbounded loop on a nightly job can run for hours unattended if self-assessed success substitutes for a real validator)

selfGuidedExercise.objective: Instrument a week of your own AI-assisted work to find out, with real numbers, where assistance actually pays off and where it costs you time.
selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: Your own ordinary working week — whatever development work you would be doing regardless of this course.
instructions: For one working week, log every task where you used AI assistance: the task, the mode chosen, time taken, whether you kept the output, and — where you can estimate it — cost.
Log three tasks where you deliberately did NOT use assistance, and why.
At week's end, calculate where the assistance actually paid off and where it cost you time. Most people are surprised by at least one category.
Design and run one bounded loop, with a real external validator and a real budget, on a genuine task from your own work. Record cost per completed task.
Write the results into `decision-log.md`.
materialsOrPrerequisites: A real week of development work, inside or outside your job
Access to a coding assistant with agentic capability, for the bounded-loop portion
Your `decision-log.md`
reflectionPrompts: Which category of task had the best payoff, and which had the worst — and did that match your prior impression before you measured it?
For the bounded loop you ran: what was the cost-per-completed-task figure, and how does it compare to your own estimated time for the same task?
Did your loop's validator catch everything that mattered, or — as in this section's worked example — did you find something only by reading the diff yourself?
What would you tell a colleague to stop doing, based on this week's numbers?

verification.mode: self-assessment against criteria, with the decision-log entry as the artifact
selfAssessmentCriteria: At least five real tasks logged with mode, time and outcome
At least three deliberately unassisted tasks logged with reasoning
One bounded loop run with a genuine external validator and a real budget, not a simulated one
A real cost-per-completed-task figure reported, not an estimate
The write-up states at least one place assistance cost time rather than saved it, if that was in fact observed

sections.title: Building Applications on LLM APIs
sections.description: Move from calling a model to engineering a service around one. The capstone begins here, and the domain you choose in this section carries through every remaining section that builds on it.

learningObjectives.description: Implement streaming, multi-turn conversation state, and token budgeting in an application-layer LLM client.
Implement schema-constrained structured output with validation and repair.
Implement tool/function calling, correctly separating model-emitted requests from application-side execution and authorization.
Handle rate limits, timeouts, partial failures, and non-determinism with retries, backoff, and graceful degradation.
Abstract the provider behind an interface enabling model substitution without call-site changes.
Select and justify a capstone domain and corpus against defined suitability criteria.
Deliver a working conversational service over that domain as the capstone baseline.

motivationHooks.prompt:
Everything up to now has been you talking to a model. From here you are building a system that talks to a model **on behalf of users who will never see the prompt and cannot tell when something has gone wrong.**

That shift changes what matters. In a playground, a malformed response is an annoyance you fix by re-running. In production it is an unhandled exception at 3am. A model that is slow is a curiosity in testing and a support ticket in production. The gap between "I called the API" and "I built a service around the API" is made of unglamorous engineering — validation, retries, timeouts, budgets, abstraction — and it is the gap that separates a demo from a product.

This is also where your capstone starts, and where you commit to a domain you will live with for six sections.

Later in this section, an airline support assistant's model emits a request: `get_booking(reference="XK4T2P")`. The user is authenticated as customer 44190. It turns out reference `XK4T2P` belongs to a **different** customer entirely.

**Before you see the design: what should happen, and precisely where in your system does that decision get made?** Write down your answer — including exactly which piece of code makes the call.

The request must be **rejected**, and the decision is made entirely in your handler — using the **session identity**, never anything the model supplied. The handler checks whether reference `XK4T2P` belongs to the authenticated session's customer, and it does not, so the call is refused before any lookup happens.

If your answer involved the model, an instruction, or a check the model performs — that is the single most common version of this mistake, and it is worth noticing now: **the model's tool request is a proposal from an untrusted source, not an authorisation.** Every design decision in this section's worked example follows from that one sentence.

sectionSummary.content:
You should now believe the following about building services on model APIs:

**Five failures define this whole section, and each has a specific, non-obvious fix.** Malformed output is routine at volume, not an edge case — fixed by schema-constrained decoding with a *bounded* repair path. A model asked about private data will invent it, unless tool calling supplies real data under real authorisation. Conversations get expensive faster than you expect, because of statelessness — fixed by an explicit context budget. Providers fail and rate-limit — fixed by retries that never touch non-idempotent operations without protection. And wanting to change models later, without an abstraction, means you never will.

**Tool calling is not execution — it is a proposal from an untrusted source.** The model emits a structured request; your code decides whether to honour it, using identity and authorisation state the model never sees. This is the entire security boundary, and it lives in one place: the handler.

**Stream prose. Buffer anything that gates an action.** You cannot validate a partial structured object, and you cannot un-display text already shown.

**Your capstone domain is chosen against five criteria, not by instinct** — and it is now locked. Every section from here to the deployment section extends the same system.
keyTakeaways: Schema-constrained output with a bounded repair path beats prompt-only JSON requests and unbounded retry loops alike.
Tool calling means the model proposes; your handler decides, using session identity — never model-supplied identity.
Statelessness means context budgets are mandatory, not optional, for any multi-turn service.
Retry on 429/5xx, never on 400, and never retry a mutating call without an idempotency key.
A provider abstraction, built before you need one, is what makes model substitution a configuration change instead of a rewrite.
Stream conversational prose; buffer and validate anything that drives a decision or an action.
Capstone domain criteria: genuinely messy corpus, you can judge answer quality, a real question space, no licensing barrier, and you care about it.
